candidates.title: The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Tops 1,900 Companies In October, With 34 Companies Joining — Half Under 4 Years Old
candidates.snippet: A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, along with a new record for the U.S. with more than 1,000 private unicorn companies.

The Crunchbase Unicorn Board Tops 1,900 Companies In October, With 34 Companies Joining — Half Under 4 Years Old

A total of 34 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in October, adding more than $96 billion in value and $14.8 billion in total funding to the board. The board also reached a new record of 1,900 private companies last month, including an all-time high of more than 1,000 such startups based in the U.S.
Last month’s new unicorn cohort also highlighted how quickly this AI cycle is awarding some companies with billion-dollar-plus valuations: Half of October’s new unicorns are less than 4 years old, and nine companies that joined the board during the month did so via seed or Series A raises.
Leading industries for unicorn formation last month were frontier labs, agentic AI, aerospace and semiconductors. The U.S. accounts for 23 of the companies, while China and Korea each added three. Estonia added two, a record for the nation in a single month. Singapore, Germany and Japan each added one new unicorn.
The most valuable of the newly minted unicorns were electrical infrastructure company Axiom Solutions International , TypeSafe AI a model developer of Jev, and agentic AI assistant company Manus AI .
Familiar names topped the list of investors backing the latest cohort. Andreessen Horowitz has led rounds across seven portfolio companies over time, Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst in four companies and Eclipse three companies from this batch.
New unicorns in October 2026
Here are October’s new unicorn companies by industry segment.
AI models, assistants and agents
TypeSafe AI : San Francisco-based AI model developer TypeSafe AI raised an $870 million Series A at a $7.5 billion valuation. Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with participation from DCVC and Sequoia Capital. The 2-year-old company develops an AI model Jev for structured decision-making, helping applications automate tasks such as classification, scoring and routing with confidence estimates.
Manus AI : Singapore-based AI assistant Manus AI raised $500 million at a $4 billion valuation. Boyu Capital and IDG Capital led the round. The 3-year-old company develops general-purpose AI agents that perform tasks including research, browser automation, content creation and software development. Meta agreed to acquire Manus in December 2025, but Chinese regulators intervened and ordered the transaction reversed.
Nous Research : Austin-based Nous Research, developer of the Hermes agent, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the financing, with investors including Nvidia , Microsoft’s M12 , Menlo Ventures and Union Square Ventures . The 3-year-old company develops open-source AI models, agents and infrastructure for AI development and deployment. Nous Research built the open-source Hermes Agent, which it is deploying for businesses.
Upstage : South Korea-based Upstage, developer of the open-source Solar model, raised $30 million in Series C funding, reaching $1.5 billion in value. The 6-year-old company develops the Solar language models and document-processing technology that converts unstructured business information into usable data for the future of work.
Wabi : San Francisco-based personal AI assistant Wabi raised a $55 million Series A at a $1.25 billion valuation. IVP led the financing, joined by investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Forerunner and Amazon’s Alexa Fund . The 1-year-old company develops an AI personal assistant for everyday activities such as planning trips, coordinating meals and organizing tasks.
Town : San Francisco-based Town, a developer of a workforce AI assistant, raised a $108 million Series B at a $1 billion valuation. Forerunner and Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, First Round Capital and other investors. The 2-year-old company develops personalized AI assistants that connect with workplace tools across teams to manage email, prepare meeting briefings, organize schedules and complete recurring tasks.
Aerospace, defense and space
Air Space Intelligence : Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which makes AI software for national security, raised a $325 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation. Spark Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz, Citadel Securities , Craft Ventures , Energy Impact Partners and Meritech Capital Partners . The 8-year-old company develops AI software for managing complex physical operations across aviation, defense, energy and logistics.
Xona : Burlingame, California-based Xona, which says it’s developing a better satellite navigation system, raised a $250 million Series D at a $2.45 billion valuation. Future Ventures led the round, with participation from Industrious Ventures and Woven Capital . The 7-year-old company says it’s developing a low Earth orbit satellite network to deliver precise positioning, navigation and timing services for applications including defense, transportation and autonomous systems.
Firehawk Aerospace : Dallas-based munitions manufacturer Firehawk Aerospace raised a $150 million Series D at a $1.4 billion valuation. Advent International and Rochefort led the round, with Nomi Capital also participating. The 7-year-old company uses additive manufacturing to produce rocket motors, engines and propellant for defense applications.

candidates.title: Anthropic Seeks Record $88.5B Tied To Public Market Debut
candidates.snippet: Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut. On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size.

Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.
On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.
Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut.
An IPO and a private placement
The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans.
For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.
Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC .
Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
Revenue and recent updates
Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.
For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.
The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.
As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

HAMBURG, Germany , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- H.I.G. Capital ("H.I.G."), a leading global private capital firm with $76 billion of capital under management, is pleased to announce that an affiliate has signed a definitive agreement to acquire a majority stake in go asia ("go asia" or the "Company"), Germany's largest retail chain for Asian food. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The transaction is subject to customary regulatory approvals.
Founded in 2008 and headquartered in Berlin, go asia operates over 70 stores in more than 30 cities across Germany. With a range of over 10,000 products from across Asia and more than 1,600 employees, the Company addresses the growing demand for authentic Asian cuisine from a well-diversified customer base.
H.I.G. and the founding family led by Wengui Ye have agreed to enter into a partnership to accelerate the Company's next phase of growth. H.I.G. will contribute its retail and consumer expertise, international network, and capital resources to support go asia's dynamic store network expansion in Germany and Europe. The founding family will reinvest and retain a significant ownership interest in the Company, and founder Wengui Ye and the Company's management team will continue to play an active role in shaping go asia's future.
Wengui Ye, founder of go asia, commented: "When I opened our first store in Berlin in 2009, my vision was to bring authentic Asian cuisine to German homes. Today, I am proud that go asia is Germany's largest Asian food retailer – and we still see significant untapped growth potential both in Germany and especially across Europe. With its vast retail experience, strong international network, and partnership-oriented, operational approach, H.I.G. is the ideal partner for our next stage of growth. My family and I will remain significantly invested, and I look forward to continuing to shape the future of go asia together with H.I.G. and our outstanding team."
Christian Kraul-von Renner, Managing Director at H.I.G., remarked: "go asia is an impressive founder-led success story. Wengui Ye and his team have built Germany's largest Asian food retailer with an authentic product range and a distinctive, scalable store concept. We see significant potential to expand the store network in Germany as well as to enter other European markets. Together with the Ye family and the management team, we look forward to accelerating go asia's next phase of growth."
About go asia
Founded by Wengui Ye in Berlin in 2008, go asia opened its first store in Berlin-Charlottenburg in 2009. Today, with over 70 stores in more than 30 cities and over 1,600 employees, go asia is Germany's largest retail chain for Asian food. Its stores are located predominantly in city-center locations, shopping centers, and transport hubs, complemented by an online shop. The Company's assortment comprises over 10,000 products from across Asia, ranging from rice, noodles, sauces, and spices to frozen and fresh products, beverages, and kitchenware. For more information, please visit the go asia website at goasia.net .
About H.I.G. Capital
H.I.G. is a leading global private capital firm with $76 billion of capital under management.* Based in Miami, and with offices in Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, New York, San Francisco, and Stamford in the United States, as well as international affiliate offices in Hamburg, London, Luxembourg, Madrid, Milan, Paris, Bogotá, Rio de Janeiro, Dubai, and Hong Kong, H.I.G. specializes in providing both debt and equity capital to middle market companies, utilizing a flexible and operationally focused/value-added approach:
H.I.G.'s equity funds invest in management buyouts, recapitalizations, and corporate carve-outs of both profitable as well as underperforming manufacturing and service businesses.
H.I.G.'s debt funds invest in senior, unitranche, and junior debt financing to companies across the size spectrum, both on a primary (direct origination) basis, as well as in the secondary markets.
H.I.G.'s real estate funds invest in value-added properties, which can benefit from improved asset management practices.
H.I.G. Infrastructure focuses on making value-add and core plus investments in the infrastructure sector.
Since its founding in 1993, H.I.G. has invested in and managed more than 400 companies worldwide. The Firm's current portfolio includes more than 100 companies with combined sales in excess of $53 billion. For more information, please refer to the H.I.G. website at hig.com .

candidates.title: Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
candidates.snippet: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.
candidates.text:
Seed funding • Startups • Venture
Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
Gené Teare
November 9, 2026
Gené Teare
@geneteare
0
Shares
Email
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.
The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.
Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)
That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.
The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.
At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.
“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan , a partner at Scale Venture Partners , which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.
This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.
Go big and early — or wait
Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.
With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.
Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”
Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.
The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.
“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”
Deals sizes trend higher
At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.
Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.
Raising a large Series A
For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.
“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures , whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.
“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.
She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.
But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

candidates.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
candidates.snippet: Nebius plans to fund its $40 billion AI infrastructure expansion through customer prepayments and loans, even as delays at a Microsoft data center raise questions about its financing model.
candidates.text:
In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks.
Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations.
“Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.”
The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip.
One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027.
The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells.
Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August , the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law.
DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center.
According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery.
Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment.
On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg.
In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays.
Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash.
Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.”
Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter.
Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey. Shares ended the day down 17%.

candidates.text:
TechFundingNews reports OpenAI’s funding round cut to $20B with UAE funds leading, with valuation at $1.25T
Dated: November 9, 2026
OpenAI’s funding round has reportedly been scaled back to $20 billion, with a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to TechFundingNews. The report says funds from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are leading the round, and it frames the move alongside expectations that Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) may be approaching.
The news reflects how major private-sector investments in advanced AI systems are being negotiated at very large dollar volumes. While the report describes the funding size, valuation, and the involvement of UAE-backed financing, it does not specify any development programs or public-interest outcomes tied to grants or humanitarian or social-sector support.
What the report says
TechFundingNews states that OpenAI’s funding round has been reduced to $20 billion from an earlier, larger target. It also cites a $1.25 trillion valuation and highlights that UAE funding is leading the round. The article further notes that Anthropic’s IPO could be a key factor in the broader AI funding environment.
Background: AI investment and valuation
Large-scale AI financing has become a defining feature of the global technology economy, where investors compete to secure stakes in frontier-model development and related infrastructure. In this context, round sizing and valuation benchmarks often shift as investor appetite, deal structure, and comparable transactions evolve.
However, the supplied source material does not provide details about the number of organizations participating, the identities of specific investors, whether funds are earmarked for research only, or how any proceeds could connect to development objectives such as health, education, livelihoods, climate resilience, or human rights.
Implications for nonprofit and development agendas
The TechFundingNews report is primarily about corporate financing rather than a documented public development initiative. As a result, it offers limited direct information for NGOs seeking program funding, partnerships, or implementation opportunities.
Still, the story is relevant to development professionals who monitor how AI governance, technology access, and investment trends may affect future demand for policy, capacity building, and responsible deployment. These themes can matter to civil society even when investment announcements are not presented as social-sector funding.
What is not specified in the source

Mercor Hits $20B Valuation After $750M Series D to Train and Test AI Agents
By James Dargan · 11 November 2026 · 1 min read
AI training startup Mercor has secured $750 million in a Series D funding round that values the company at $20 billion, the firm said on Tuesday. Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, Nvidia and funds managed by affiliates of Apollo were among the participants.
The San Francisco-based company started out as an AI-powered hiring platform but now connects technology companies with subject-matter experts whose knowledge is used to train, test and improve AI models and agents. Mercor said the new capital will go towards training and testing AI agents on professional tasks.
Co-CEO Brendan Foody said every job in the economy will require its own AI agents, and every company will need a way to train and evaluate those agents on its own work.
The latest valuation roughly doubles the approximately $10 billion figure Mercor reached after raising $350 million in October last year. The company counts Jack Dorsey and venture capitalist Peter Thiel among its backers.
The deal reflects strong investor appetite for AI, which has driven a sharp rise in private funding this year and produced a growing group of heavily capitalised startups with multibillion-dollar valuations. According to Crunchbase, AI-driven startups raised $102 billion in the third quarter of 2026, accounting for 64% of global venture capital.

candidates.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
candidates.snippet: Hugging Face's CEO pledged to keep fighting for open source AI after Huang's exit, raising questions about Nvidia's $12.9 billion acquisition.
candidates.text:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.
This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!
But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026
The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.
As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.
After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.
The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.
Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”
Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.
For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter.
AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country.
Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026
In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
Earlier this year, Huang promoted open source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.”

candidates.text:
Ferguson: $9 Billion In Third-Quarter Sales, 9.5% Growth, And Raised 2026 Guidance
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 3:07 AM
Ferguson: $9 Billion In Third-Quarter Sales, 9.5% Growth, And Raised 2026 Guidance
Ferguson Enterprises, a North American distributor of water and air solutions, reported third-quarter 2026 sales of $9.03 billion, representing a 9.5% increase from the prior year, supported by organic growth, acquisitions, and strong demand across non-residential markets. The company also raised its full-year sales growth outlook following continued operating momentum and the acquisition of FloWorks.
For the quarter ended September 30, 2026, Ferguson generated organic sales growth of 7%, while acquisitions contributed an additional 2.7 percentage points. The company reported operating profit of $885 million, up 4.9% year over year, and adjusted operating profit of $962 million, an increase of 8.9%.
Gross margin declined 40 basis points to 30.9%, while reported operating margin decreased to 9.8% from 10.2% a year earlier. Adjusted operating margin remained unchanged at 10.7%.
Reported diluted earnings per share declined 4.9% to $3.08, compared with $3.24 in the prior-year quarter. However, adjusted diluted earnings per share increased 7.9% to $3.43, reflecting higher adjusted operating profit.
Ferguson’s U.S. business continued to drive growth, with sales increasing 10.2% year over year. Non-residential sales rose 15%, supported by large capital projects, healthy bidding activity, and demand for specialized solutions. Residential sales increased 6% despite continued weakness in new construction and repair, maintenance, and improvement activity.
The Canadian business experienced more challenging conditions, with sales declining 4.5%, reflecting divestments and unfavorable foreign exchange movements.
Acquisitions remained a central component of Ferguson’s expansion strategy. The company completed three acquisitions during the quarter, including FloWorks, Brax Company, and Rogers Supply Company. Following the quarter, Ferguson also acquired Canyon Systems, expanding its water and wastewater treatment capabilities.
Ferguson has completed 11 acquisitions during 2026, representing approximately $1.5 billion in aggregate annualized revenue. The company invested $1.7 billion in acquisitions during the third quarter, including FloWorks, while deploying $108 million in capital expenditures.
Following the FloWorks acquisition, Ferguson reported net debt to adjusted EBITDA of 1.7 times, compared with 1.0 times a year earlier.
For the first nine months of 2026, Ferguson generated $25.25 billion in sales, an increase of 6%, while adjusted operating profit increased 6.5% to $2.54 billion. Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.73 billion, up 6.9%.
Based on its year-to-date performance and the contribution from FloWorks, Ferguson increased its calendar 2026 sales growth guidance from mid-single-digit growth to approximately 7%. The company also raised the lower end of its adjusted operating margin outlook, establishing a revised range of 9.6% to 9.8%, compared with the previous range of 9.5% to 9.8%.
The updated outlook includes approximately $235 million in interest expense and $425 million in capital expenditures.
Ferguson also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.89 per share, payable January 8, 2027, to shareholders of record as of November 20, 2026.
KEY QUOTES:
“Our expert associates delivered strong third quarter results, with non-residential sales up 15% and residential growth of 6%. We continue to invest organically and through acquisitions to expand our value-added solutions and geographic footprint. We have completed eleven acquisitions this year with an aggregate annualized revenue of approximately $1.5 billion, while preserving a strong balance sheet.
“While our markets remain mixed, our year-to-date performance and the addition of FloWorks enable us to raise our full year guidance. We expect to continue delivering market outperformance by deploying scale locally and leveraging the long-term growth drivers of water infrastructure, large capital projects, climate and comfort and aging and underbuilt housing. We remain confident in our ability to capitalize on these growth drivers as we provide essential water and air solutions for the complex project needs of the specialized professional.”
Kevin Murphy, Chief Executive Officer, Ferguson

SolaREIT Supports Over $8.5 Billion In Clean Energy Project Value
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 12:56 PM
SolaREIT Supports Over $8.5 Billion In Clean Energy Project Value
SolaREIT has surpassed $8.5 billion in project value supported through its real estate financing, covering approximately 4.6 gigawatts of solar and battery storage capacity.
The milestone represents more than $3.5 billion in additional project value since November 2025. It measures the value of associated energy projects rather than the amount of financing directly provided by SolaREIT.
The Virginia-based company offers land purchases, lease purchases and land loans across all 50 states.
Its services cover utility-scale and distributed solar, battery energy storage and related infrastructure, including substation and transmission land.
The model allows developers and project owners to access capital tied to project real estate. Management said that flexibility is important when financing conditions, procurement plans and interconnection schedules change.
Co-Founder and CEO Laura Pagliarulo described land as an asset developers can use to raise capital in a constrained funding environment.
Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer Laura Klein said transactions can close within 30 to 45 days of signing, using diligence built around information developers already hold about their projects.
Founded in 2020 as a real estate investment trust, SolaREIT is a woman-owned and led business established by clean energy industry executives.
Its team brings experience across project development, finance, real estate and community solar. The company works with both developers and landowners.
The milestone reflects growth in real estate financing as one component of renewable energy project funding.
SolaREIT’s offering focuses specifically on land, providing developers with an additional source of capital alongside the other financing needed to build and operate solar, storage and associated infrastructure.
The company said its team’s industry experience helps it evaluate complex transactions and structure financing around project timelines.
KEY QUOTES:
“We pride ourselves on being a trusted partner to developers and project owners, helping them create additional value in a capital-constrained environment. It’s been another turbulent year, with higher interest rates and shifting policy, and the land under their projects is one of the few assets developers can turn into capital quickly. Surpassing $8.5 billion in project value financed reflects the trust our partners place in us. Our team has over 300 years of collective experience in the clean energy space, which allows us to help developers finance even their most complex deals.”
Laura Pagliarulo, Co-Founder And CEO Of SolaREIT
“In this market, speed and flexibility matter. With interconnection deadlines and procurement plans constantly shifting, developers need capital solutions that work on their timeline. We build our diligence on what developers already know about their projects, so we can close in 30 to 45 days from signing, providing developers with capital on a schedule they can plan around.”
Laura Klein, Chief Financial Officer And Chief Operating Officer Of SolaREIT

By Sam Tabahriti
LONDON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – AI chip startup Fractile was valued at $7 billion in its latest fundraising round, which included backing from the British government, a person involved ​in the deal said on Wednesday, making it one ‌of Britain’s most valuable technology startups.
The London- and Bristol-based company is developing chips designed to improve AI inference, the process through which AI models generate responses. Fractile says its technology can deliver faster performance while cutting energy use ‌and ​costs.
The company raised $720 million in a Series ⁠C funding round led ⁠by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, it told Reuters.
Other investors included Google’s venture arm CapitalG, BlackRock, DST Global, Elad Gil, Balderton, SV Angel, Britain’s Sovereign AI fund and the ​British Business Bank.
BRITAIN’S AI AMBITIONS
The investment marks a major vote of confidence in Britain’s efforts to build domestic AI infrastructure, rather ⁠than solely relying on overseas suppliers ⁠for the computing power that underpins the technology.
It also ​highlights growing investor interest in companies developing the hardware behind AI, ​a market dominated by Nvidia and a handful of Asian ‌semiconductor manufacturers.
Britain has made becoming an AI superpower a key part of its economic strategy, seeking to build on strengths in AI research and chip design while retaining more of the jobs, ⁠investment and economic value generated by the technology.
“For too long, Britain has produced some of the world’s best scientific ideas, only to see too ⁠much of the ‌technology, industry and wealth they create built elsewhere,” ⁠AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said in a statement ​on the ‌funding round.
“We are determined to change that.”
Britain is ​home to ⁠chip designer Arm, whose technology is used in billions of devices worldwide, but its semiconductor manufacturing industry remains small compared with those in the US and Asia.
Fractile plans to launch its first commercial chip next year.
($1 = 0.7492 pounds)

candidates.snippet: Nvidia Rival Fractile Hits $7B Valuation With $720M AI Chip Funding Coinpaper
candidates.text:
News / Technology
Nvidia Rival Fractile Hits $7B Valuation With $720M AI Chip Funding
British AI chip startup Fractile raises $720M at a $7B valuation, backed by Google, BlackRock and the UK government ahead of its 2027 chip launch.
Emir Abyazov 2 min read
12 November 2026, 01:14 PM Prefer us on Google
Key takeaways
Fractile raises $720 million at $7 billion valuation
Google and UK government back Nvidia challenger
First commercial AI chips expected in 2027
British AI chip startup Fractile has raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, attracting backing from Google-linked investors, BlackRock and the UK government as competition intensifies to develop alternatives to Nvidia's artificial intelligence processors.
The November 11 Series C round was co-led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. Alphabet's CapitalG, DST Global, Balderton and several other investors also participated.
The UK government's announcement confirmed investments from its Sovereign AI fund and the British Business Bank, describing the financing as part of Britain's strategy to develop domestic semiconductor capabilities.
Fractile's $720M Funding Targets Nvidia's AI Chip Dominance
Founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin, Fractile is developing processors specifically designed for AI inference, the process of generating responses after a model has been trained.
Unlike conventional AI accelerators, Fractile's architecture places dynamic random-access memory directly above processing components, seeking to reduce the delays caused by moving data between memory and computing units.
The company argues that memory bandwidth increasingly limits AI performance, particularly as reasoning models and autonomous agents generate longer outputs.
Its technology could eventually challenge Nvidia's dominant position in AI inference, although commercial performance remains unproven.
The financing arrives as Google expands its exposure to alternative AI chip developers, including a recently disclosed $548 million Qualcomm stake.
Other companies are pursuing similar opportunities through custom AI accelerators , as cloud providers seek more specialized computing hardware.
Google and UK Government Back Fractile's Expansion
Fractile's investors include major technology-focused funds alongside British public institutions, reflecting growing demand for alternatives to foreign semiconductor suppliers.
The British government said the investment would help the company expand its engineering operations across London and Bristol while strengthening domestic AI infrastructure.
The round also comes amid Nvidia's continued investment in AI chip research , where rapid innovation remains essential to protecting its competitive advantage.
However, Fractile faces significant execution challenges.
The company expects to introduce its first commercial chip in 2027, meaning its current valuation largely reflects investor expectations rather than established product revenue.
Can Fractile Challenge Nvidia in AI Inference?
Fractile is entering a competitive market that includes established semiconductor companies and emerging developers such as Groq and Etched.
Nvidia has already pursued inference technology investments to strengthen its position as AI workloads expand beyond model training.
Fractile must demonstrate that its architecture delivers meaningful improvements in speed, energy consumption and cost under real-world conditions.
Its financing also reflects the broader AI infrastructure investment boom , where substantial capital is flowing into companies before their technologies achieve commercial scale.

candidates.text:
Surgery Partners: HealthSpan Partners Raises Merger Offer To $25 Per Share In Deal Valued At Up To $6 Billion
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 3:32 PM
Surgery Partners: HealthSpan Partners Raises Merger Offer To $25 Per Share In Deal Valued At Up To $6 Billion
Surgery Partners and HealthSpan Partners have amended their merger agreement to increase the cash consideration for Surgery Partners shareholders to $25 per share, with the total enterprise value potentially reaching approximately $6 billion. The revised agreement follows an unsolicited competing acquisition proposal and includes additional payments for certain shareholders if the transaction closes after March 1, 2027.
HealthSpan Partners is affiliated with Bon Secours Mercy Health and is pursuing the acquisition of Surgery Partners, an operator of outpatient surgical facilities across the United States.
The amendment represents an increase in the merger consideration and introduces a mechanism to compensate eligible shareholders for certain closing delays.
Under the amended agreement, shareholders other than affiliates of Bain Capital will receive $25 per share in cash if the transaction closes before March 1, 2027.
If the required shareholder approval has been obtained but the transaction remains incomplete after that date, eligible shareholders will receive additional monthly payments.
These payments will accrue at a rate equivalent to 10% annually on the $25-per-share merger consideration.
If the transaction closes on its October 23, 2027 outside date and the applicable conditions are satisfied, those payments could total up to $1.61 per share.
That would increase the maximum consideration for eligible shareholders to $26.61 per share.
The revised merger agreement follows an unsolicited, nonbinding competing proposal received on November 3, 2026, and updated on November 8.
The competing bidder offered $28 per share in cash to acquire all outstanding Surgery Partners shares.
Although the competing proposal offered a higher stated price, Surgery Partners’ independent special committee considered additional factors involving transaction certainty and closing timing.
The committee evaluated the likelihood that the competing transaction would receive regulatory approvals and the potential consequences of a longer completion process.
It also considered the contractual protections available under each proposal.
Following consultation with legal and financial advisors, the special committee unanimously determined that the competing offer did not constitute a superior proposal under the existing merger agreement.
The committee recommended that Surgery Partners proceed with the amended HealthSpan transaction.
The company’s Board of Directors approved the revised agreement and reaffirmed its recommendation that shareholders vote in favor of the merger.
Bain Capital, which owns approximately 39% of Surgery Partners’ outstanding shares, has agreed to support the transaction.
Rather than receiving cash consideration, Bain Capital affiliates will exchange their Surgery Partners shares for ownership interests in the acquiring entity.
The arrangement will allow Bain Capital to remain a significant investor alongside HealthSpan Partners after closing.
Surgery Partners operates more than 200 locations across 30 states.
Its facilities include ambulatory surgery centers, surgical hospitals, multispecialty physician practices, and urgent care locations.
The company focuses on providing surgical care through outpatient and other short-stay healthcare settings.
The combination with HealthSpan is intended to support expansion of outpatient care services through relationships with physicians and healthcare systems.
HealthSpan plans to finance the acquisition using cash on hand and new debt financing supported by existing commitments.
The merger is expected to close during the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder approval, regulatory clearances, and other closing conditions.
Centerview Partners is serving as lead financial advisor to Surgery Partners, while Leerink Partners is also providing financial advice.
Moelis & Company is advising the independent special committee.
Jefferies is serving as exclusive financial advisor to HealthSpan and has provided committed financing support.
The revised transaction reflects Surgery Partners’ decision to prioritize the combination of increased cash consideration, contractual protections, and expected closing certainty.
KEY QUOTE:
“We are pleased to have reached this outcome, which reflects the rigorous focus of our Board of Directors and Special Committee throughout this process on delivering the best possible result for Surgery Partners and our stockholders. This transaction provides exceptional value for our stockholders, along with regulatory certainty and a closing expected in the near term. We continue to believe combining with HealthSpan Partners is the right next chapter for our company as, together with our physician and health system partners, we expand access to high-quality outpatient care across the communities we serve.”
Eric Evans, CEO Of Surgery Partners

SoftBank Bets approximately $5.4 Billion on Swiss Robotics as Foreign Capital Influx Deepens
Add preferred source
Japan's SoftBank Group is pouring large sums into Switzerland's robotics industry, agreeing to acquire ABB's robotics division for $5.4 billion and investing $200 million in Gravis Robotics, a construction-robotics startup spun out of ETH Zurich. Foreign investors account for 88% of capital in deep-tech funding rounds of $100 million or more, and 43% of Swiss scale-ups are university or research-institute spin-offs. However, the share of Swiss investors in later-stage rounds has fallen from 27% to 13%, with limited mass-production experience and the flight of domestic capital cited as challenges at the growth stage.
Key Elements
SoftBank Group ABB Gravis Robotics ETH Zurich Deep Tech Nation Switzerland Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE) Neura Robotics Swissmem Swisscom Ventures EPFL
Japan's SoftBank Group is injecting large sums into Switzerland's robotics industry in quick succession. After agreeing to acquire the robotics division of Swiss automation company ABB for $5.4 billion (~7.2 trillion won), SoftBank in August invested $200 million (~270 billion won) in Gravis Robotics, a construction-robotics startup spun out of ETH Zurich. Gravis said the round was the largest Series A investment ever in the construction-robotics sector.
SoftBank's string of bets encapsulates the recent surge of foreign capital into Swiss deep-tech companies. According to the "Swiss Scale-up Report 2026" published this year by Deep Tech Nation Switzerland, foreign investors accounted for 88% of the capital in deep-tech funding rounds that raised $100 million or more. In effect, Swiss companies are raising their growth capital from abroad.
Speaking at a robotics and automation event hosted by Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE) in Zurich, Switzerland, on the 11th (local time), investment and industry officials agreed that foreign capital looks at the depth of research accumulated before a company's founding rather than its short history. They explained that technology and intellectual property (IP) built up over years in university labs, combined with research talent from around the world, heighten investment appeal.
Alexandre Meldem, head of international communications at Deep Tech Nation Switzerland, said, "Even if a company was only recently founded, there may be 10 years of science behind it," adding, "Switzerland is a relatively stable country with a predictable policy environment, which is an advantage because it allows investors to look 10 years ahead."
Indeed, research institutions are the key starting point for deep-tech companies in Switzerland. Of 265 Swiss scale-ups, 115—or 43%—are spin-offs from universities or research institutes. Forty-two came from ETH and 41 from EPFL. Some foreign robotics companies have even set up bases in Zurich directly to tap the research ecosystem. German robotics company Neura Robotics is developing core hardware technology for humanoid robots in Zurich.
Urs Laupi, chief strategy officer (CSO) of Neura Robotics, cited cooperation with ETH, physical AI research talent, and the capital environment as reasons for choosing Zurich as its base. "Switzerland has a solid knowledge base in the field of physical AI," he said, stressing that "we can combine world-class Swiss research capabilities with Germany's industrialization capabilities."
Switzerland also operates a separate intermediate stage to validate research results before they are applied on actual factory floors. The Swiss Cobotics Competence Center (S3C) at the Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne supports proof-of-concept (PoC) testing of robotics technology before companies invest in automation equipment, and once validation is complete, hands the results to system integrators and others to connect them to industrialization.
The competitiveness of Swiss robotics companies was not built on university research alone. As the precision machinery and automation industries developed long ago, a manufacturing base for applying lab technology to real industry was built alongside them. A Chinese venture capital (VC) official also cited precision machinery technology and the manufacturing base supporting it as reasons for paying attention to Swiss robotics companies.
Roger Sonderegger, industry sector manager at Swissmem, the Swiss association for the mechanical, electrical, and metal industries, explained that "high labor costs accelerated automation in Swiss manufacturing," adding that "from the 1970s and 1980s, automation was adopted to cope with high production costs, and competitiveness was built around precision machinery and high-value-added products rather than mass production."
Category Key Figure
Size of ABB robotics acquisition $5.4 billion (~7.2 trillion won)
Size of Gravis Robotics investment $200 million (~270 billion won)
Foreign capital share in rounds of $100 million+ 88%
Share of university/research-institute spin-offs 43% (115 of 265)
Swiss investor share in later-stage rounds 27% average in 2019–2022 → 13% last year
Note: Based on the Swiss Scale-up Report 2026 and event presentations
However, this industrial structure can also become a weakness when robotics startups reach the stage of growing into large companies. Alexander Schläpfer, managing partner at Swisscom Ventures, said, "Switzerland has focused on making high-value-added products for relatively small markets, like watches," adding, "It is not a country that has nurtured mass-production companies making millions of units." He added, "Because we are not accustomed to large-volume production, partnerships with countries that have much larger markets are necessary."

Mubadala Capital: LSV Advisors $5 Billion Secondaries Platform To Receive Strategic Minority Investment
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 9:38 AM
Mubadala Capital: LSV Advisors $5 Billion Secondaries Platform To Receive Strategic Minority Investment
Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset management subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Company, has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire a minority ownership stake in LSV Advisors, a New York-based investment manager specializing in GP-led secondary transactions. The partnership will expand Mubadala Capital’s alternative investment capabilities while supporting the continued growth of LSV, which manages approximately $5 billion in assets and commitments.
Founded in 2005, LSV has established a specialized investment strategy focused on general partner-led continuation vehicles, particularly single-asset transactions involving middle-market companies.
The firm has completed more than 75 transactions since executing one of the industry’s earliest GP-led investments in 2011.
Continuation vehicles have become an increasingly important segment of the private equity secondary market, providing investment managers with an alternative to selling portfolio companies through traditional exit transactions.
These structures allow general partners to transfer investments from an existing fund into a new investment vehicle, often providing existing limited partners with an opportunity to receive liquidity or maintain exposure to the underlying business.
For fund managers, continuation vehicles can create additional time to execute growth strategies at portfolio companies while introducing new capital partners.
LSV focuses on identifying established, cash-generative businesses and structuring investments that emphasize governance, risk management, and alignment among stakeholders.
The company’s approach combines investment due diligence with transaction structures designed to address the interests of general partners, existing investors, and new capital providers.
The investment will add dedicated GP-led secondaries expertise to Mubadala Capital’s expanding portfolio of strategic partnerships.
Mubadala Capital currently maintains investment relationships across private wealth, insurance, credit, and real estate.
The LSV partnership will complement those activities by providing exposure to a specialized segment of the private equity market.
Mubadala Capital manages, advises, and administers more than $755 billion in assets through its core alternative investment businesses and strategic partnerships.
Its core alternatives operations manage and invest more than $60 billion across private equity, venture capital, credit, special opportunities, and related investment strategies.
The company operates as a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi-based Mubadala Investment Company, combining institutional capital resources with a global alternative asset management platform.
Mubadala Capital maintains offices in Abu Dhabi, London, New York, Rio de Janeiro, and Menlo Park, with more than 250 professionals.
The investment in LSV represents part of its strategy to develop long-term relationships with specialized alternative investment managers.
Through these partnerships, Mubadala Capital aims to provide access to institutional capital, private wealth distribution relationships, and its international network.
For LSV, the transaction creates opportunities to expand its investment platform while maintaining the firm’s existing leadership and investment strategy.
The company will continue operating under its established management team.
LSV’s principals also intend to reinvest the majority of their net proceeds from the transaction into future funds.
This reinvestment is intended to maintain alignment between the firm’s leadership, its investment strategies, and its limited partners.
The arrangement will allow LSV to access Mubadala Capital’s institutional relationships without fundamentally changing the investment philosophy that has guided its development.
LSV serves institutional investors, family offices, and other clients internationally.
In addition to continuation vehicle investments, the firm and its affiliates provide restructuring and liquidity solutions involving different types of investment funds.
The transaction comes as alternative asset managers increasingly seek strategic partnerships to expand distribution capabilities, strengthen their capital resources, and enter specialized investment markets.
Mubadala Capital plans to continue evaluating additional partnerships in complementary asset classes, with an emphasis on selectively identifying managers whose strategies align with its broader investment platform.
LSV will join its network of strategic and institutional partners while maintaining relationships with its existing private wealth investor base.
The transaction is expected to close during the first half of 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals.
Evercore is serving as exclusive financial advisor to Mubadala Capital, while Houlihan Lokey is acting as exclusive financial advisor to LSV.
The strategic investment positions Mubadala Capital to expand its exposure to GP-led secondary transactions while providing LSV with additional institutional resources to support its next phase of growth.

Mubadala Capital’s global reach, institutional perspective, and long-term investment orientation make them an ideal partner as we continue building the firm for the years ahead. The investment further strengthens our platform and expands our capabilities while allowing us to remain steadfast in the approach that has defined LSV for the past 17 years.”
David G. Tisch, Founder And CEO Of LSV Advisors

candidates.text:
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Announces $5 Billion AWS Data Center Transaction
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 1:04 PM
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Announces $5 Billion AWS Data Center Transaction
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust has agreed to acquire a 75% majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion.
The acquisition represents the recently listed company’s first investment and carries an initial capitalization rate of 7%. The joint ventures will own 13 newly constructed powered shells across two AWS data center campuses.
AWS will retain a 25% interest in the ventures and lease the entire portfolio on a triple-net basis. The initial lease term is 12 years, with extensions potentially taking the total term to 32 years.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to closing conditions.
The investment establishes a starting portfolio aligned with the trust’s strategy of acquiring stabilized data centers leased to major cloud providers under long-term contracts.
CEO and President Nick Pell identified asset quality, pricing and the tenant relationship as reasons for deploying proceeds from the company’s initial public offering into the portfolio.
For AWS, the arrangement combines continued occupancy with minority ownership. The company said the partnership supports its expansion while maintaining its focus on local employment, workforce training and community priorities.
Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust targets newly constructed, income-generating facilities leased to investment-grade hyperscale tenants. Its strategy emphasizes contractual cash flows, rent increases and further acquisitions.
The company is externally managed by a Blackstone affiliate. Blackstone manages nearly $1.4 trillion across real estate, private equity, credit, infrastructure and other strategies.
Morgan Stanley, CBRE Capital Markets, Citi, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan and Wells Fargo are serving as financial advisors on the transaction. Simpson Thacher & Bartlett is advising Blackstone legally.
KEY QUOTES
“We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation. The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders.”
Nick Pell, CEO And President Of Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust
“As we scale to meet growing demand for our customers, we’re committed to building in a way that strengthens the communities where we operate. We’re focused on delivering long-term local benefits, from creating good jobs and free workforce training programs to supporting local priorities. Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build.”
Prasad Kalyanaraman, Vice President Of AWS Infrastructure

candidates.text:
Norwest: $4 Billion Fund Expands Global Multi-Stage Investment Strategy
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:42 AM
Norwest: $4 Billion Fund Expands Global Multi-Stage Investment Strategy
Norwest has closed Norwest 18, a $4 billion global investment fund that will back venture and growth equity opportunities across technology, healthcare, and consumer markets. The vehicle is the largest fund in the firm’s 65-year history and increases its total capital under management to $18 billion.
Norwest will deploy the new fund across the United States, India, and Israel, continuing a strategy that spans early-stage venture investments through later-stage growth equity. The firm said this flexible approach allows it to begin working with companies at different stages and continue supporting them as their capital requirements and operating priorities evolve.
Since launching Norwest 17 in April 2024, the firm has completed more than 87 investments and worked with over 30 portfolio companies on liquidity events. Initial public offerings during that period included Amagi Media Labs, BillionToOne, MBX Biosciences, Omada Health, and Swiggy.
Strategic acquisitions involving Norwest-backed businesses included EQT’s acquisition of Avetta, Luminate Capital Partners’ purchase of AbsenceSoft, Gilead Sciences’ acquisition of Ouro Medicines, Salesforce’s purchase of Qualified, Pinterest’s acquisition of tvScientific, and ServiceNow’s purchase of Veza.
Norwest 18 will maintain the firm’s primary sector focus while increasing its exposure to emerging categories. Areas of interest include next-generation financial infrastructure, physical and voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, technology-enabled industrial and aerospace businesses, and healthcare AI.
Recent financial infrastructure investments include Beltic, Rain, and Stablecore. Norwest has also backed Coval, Generalist AI, and LlamaIndex in intelligent AI systems; Above Security, ORION Security, Red Access, and Zenity in cybersecurity; and East Range Group, Padmini VNA, JJG Aerospace, and Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group in industrial and aerospace markets.
Healthcare investments include Infinx, Matchpoint Therapeutics, Rezo Therapeutics, Tokaido Health, and Vitalize Care. These businesses are applying AI to drug discovery, clinical and administrative workflows, healthcare access, and care-team productivity.
Beyond financing, Norwest provides portfolio companies with operating support and strategic guidance. The firm has doubled the size of its Senior Advisor Network, added operating executives, and launched the Norwest Operator Collective and Norwest Kinetic. These resources are intended to help management teams address technology, go-to-market, talent, and organizational challenges.
Since its founding in 1961, Norwest has invested in more than 750 companies and currently works with over 275 venture and growth equity portfolio companies. Its offices are in Menlo Park, San Francisco, Mumbai, and Tel Aviv.
KEY QUOTES
“Building and scaling a company has never been a linear journey, and today that journey is becoming more complex. Companies are staying private longer, scaling across markets, and navigating critical decisions around technology, talent, and growth. Capital is only one part of what they need. Our role is to be a long-term partner and bring the experience, networks, and resources that can help leadership teams make those decisions with confidence.”
Jeff Crowe, Senior Managing Partner at Norwest
“Markets and technology change, but what has remained consistent at Norwest is our ability to identify strong businesses, invest patiently, and stay closely aligned with the founders, CEOs, and leadership teams we partner with. Our multi-stage strategy allows us to meet companies where they are and continue supporting them as they grow. candidates.snippet: Science Corp. raised a $400 million Series D to scale up its anti-blindness business.
candidates.text:
In Brief
Posted:
6:26 AM PST · November 17, 2026
Image Credits: Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch
Tim Fernholz
Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding
Science Corporation , the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post .
Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.
Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.
Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.
Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.
With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.
Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

LPL Financial Brings In $2.035 Billion In Combined Client Assets Represented By Four Joining Practices
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 4:03 PM
LPL Financial Brings In $2.035 Billion In Combined Client Assets Represented By Four Joining Practices
LPL Financial has welcomed four wealth management practices reporting approximately $2.035 billion in combined client assets, expanding its advisor network through affiliations announced over the last couple of days. SteadRock Private Wealth, FHT Advisors, Impel Wealth Management and Sound Foundation Wealth Advisors joined LPL’s broker-dealer and Registered Investment Advisor platforms. The reported assets include advisory, brokerage and retirement plan assets.
SteadRock Private Wealth
Nathan J. “Nate” Hershman joined LPL from Edward Jones to launch SteadRock Private Wealth in North Canton, Ohio. He reported serving approximately $185 million in advisory, brokerage and retirement plan assets.
SteadRock serves families, individuals approaching or living in retirement, and business owners, including those in manufacturing. Its planning approach connects investments and retirement needs with business interests, charitable priorities and financial legacies.
For business owners, planning can include preparing for a transition and evaluating how a sale or succession could affect retirement and family objectives. Hershman selected LPL to establish an independent practice with access to its technology, investment platform and business support.
FHT Advisors
FHT Advisors joined LPL from Cetera alongside Impel Wealth Management. The two Ohio-based practices reported approximately $1.15 billion in combined client assets and will retain their separate identities.
Led by Brian Toma, FHT serves clients across 32 states, including professionals, medical professionals, younger families, people approaching retirement and retirees.
The firm operates as an ensemble practice, bringing multiple advisors’ experience and planning perspectives to client relationships. Its advisory team includes Sarah Stewart, Tom Drager, Tammy Hafner, Bruce Baker, Bear Rupert, Jonathan Goldston, Seann Schaller and financial consultant Stephen Ehrhardt.
FHT identified LPL’s technology, planning capabilities and resources as factors supporting its next stage of development.
Impel Wealth Management
Jesse Hurst leads Impel Wealth Management, which began by serving corporate executives around Akron and has expanded into multigenerational wealth management.
Hurst works alongside advisors Nathan Ollish and Irene Zurowski. Ollish serves many next-generation clients, while Zurowski’s focus includes retirement plans and female executives.
Impel works with dozens of families across at least two generations and more than a dozen across three generations. The team also produces market and financial planning commentary through recurring blog posts and videos.
Hurst and FHT’s Toma have worked alongside one another for 25 years, exchanging ideas and best practices while independently leading their firms. Impel selected LPL for its technology, advanced planning resources and growth opportunities.
Sound Foundation Wealth Advisors
Sound Foundation Wealth Advisors joined from Cambridge Investment Research Advisors, reporting approximately $700 million in advisory, brokerage and retirement plan assets.
Founded by Nathan Downs and Cory Thomas, the Boise, Idaho-headquartered practice traces its beginnings to 2018. It has developed shared operations and business processes to support a nationwide advisory team.
Its advisors also include Seth Church, Cameron Church, Caleb Whalen, Kason Wedel, Dustin Olson and Cory McLeaf.
Sound Foundation serves clients including technology, healthcare and higher education professionals, as well as business owners. Its planning process starts with each household’s income, expenses, assets and objectives before developing individualized recommendations.
The founders cited LPL’s investment in technology and systems, along with its ability to support the practice’s evolving needs, as reasons for joining.
LPL supports more than 32,000 financial advisors and the wealth management practices of approximately 1,100 financial institutions. It services and custodies approximately $2.6 trillion in brokerage and advisory assets on behalf of approximately 8 million Americans.

India's AI startups raise $1.91 billion across 102 funding rounds in 2026 so far

Sarvam subsequently raised another $90.4 million in August, while Freehand secured $75 million through a Series B round in July. India's artificial intelligence (AI) startup ecosystem has attracted approximately $1.91 billion across 102 funding rounds between January 1 and November 5, 2026, with a handful of large-ticket transactions accounting for a significant portion of the capital raised, according to data compiled by Tracxn .
The funding activity includes investments across companies developing AI infrastructure, generative AI platforms and enterprise applications, with some of the largest transactions involving businesses operating in the infrastructure and computing ecosystem.
Advt
Neysa's $600 million Series B round in February was the largest funding transaction recorded during the period. Sarvam followed with a $255.1 million Series B round in June, while semiconductor technology company Kandou raised $225 million through a Series E round in March.
Other significant transactions included Yotta's $150 million Series D round in July and Emergent's $130 million Series C round in the same month. Emergent had also raised $70 million through a Series B round in January.
Sarvam subsequently raised another $90.4 million in August, while Freehand secured $75 million through a Series B round in July.
The four largest funding transactions — involving Neysa, Sarvam, Kandou and Yotta — together accounted for approximately $1.23 billion, or nearly 64 per cent of the total funding recorded during the period.
Peak XV Partners leads investor participation
Sarvam subsequently raised another $90.4 million in August, while Freehand secured $75 million through a Series B round in July. On the investor side, Peak XV Partners emerged as the most active investor in India's AI startup funding landscape, participating in six funding rounds during the period.
Khosla Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Together, Info Edge Ventures, Capital 2B, IvyCap Ventures, Antler, Venture Catalysts and Wyser followed, with participation in three rounds each.
Advt
In terms of lead-investor participation, Peak XV Partners led three funding rounds, while IvyCap Ventures and Info Edge Ventures led two rounds each.
The investor activity reflects participation by established venture capital firms, as well as funds backing emerging AI companies at different stages of development.
The funding rounds recorded during the period included seed, Series A, Series B, and later-stage investments, as well as venture debt, conventional debt, and grant-related entries.
