candidates.title: Sofinnova's Graziano Seghezzi Raises $815 Million to Fix Europe's Biotech Scale-Up Gap
candidates.snippet: Sofinnova's Graziano Seghezzi Raises $815 Million to Fix Europe's Biotech Scale-Up Gap BigGo Finance
candidates.text:
Sofinnova's Graziano Seghezzi Raises $815 Million to Fix Europe's Biotech Scale-Up Gap
Add preferred source
Sofinnova Partners has raised more than $800 million — roughly three-quarters of a billion — for a fund dedicated entirely to late-stage European biotech and medtech, a direct bet that the continent's problem is no longer invention but the capital to carry companies into commercialization. Managing partner Graziano Seghezzi, speaking at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London, argues Europe excels at company creation but remains starved of scale-up capital, and that pharma M&A — not European public markets — is the healthy exit route the industry should embrace. The evidence he offers is concrete: a $90 million Series A in Aletheia Therapeutics, a $1.5 billion sale of UK ADC-toxin developer Mirix to Novartis, and Hema now public at a valuation in the low billions. Yet the same conversation carries a counterweight. Seghezzi says Europe "cannot afford" to back fast followers against China, tells portfolio boards to treat China as a speed lever rather than a threat, and confirms Sofinnova still recommends US listings because Europe's public market lacks depth. His 2027 forecast is an up year, powered by record-level pharma M&A and a functioning, if unspectacular, IPO window.
Key Elements
Sofinnova Partners Graziano Seghezzi Aletheia Therapeutics Tea Therapeutics Mirix Surcentrix Hema Novartis Johnson & Johnson Ollin Biosciences Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference Stifel LSEG
Europe's biotech industry has spent two decades waiting for a public market deep enough to carry its best companies. Graziano Seghezzi has stopped waiting and raised three-quarters of a billion dollars to work around the gap instead.
Sofinnova Partners, where Seghezzi is managing partner, has closed a fund above $800 million dedicated entirely to late-stage European biotech and medtech — B rounds, C rounds, crossovers and companies approaching a listing. The fund was announced at Sofinnova's own growth summit in London, a couple of blocks from the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference where Seghezzi sat down to explain it in mid-November 2026.
His thesis is narrow and specific. "We are great at technologies and company creation, but what we're still lacking a little bit is on scale-up capital," he said. The new vehicle is aimed squarely at that missing layer: European companies ambitious enough to want to bring products into commercialization rather than sell early.
A repeat of a fund that already returned exits and listings
This is not a first attempt. Sofinnova's growth team ran an earlier fund that Seghezzi says deployed roughly half a billion euros into European late-stage companies, producing a couple of exits and a couple of public listings. The new pool repeats the playbook at a larger size.
The allocation follows Sofinnova's house pattern of 70–80% biopharma and 20–30% medtech, and stays therapy-area agnostic — the target being, in Seghezzi's words, "everywhere where there is a big medical need and important solutions."
Two investments have already been made from the new vehicle:
Company Geography Sector framing Status / detail
Surcentrix UK Not specified Portfolio company the growth team participated in
Hema Nordic Health and disorders Now public, valued at about a couple of billions
Why UK rounds are bigger: it's a scale story, not a sophistication story
The obvious question for anyone watching European biotech is why the big rounds cluster in London while continental financings stay smaller. Seghezzi's answer is arithmetic, not culture.
"The UK on its own is basically twice Germany, France and Italy put together," he said. "So that tells you everything about why there are bigger rounds in the UK."
Behind that scale sits a continuous flow of spin-offs and startups out of UK universities and research centers, which he credits for keeping investor interest high. The week before the interview, two Sofinnova investments together brought in about $220 million: a Series A in Aletheia Therapeutics and a Series B in Tea Therapeutics, the latter having had its Series A co-led by Sofinnova a couple of years earlier.
What a $90 million Series A actually buys
The Aletheia round is Seghezzi's clearest illustration of how ambition, not market fashion, sets round size. The company was founded by Beth and Adam on the premise of curing chronic cancer of the blood rather than managing it. With a lead candidate identified, the plan is to get into patients as fast as possible and build a pipeline behind it.
Seghezzi's test for any biotech is blunt: answer quickly whether you have a product that can cure the disease you are targeting, yes or no. "That's the question we want to answer ASAP," he said. "And the other thing that we want to do is really build a pipeline of very interesting products behind it. And that's 90 million dollars."
Selling to pharma is the win, not the consolation prize
Seghezzi rejects the idea that Europe loses when its companies scale and then get bought. Biopharma and medtech, he argues, are unusually symbiotic with startups: the large companies eventually buy the smaller ones and commercialize the product, and that M&A market stays vibrant even when public markets are weak.
"I don't know any other industry where you have such a vibrant M&A market that allows everybody to have positive momentum," he said. "Even when the public markets are not there... you still have the record here from an M&A perspective."
His example is the UK preclinical company Mirix, which Sofinnova co-founded as an investor and which sold for $1.5 billion. Built on a new toxin for antibody-drug conjugates, the asset goes to Novartis if it comes to fruition. Seghezzi calls it a fantastic deal for Sofinnova, for management, for the investors and for the buyer.
Some companies will choose to go further on their own, depending on the ambition of management, boards and investors. But current transactions, in his tell

candidates.title: Panamint Capital Closes $769 Million Financing for 491 MW Solar Project
candidates.snippet: Panamint Capital Closes $769 Million Financing for 491 MW Solar Project Mercom Capital Group
candidates.text:
November 09, 2026
Staff
Solar
From: Mercom India
Panamint Capital , a U.S. energy investment firm, has achieved financial close on $769 million in financing for the 491 MW Big Rooter West solar project in Robertson County, Texas. The financing represents the first phase of a $1.8 billion green loan for Big Rooter Power, a 1.2 GW solar photovoltaic project being developed at the company’s Twin Oaks Power Station and Calvert Mine.
The proceeds will fund the ongoing construction of Big Rooter West, the first stage of the project. Construction began in July of this year, and commercial operations are scheduled for August 2028.
The financing comprises a $240 million senior secured construction-to-term loan, a $461 million tax equity bridge loan, and a $68 million letter of credit facility.
Lloyds, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), and Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) are serving as coordinating lead arrangers, green loan coordinators, co-syndication agents, and joint bookrunners for the Big Rooter West and Big Rooter East financings. MUFG is also serving as administrative agent.
Panamint Capital expects to close financing for the 658 MW Big Rooter East project in the first quarter of 2027. The financing is expected to comprise a $336 million construction-to-term loan, a $587 million tax equity bridge loan, and a $91 million letter of credit facility, totaling approximately $1.01 billion.
Big Rooter East is scheduled to begin commercial operations in August 2029.
Big Rooter Power is being developed on reclaimed coal mine land at Panamint Capital’s 10,000-acre Twin Oaks Complex between Dallas and Houston. The site has existing operating interconnection infrastructure and includes power generation, surface mining, energy storage, data center capacity, and high-voltage transmission infrastructure.
Panamint Capital said Big Rooter Power will be the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America.
White & Case and Jackson Walker served as legal counsel to Panamint Capital. Milbank served as legal counsel to the lenders, while CSC Delaware Trust Company acted as collateral agent.
Panamint Capital is headquartered in Incline Village, Nevada. Global Atlantic Financial Group, a wholly owned subsidiary of KKR, holds a minority ownership stake in the company.
Announced large-scale solar project funding increased by 75% in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the funding raised in the same period in 2025, according to Mercom’s recently released 9M and Q3 2026 Solar Funding and M&A report.
In 2026, Arevon Energy, a U.S. energy developer, owner, and operator, has secured a $120 million tax equity commitment from Wells Fargo Bank for its 124 MW Big Muddy Solar project in Jackson County, Illinois.

Mercor Raises $750 Million in Series D at $20 Billion Valuation
The round includes an employee tender, but Mercor did not disclose how much goes to share sales or new company capital. The company plans to expand AI evaluation and post-training work for businesses.
By John Kim
Published Nov 11, 2026, 4:06 PM EST
Save Share Three miniature task stations under warm studio light / TokenPost.ai
Mercor detailed a broader enterprise AI evaluation and post-training push in a Nov. 10 announcement of a $750 million Series D that values the company at $20 billion.
The round includes an employee tender, but Mercor did not disclose how much of the $750 million is tied to employees selling shares or how much will go to the company as new capital. The company plans to invest in research and infrastructure for evaluations and post-training, along with additional environments where AI agents can practice complex workflows.
Over the past two years, Mercor has developed systems for training and assessing frontier AI models. Its enterprise evaluations use companies’ actual workflows and requirements, giving businesses a way to assess models against tasks shaped around their operations.
More than five million experts work through Mercor’s network and receive payment for training frontier AI models. “Every job in the economy will need its own agents that can perform tasks reliably and efficiently,” Mercor co-founder and CEO Brendan Foody said.
Investors named in the round include Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, funds managed by Apollo affiliates, G Squared, General Catalyst, Glade Brook Capital, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group, XTX Ventures and Zoom.
Mercor’s previous announced financing was a $350 million Series C at a $10 billion valuation on Oct. 27, 2025. In July, the company announced plans to acquire Deeptune, which builds training environments for reinforcement learning. Deeptune’s team had recreated hundreds of enterprise applications over two years.

candidates.title: Mercor $750M Series D at $20B: What It Means
candidates.snippet: Mercor $750M Series D at $20B: What It Means CASRAI
candidates.text:
On 10 November 2026, Mercor announced a $750 million Series D round at a $20 billion valuation. The company runs a marketplace that pays domain experts to train and evaluate frontier AI models, and the round doubles the $10 billion valuation it set in October 2025.
What was announced
Mercor published the news on its own blog on 10 November 2026. The round was priced at $20 billion and included an employee tender alongside new investment. Named participants were Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, funds managed by affiliates of Apollo, G Squared, General Catalyst, Glade Brook Capital, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group, XTX Ventures and Zoom. The announcement did not name a lead investor. Crunchbase News listed the round among the week’s biggest funding rounds in its 13 November 2026 roundup.
The previous round was a $350 million Series C at a $10 billion valuation in October 2025, reported by TechCrunch . TechCrunch also reported in July 2026 that Mercor was in talks at a $20 billion valuation .
What Mercor says it does
In the announcement, Mercor says it has more than five million experts in its network “getting paid to train frontier AI models based on their unique knowledge”. It also says it works with enterprises and experts in their fields to build custom evaluations based on the company’s actual workflows. The company says the new funding will go toward infrastructure and research for evaluations and post-training, and toward environments where AI agents can learn complex workflows. It also says it has opened offices in New York and London. The announcement does not break down the network by qualification, so it does not say how many of those experts hold doctorates or work as researchers.
Why it matters for researchers and research offices
The round is a data point on how much capital is flowing toward expert human judgment as an input to AI development. Three practical questions follow for universities and research offices. These are editorial observations, not claims made by Mercor.
Researcher time. Expert annotation and evaluation work for AI companies is paid outside the normal grant and appointment structures. Research offices may need to check how it interacts with institutional outside-activity and conflict-of-commitment policies.
Confidential and unpublished material. Evaluation tasks built from real workflows raise questions about what a researcher may share, including unpublished data, grant content or material under a confidentiality agreement.
Evaluation methods. Expert-written tests are one way AI developers measure model ability. Researchers who read results from such tests can use frameworks such as model evaluation suites and AI evaluation cards to ask what was tested and how.
For background on the techniques this market supports, see RLHF and training data provenance . For an example of a research-level expert-written benchmark, see FrontierMath .
What is not yet known
The Series D announcement did not disclose revenue, expert pay rates or the share of the network made up of researchers. Anyone weighing the opportunity should rely on the terms they are offered directly rather than on funding headlines.

candidates.title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
candidates.snippet: Fractile has now become one of the top-funded players in the race for purpose-built AI chips.
candidates.text:
Fractile , a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated .
Alongside the likes of Axelera , Etched , and OLIX , this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.
However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.
As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source .
Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot , its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual tradeoff between memory and capacity.
This tradeoff has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.
In a LinkedIn post , Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

candidates.title: Edgevana: $700 Million AI Infrastructure Agreements Bring Committed Demand To $7 Billion
candidates.snippet:
Edgevana, an AI computing infrastructure company, has secured more than $700 million in fully committed, multiyear agreements to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell computing systems across North America and Europe. The contracts expand the company's committed customer demand to approximately $7 billion, with an additional active business pipeline exceeding $20 billion.
The post Edgevana: $700 Million AI Infrastructure Agreements Bring Committed Demand To $7 Billion appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
Edgevana: $700 Million AI Infrastructure Agreements Bring Committed Demand To $7 Billion
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 3:26 PM
Edgevana: $700 Million AI Infrastructure Agreements Bring Committed Demand To $7 Billion
Edgevana, an AI computing infrastructure company, has secured more than $700 million in fully committed, multiyear agreements to deploy NVIDIA Blackwell computing systems across North America and Europe. The contracts expand the company’s committed customer demand to approximately $7 billion, with an additional active business pipeline exceeding $20 billion.
The agreements involve take-or-pay commitments under which customers contract for computing capacity over multiple years.
Edgevana intends to deploy NVIDIA B300 GPUs and GB300 systems through its distributed data center infrastructure.
The company is developing a model that combines existing power availability, data center facilities, computing equipment, and high-speed network connectivity.
By coordinating these resources across multiple locations, Edgevana aims to accelerate the delivery of production-ready AI computing capacity.
The company says its approach can bring tens of megawatts of high-density AI infrastructure online within approximately 90 to 120 days.
Traditional data center development projects can require substantially longer timelines because of challenges involving land acquisition, utility connections, power infrastructure, equipment procurement, and construction.
Edgevana’s strategy centers on identifying locations where power and other essential infrastructure are already available.
The company then coordinates deployment of computing systems across its network, creating what it describes as a virtual campus.
This approach allows customers to access distributed infrastructure through a unified management environment.
Edgevana believes the model is particularly relevant as AI workloads shift from centralized model training toward inference applications supporting active users and business systems.
Inference workloads can require low latency, reliable network connectivity, and geographically distributed computing resources.
These requirements create opportunities for infrastructure providers capable of deploying AI compute closer to end users.
Edgevana’s experience includes providing low-latency infrastructure for high-frequency trading and supporting edge computing operations for two major hyperscale technology companies.
The company is applying those capabilities to the deployment of advanced AI accelerators.
Its global infrastructure network includes 17 operational data center locations, with another 10 sites under active development.
According to Edgevana, platforms supported by its infrastructure serve more than 10,000 downstream enterprise customers.
The company’s business model combines long-term energy supply arrangements, access to GPU computing equipment, and committed customer contracts.
By securing customer demand before deployment, Edgevana seeks to reduce financial exposure and improve capital efficiency.
The approach is also intended to help customers avoid delays associated with constructing entirely new data centers.
Edgevana believes pre-energized infrastructure can provide a competitive advantage as demand for high-performance AI computing increases.
Power availability has become an important constraint in the development of large AI data centers.
Companies seeking to deploy substantial computing capacity must secure reliable electricity supply while coordinating physical infrastructure and network requirements.
Edgevana’s platform is designed to address these challenges through coordinated deployment across multiple sites.
The latest $700 million in agreements will support deployment of next-generation NVIDIA computing systems in North America and Europe.
The company’s broader $7 billion in committed demand reflects customer contracts, while its more than $20 billion pipeline represents potential additional business rather than completed commitments.
Founded in 2019, Edgevana intends to continue expanding its network and accelerating deployment of AI infrastructure.
The company is positioning its distributed model as an alternative to relying exclusively on large, centralized data center campuses.
By combining available power, high-performance computing equipment, and network infrastructure, Edgevana aims to reduce deployment timelines and support customers requiring dedicated AI capacity.
KEY QUOTES:
“We stayed in stealth through the initial training boom on purpose, and in many ways, we still operate that way because our model isn’t obvious to the broader market. Training rewards centralized mega–campuses, but inference is live production traffic. As performance demands increase, it plays directly into our core strengths. We cut our teeth delivering ultra-low latency for high-frequency trading and managing edge production for two of the world’s largest hyperscalers. Now that AI is pivoting to inference, the market has come to us.”
Ryan Fay, Co-CEO Of Edgevana
“The defining constraint on AI isn’t algorithms or software, it’s physical, heavy-duty infrastructure. While the market focused exclusively on mega-gigawatt campuses, we spent years quietly securing the power, land, and compute required to bring infrastructure closer to the end user. Getting high-performance GPUs to the edge reliably and at scale is incredibly difficult. As our name suggests, Edgevana makes edge deployment seamless.”
Subhan Jahromi, Co-CEO Of Edgevana

candidates.title: Peloton: $700 Million Senior Secured Notes Offering Upsized From $600 Million As Part Of Debt Refinancing
candidates.snippet:
Peloton Interactive has announced the pricing of an upsized $700 million senior secured notes offering carrying an annual interest rate of 8.625% and maturing in 2032. The offering, increased from an originally announced $600 million, is part of a broader refinancing initiative that also includes a proposed $200 million revolving credit facility.
The post Peloton: $700 Million Senior Secured Notes Offering Upsized From $600 Million As Part Of Debt Refinancing appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
Peloton: $700 Million Senior Secured Notes Offering Upsized From $600 Million As Part Of Debt Refinancing
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 8:20 AM
Peloton: $700 Million Senior Secured Notes Offering Upsized From $600 Million As Part Of Debt Refinancing
Peloton Interactive has announced the pricing of an upsized $700 million senior secured notes offering carrying an annual interest rate of 8.625% and maturing in 2032. The offering, increased from an originally announced $600 million, is part of a broader refinancing initiative that also includes a proposed $200 million revolving credit facility.
The New York-based connected fitness company expects the notes offering to generate approximately $700 million in gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions, and other transaction expenses.
The transaction is expected to settle on November 20, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions.
Peloton intends to use the net proceeds, together with existing cash, to repay all outstanding borrowings under its current $1 billion five-year term loan facility.
The existing term loan agreement will be terminated following repayment.
The refinancing is designed to restructure Peloton’s debt obligations by replacing its outstanding term loans with senior secured notes carrying a maturity date in 2032.
The notes will represent senior secured obligations of the company, meaning they will benefit from specified collateral arrangements and rank according to the terms established in the financing documents.
The annual interest rate of 8.625% determines the stated interest expense associated with the notes.
At the full $700 million principal amount, the stated annual interest obligation would total approximately $60.4 million before considering any applicable adjustments or other financing costs.
The refinancing also includes Peloton’s proposed entry into a new $200 million revolving credit facility with a five-year term.
A revolving credit facility allows a company to borrow, repay, and potentially borrow again within an established credit limit, subject to the agreement’s terms.
Such facilities can provide financial flexibility for working capital needs, operating expenses, and other corporate requirements.
Peloton’s proposed revolving facility would complement its longer-term debt financing by providing an additional source of potential liquidity.
However, the company emphasized that completion of the senior secured notes offering is not dependent on entering into the new revolving credit facility.
The notes offering is also not conditioned on repayment of the existing term loan facility.
These provisions allow the offering to close independently of the other components of the broader refinancing initiative.
Expanded Offering And Use Of Proceeds
Peloton increased the offering from $600 million to $700 million, representing an additional $100 million in planned debt issuance.
The expansion provides additional proceeds that can be applied toward the company’s refinancing requirements.
Peloton plans to combine the proceeds with cash on hand to repay the remaining loans outstanding under its existing term loan facility and cover associated transaction expenses.
The announced $1 billion figure refers to the size of the existing facility rather than a confirmed amount currently outstanding.
Consequently, the company has not specified the precise cash contribution required to complete the repayment.
Following the refinancing, any remaining net proceeds may be used for general corporate purposes.
Potential uses include working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions, and other business opportunities.
Peloton also identified possible repurchases of its Class A common stock among the permitted uses of remaining proceeds.
These potential applications provide flexibility for management to allocate capital according to future corporate priorities.
The company’s financing plan reflects an effort to manage its capital structure while preserving resources for ongoing operations and strategic initiatives.
By extending a portion of its debt obligations through 2032, Peloton is seeking to establish a longer-term financing structure.
The company has not announced specific acquisitions, capital expenditure projects, or share repurchases associated with any remaining proceeds.
Private Placement Structure
The senior secured notes are being offered through a private placement rather than a registered public securities offering.
Eligible purchasers include qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A of the Securities Act of 1933.
The offering is also available to certain investors outside the United States pursuant to Regulation S.
These provisions establish the regulatory framework for distributing the notes to eligible institutional and international investors.
The financing remains subject to customary closing conditions.
Peloton’s expanded $700 million debt offering and proposed $200 million revolving credit facility represent significant components of its broader refinancing strategy.
The transactions are intended to replace existing term loan obligations, extend the company’s debt maturity profile, and provide additional financial flexibility as it manages its capital structure and future business requirements.

candidates.snippet: Uforce Raises $700M in Series A Funding to Expand Ukraine-Focused Autonomous Defense Production AI Insider
candidates.text:
Physical AI · Defence & Autonomous Systems
Uforce Raises $700M in Series A Funding to Expand Ukraine-Focused Autonomous Defense Production
By Greg Bock · 13 November 2026 · 3 min read
Credit: Uforce
Insider Brief
Ukraine-founded defense technology company Uforce raised $700 million in Series A funding at a $6 billion valuation to expand production of autonomous military systems for Ukraine and allied nations.
The round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the UK National Wealth Fund, with participation from the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund and investors including Menlo Ventures, Xantium and Hiro Capital.
Uforce plans to expand manufacturing of its MAGURA maritime drones, NEMESIS aerial drones, LIUT ground vehicles and PREDATOR turret systems across allied countries, while supporting operations and research in Ukraine.
Ukraine-founded defense technology company Uforce has raised $700 million in Series A funding at a $6 billion valuation to expand production of autonomous military systems for Ukraine and allied nations.
The round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the UK National Wealth Fund, with participation from the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, according to Uforce . Other investors included Menlo Ventures , Xantium and Hiro Capital, while existing backers Shield Capital , Ballistic Ventures , Lakestar and Squadra increased their stakes.
Headquartered in London, with major operations in Kyiv and Washington, Uforce develops uncrewed systems for air, land and sea operations, along with AI software for coordinating and controlling them. The company said the funding will support manufacturing expansion across the United States, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, while maintaining production and supplies for Ukrainian forces despite continued attacks in Ukraine.
Expanding Autonomous Defense Production
Uforce plans to increase production and research and development across four product families: MAGURA uncrewed surface vessels, NEMESIS aerial drones, LIUT ground vehicles and PREDATOR turret systems.
The company also anticipates working with partners in allied countries to adapt existing maritime and automotive manufacturing facilities for defense production.
Uforce recently announced a partnership with ReconCraft to expand U.S. manufacturing of its Maritime Autonomous Guard Unmanned Robotic Apparatus (MAGURA) vessels. It also plans to build on relationships within NATO and Joint Expeditionary Force networks and continue participating as a founding member of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance.
CEO Oleg Rogynskyy said the financing will help increase production for Ukraine while providing allied nations with autonomous systems they can deploy, integrate and maintain.
“The war in Ukraine has shown that in an increasingly volatile world, effective defense requires systems that can keep improving as threats change,” noted Rogynskyy. “Governments and the technology ecosystem need to come together to develop cost-effective, interoperable, and autonomous platforms that are ready to fight now, and can evolve to meet future needs.”
Investment Supports Ukrainian Operations
The U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund’s participation will specifically support Uforce’s operations in Ukraine, including staffing, research and development, and new products. The fund was established jointly by the United States and Ukraine to attract investment into reconstruction, economic development and strategic industries.
Uforce also announced that retired Gen. Christopher G. Cavoli, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe and a partner at Valor Equity Partners, will join its board of directors.

candidates.text:
African tech startups raised $684M in first nine months of 2026, led by Nairobi with $277M following Spiro’s $215M Series E
Dated: November 9, 2026
African tech companies raised $684 million in the first nine months of 2026, according to a Tracxn Technologies report cited by AU-Startups, representing a 30% year-on-year increase from $527 million in the same period of 2025. The total was deployed across 100 funding rounds, slightly fewer than the 103 rounds recorded the year before.
The report found that Nairobi led African startup fundraising, attracting $277 million—about 41% of the continent-wide total for the period. The concentration is largely linked to a single transaction: Spiro’s $215 million Series E round in Nairobi, which followed the company’s broader $270 million funding round completed in June 2026.
Funding growth alongside fewer deals
While overall capital increased, the number of rounds fell by 3% year on year, signaling a more selective environment for investors. The report describes a trend in which capital is increasingly directed toward larger transactions and businesses demonstrating clear commercial potential, rather than earlier-stage ventures.
For early-stage founders—particularly those at pre-seed and seed—this environment can make fundraising more challenging, the report suggests, as investors focus on later-stage traction and scale-ready models.
Spiro’s Series E and the shift toward infrastructure-style cleantech
Spiro, an electric vehicle and battery-swapping company, finalized its $270 million funding round in June 2026, with $215 million of that amount coming as equity financing. The Series E included participation from institutional investors Impact Fund Denmark and Equitane, according to the report.
The company operates across seven African countries, including Kenya, Rwanda and Nigeria. Spiro says it has deployed more than 100,000 electric vehicles and established over 2,500 battery-swapping stations on the continent, framing the investment as support for scaling electric mobility infrastructure.
The funding also reflects a broader pattern described by the report: greater attention to asset-heavy, infrastructure-style businesses in mobility and clean energy. It notes that this emphasis contrasts with earlier funding cycles that often favored software-only models, and it highlights an increased use of debt and blended finance alongside equity.
Nairobi’s dominance and other emerging hubs
Nairobi’s $277 million share in the first nine months of 2026 rose sharply from $61 million in the same period of 2025, with the increase attributed almost entirely to Spiro’s $270 million contribution to the city’s total. Other hubs cited include Cairo, which raised $126 million, and Abuja, which attracted $52 million.
In Abuja, the report states that the funding was driven entirely by Terra across three seed rounds. The geographic concentration matters because it suggests that growth in headline capital does not automatically translate into evenly distributed investment opportunities across Africa’s ecosystems.
The article also notes discrepancies between data providers: Tracxn reported $684 million, while other analyses pointed to higher totals—TechCabal Insights estimated $2.49 billion across 315 deals, and Condia reported about $2.45 billion in disclosed funding for the same period. The differences are attributed to varying inclusion criteria across trackers.
What this means for African operators
The reporting frames the 2026 fundraising pattern as a call for African founders to recalibrate strategy toward revenue-generating models and operational efficiency, particularly as investors appear to favor later-stage and infrastructure-heavy sectors. It also points to the growing relevance of debt financing, where requirements such as collateral and predictable cash flows can become more important.
For regulators and development stakeholders, the report’s emphasis on uneven capital flows across cities and sectors suggests a need for policies that support a more diversified innovation ecosystem—one that extends beyond a small number of standout deals and hubs.
The transaction also provides Spiro additional runway, the report states, to scale its electric mobility and energy infrastructure across its existing seven African markets and to expand into additional countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia.

Initiative or programme: Tracxn Technologies-reported African tech startup funding trends (capital raised and number of rounds)
Lead organization: Tracxn Technologies (report cited by AU-Startups)
Partners: Impact Fund Denmark; Equitane (listed as participants in Spiro’s Series E)
Funding amount: $684M raised across 100 rounds (first nine months of 2026); Nairobi $277M; Spiro Series E equity $215M (within a $270M funding round)
Geographic focus: Africa, with Nairobi (Kenya) as the leading hub; other hubs mentioned include Cairo and Abuja
Target groups: The reporting focuses on African tech startups and investors; it highlights implications for pre-seed and seed founders
Duration or timeline: First nine months of 2026 (data period); Spiro round closed in June 2026
Expected reach or outcomes: Spiro states it plans to use the funding to scale electric mobility and battery-swapping infrastructure across seven African countries and expand to the Democratic Republic of Congo and Ethiopia

African tech fundraising trends can influence how quickly innovations—particularly those tied to infrastructure such as clean mobility—reach real-world use. Twelve Secures $645 Million to Revolutionize Sustainable Aviation Fuel
Twelve raised $645 million, led by TPG Rise Climate, to scale technology that turns captured CO2, water, and renewable energy into E-Jet sustainable aviation fuel. The round funds AirPlant One in Moses Lake, Washington.
Written by Causeartist
Tagged
Carbon Climate Tech Climate Change Funding Round Sustainable Aviation
Last updated: November 13, 2026
Photo credit: Causeartist
Featured companies
Twelve A world made from air.
Key takeaways
Twelve announced a $645 million funding round led by TPG Rise Climate to scale carbon-to-fuel technology.
The financing combines $400 million in project equity from TPG Rise Climate, about $200 million in Series C funding, and $45 million in credit facilities.
Series C was co-led by Capricorn Investment Group and Pulse Fund, with DCVC, Munich Re Ventures, and Emerson Collective participating.
AirPlant One, Twelve's sustainable aviation fuel facility in Moses Lake, Washington, was scheduled to start operations in 2025 and produce E-Jet fuel from biogenic CO2, water, and renewable energy.
Twelve says the fuel is projected to cut lifecycle emissions by up to 90% versus conventional fossil jet fuel, with future plants supplying Alaska Airlines and International Airlines Group.
Twelve, an innovative carbon transformation company, has announced a $645 million funding round led by TPG Rise Climate.
This funding is set to propel Twelve's mission of converting captured carbon dioxide into valuable chemicals, fuels, and essential products traditionally derived from fossil fuels.
The financing includes a strategic blend of $400 million in project equity from TPG Rise Climate , $200 million in Series C financing, and an additional $45 million in credit facilities from prominent renewable energy sector funders, marking it as one of the largest rounds in the e-fuels industry to date.
About Twelve
Twelve is a leader in carbon transformation technology, dedicated to eliminating global emissions and forging a fossil-free future.
Through their Opus™ Carbon Transformation System , Twelve converts CO2, water, and renewable energy into essential hydrocarbons used in chemicals, materials, and fuels, displacing the need for fossil fuels across industrial and everyday product supply chains.
Transforming Aviation with Sustainable Solutions

"Our financing strategy has been to build a comprehensive capital stack that enables us to deliver product to customers at scale while continually driving down costs," said Nicholas Flanders, Chief Executive Officer at Twelve. "We're proud to work with visionary financing partners and collaborators who share our commitment to deploying first of a kind technologies that address climate change at scale."
The funding accelerates Twelve's efforts to decarbonize manufacturing, initially targeting emissions from aviation . A key milestone for the company is the completion of AirPlant™ One, Twelve's pioneering sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility located in Moses Lake, Washington.
Scheduled to commence operations in 2025, AirPlant One will utilize Twelve's patented technology to produce E-Jet® fuel from biogenic CO2, water, and renewable energy sources.
This approach is projected to achieve lifecycle emissions up to 90% lower than conventional fossil jet fuel.
Strategic Partnerships and Market Expansion
TPG Rise Climate's commitment of up to $400 million in project equity underscores their confidence in Twelve's technology and its potential to revolutionize SAF production.
Future AirPlants will supply E-Jet fuel to key customers like Alaska Airlines and International Aviation Group (IAG), parent company of British Airways.
TPG Rise Climate, launched in 2021 as a $7.3 billion climate impact fund, focuses on investments that drive substantial environmental benefits.
Broadening Investment Support
In addition to TPG's significant investment, Twelve raised approximately $200 million in its Series C round, co-led by Capricorn Investment Group and Pulse Fund .
Existing investors, including DCVC , Munich Re Ventures , and Emerson Collective , also participated, highlighting their continued confidence in Twelve's innovative approach.

UFORCE, the Ukrainian company behind the MAGURA sea drones , has raised €630 million ($700 million) . The round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the UK National Wealth Fund (NWF). New investors include the US–Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF), Menlo Ventures, Xantium and Hiro Capital. Existing backers Shield Capital, Ballistic Ventures, Lakestar and Squadra increased their stakes.
Worker.ai , a company operating system for small businesses backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev, has acquired DeltaGen , a Prague-based startup that builds real-time voice AI. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. All three of DeltaGen’s founders are moving to Worker. DeltaGen’s team of around 10 people will stay in Prague.
Vilnius-based Biomatter , which uses AI to design enzymes, has raised an oversubscribed €16.2 million ($18 million) Series A . The round was led by Astanor , with existing investors UVC Partners, Inventure and Metaplanet also taking part. Founded in 2018, Biomatter designs enzymes by starting from the chemical reaction a customer needs .
Czech medtech startup Kardi AI has raised €5.3 million in a Series A round led by German healthtech fund Callisto Health. According to the company, this is the largest round a Czech medtech startup has raised to date. Česká spořitelna and Slovenská sporiteňa joined through their corporate venture programmes. Earlier backers BrightCap Ventures, Purple Ventures, DEPO Ventures and Garage Angels also put in money. After the round, Kardi AI is valued at €23 million.
Hedepy, the Prague-based online therapy platform operating in nine European countries, has secured €4 million in venture debt from Orbit Capital to fund acquisitions and expand into clinical care and AI tools — aiming to consolidate Europe’s fragmented mental health market.
Valkyrie Dynamics, the Ukrainian-Lithuanian defense startup building a 100-gram radar seeker that lets low-cost drones intercept targets through cloud and fog, raised €1 million in a pre-seed round led by Paris-based venture studio Hexa — developed and field-tested alongside operators in Kyiv.
Romanian edtech company Kinderpedia , which has developed a management and communication platform for schools and kindergartens, has secured a €500,000 investment from BCR Seed Starter , the corporate venture capital arm of BCR. The investment completes Kinderpedia’s €2.7 million funding round , led by Polish fund Simpact Ventures, with participation from existing investors Early Game Ventures and ROCA X.
Italian-founded legal AI company Lexroom has launched lex , an AI-powered personal assistant for lawyers accessible through WhatsApp, just two months after acquiring Bulgarian legal tech company Praven Intelekt . The new product aims to help legal professionals manage administrative tasks, conduct legal research, and prepare documents directly through a messaging app.
New funds launching
BlackPeak Capital , a private equity firm that invests growth equity in Southeast Europe, has announced the first close of BlackPeak Southeast Europe Growth Equity Fund II (BPSEEF II) at €125 million . That is almost as much as the €126 million its first fund raised in total. The Luxembourg-domiciled fund is targeting €150 million, has a hard cap of €200 million, and expects to hold its final close in 2027. BPSEEF II will invest between €7 million and €20 million per deal in fast-growing companies. Its primary markets are Bulgaria, Romania, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia, and it may also invest opportunistically in Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, the Baltic states and other Western Balkan countries.
Polish venture capital firm Bitspiration VC is preparing to launch a new €50 million biotech fund , supported by investors including Snowflake co-founder Marcin Żukowski and Tomasz Onyszko, co-founder of Predica and CTO of Morning Brew. The firm has already secured investor commitments for a first close of €15–20 million, scheduled for November.

Funding
Apollo Raises $600 Million With 7.550% Junior Notes Due 2056
Published
November 9, 2026
By
Nikhil Rao Bonds, Credit & Rates, AI Research Agent
Add Securities.io to your preferred sources on Google
Table Of Contents
Apollo Global Management ( N7I.DE ) announced on November 9, 2026 that it priced $600 million of fixed-rate resettable junior subordinated notes and estimated net proceeds of approximately $594 million after the underwriting discount but before offering expenses. The notes carry a 7.550% initial coupon and mature on December 15, 2056.
The final pricing terms set the public price at 100.000% of principal, plus accrued interest, if any. Settlement is expected on November 13, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions. Apollo intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, including funding its previously announced investment in Mubadala Capital Asset Management, and to pay related fees and expenses. J.P. Morgan, BofA Securities, Morgan Stanley ( MS ) and Wells Fargo Securities are the joint book-running managers.
Guarantees Leave Structural Subordination in Place
The securities are junior subordinated unsecured notes, ranking behind current and future senior indebtedness and structurally behind the liabilities of subsidiaries that do not guarantee them. Six holding companies will fully and unconditionally guarantee the notes jointly and severally on an unsecured subordinated basis: Apollo Asset Management, Apollo Principal Holdings A, B and C, AMH Holdings (Delaware), and Apollo Management Holdings.
Athene and its subsidiaries, Apollo-managed funds and businesses generating significant fees are not guaranteeing the notes. The preliminary prospectus describes the issuer and guarantors as holding companies dependent on transfers from their subsidiaries. As a result, the guarantees sit at intermediate holding companies and do not remove the prior claims of creditors at the significant fee-generating operating businesses.
As of September 30, 2026, the issuer and guarantors had $4.684 billion of senior indebtedness and $1.078 billion of indebtedness ranking on a parity with the notes. The notes do not limit additional borrowing by Apollo or its subsidiaries, including borrowing senior to this issue.
The expected ratings are A3 from Moody’s and BBB+ from both S&P and Fitch. Apollo does not intend to list the notes on an exchange or quotation system, and there was no established public market for them.
Coupon Resets and Deferral Preserve Issuer Flexibility
That initial coupon applies until December 15, 2036, the first reset date. For each subsequent reset period, the rate will equal the five-year U.S. Treasury rate as of the most recent reset determination date plus 2.672%. Interest is scheduled semiannually on June 15 and December 15, beginning June 15, 2027, subject to Apollo’s deferral right. The structure fixes the coupon for the initial ten-year period and then resets it from Treasury yields while retaining the spread.
Apollo may defer interest for up to five consecutive years on one or more occasions. Interest continues accruing during deferral, and deferred payments accrue additional interest at the then-applicable note rate, compounded semiannually to the extent permitted by law. During a deferral period, Apollo and the guarantors generally face restrictions on payments on, or redemptions and purchases of, their equity and parity or junior debt, subject to enumerated exceptions. Deferral therefore postpones cash payments rather than canceling the interest obligation.
Apollo may redeem some or all of the notes at 100% of principal plus accrued and unpaid interest during the three months before and including the first reset date or any later reset date. Separate rights permit whole-issue redemption within 120 days of a tax redemption event at the same price or a rating agency event at 102% of principal, in each case plus accrued and unpaid interest. Holders do not have an option to require redemption before maturity.
Mubadala Transaction Provides the Named Use of Proceeds
The October 26, 2026 transaction announcement said Apollo will take a minority equity stake in Mubadala Capital and commit capital across its investment strategies. Additional strategic investors will also join as minority shareholders. Apollo and those investors are expected to commit an aggregate $5 billion to Mubadala Capital’s strategies at initial close, a combined amount rather than an Apollo-only commitment.
Mubadala Investment Company will remain the majority shareholder, while Mubadala Capital will continue to operate independently with its own governance structure and its existing management retaining full authority over investment decisions and operations.
Mubadala Capital reported that its core alternatives business managed and invested more than $60 billion across five strategies. The October announcement targeted a fourth-quarter 2026 closing, subject to regulatory and legal approvals.
The offering pairs long-dated funding and a named strategic use with considerable issuer flexibility through reset-date redemptions and interest deferral. The offset is in the creditor claim: repayment ranks behind senior debt and non-guarantor subsidiary liabilities, while the six guarantees come from holding companies rather than Athene or the businesses generating significant fees.

OneWater Marine: $547 Million Inventory Financing Facility And Term Loan Extended Through 2029
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 8:19 AM
OneWater Marine: $547 Million Inventory Financing Facility And Term Loan Extended Through 2029
OneWater Marine, one of the largest premium marine retailers in the United States, has amended its senior secured term loan and floor plan credit facilities to extend their maturities by two years while increasing its inventory financing capacity by $50 million. The amendments raise the company’s available floor plan financing capacity to as much as $547 million, providing additional financial flexibility as OneWater focuses on inventory management and balance-sheet improvements.
Under the amended agreements, the maturity of OneWater’s senior secured term loan has been extended to July 31, 2029, while its floor plan credit facility will now mature on March 1, 2029.
The extensions provide additional time before the company must address the scheduled maturities of these financing arrangements.
Truist Bank continues to lead the senior secured term loan facility, while Wells Fargo remains the lead lender for the floor plan financing arrangement. The expansion of inventory financing capacity also includes the addition of a new lender to the lending syndicate.
Both facilities remain subject to customary financial and non-financial covenants.
Expanded Inventory Financing Capacity
The increase in floor plan financing capacity is particularly relevant to OneWater’s retail operations, which depend on maintaining inventories of new and pre-owned boats across its dealership network.
Floor plan financing is a specialized form of credit commonly used by vehicle and marine retailers to finance inventory before products are sold to customers.
Rather than using operating cash to purchase every boat held in inventory, retailers can use these financing arrangements to support the acquisition and management of available products.
As inventory is sold, the associated financing obligations are generally repaid according to the terms of the lending agreements.
This structure allows retailers to maintain product availability while managing working capital requirements.
OneWater’s amended agreement increases its maximum inventory financing capacity from approximately $497 million to $547 million.
The additional $50 million provides potential borrowing capacity to support inventory requirements across the company’s operations.
However, the expanded facility represents available financing capacity rather than an immediate increase in cash or an indication that the entire amount has been borrowed.
The company believes the additional flexibility will help it manage inventory levels more effectively as it navigates challenging conditions in the marine retail market.
Focus On Balance-Sheet Strengthening
The amendments reflect OneWater’s efforts to improve its financial flexibility and extend its debt maturity profile.
By pushing the maturities of both facilities into 2029, the company has reduced near-term refinancing pressures associated with these arrangements.
Management indicated that the changes are part of a broader strategy to strengthen the balance sheet and maintain appropriate inventory levels.
Inventory management is an important consideration for marine retailers because boats represent relatively expensive products that can require substantial financing.
Demand can also be influenced by consumer confidence, interest rates, financing availability, and broader economic conditions.
Maintaining an appropriate balance between available inventory and expected customer demand can help retailers manage borrowing requirements and operating expenses.
OneWater expects the amended facilities to provide greater flexibility as it enters fiscal 2027.
The company intends to remain focused on maintaining suitable inventory levels while continuing efforts to strengthen its financial position.
OneWater’s Nationwide Retail Operations
Headquartered in Buford, Georgia, OneWater Marine operates 88 retail locations and six distribution centers and warehouses across 17 states.
The company also maintains multiple online marketplaces supporting its retail activities.
Its geographic footprint includes several states ranked among the nation’s largest markets for marine retail expenditures.
OneWater sells new and pre-owned boats while providing a range of related products and services.
Its revenue sources include boat sales, financing and insurance products, parts and accessories, maintenance, repairs, and other marine services.
This diversified operating model allows the company to generate revenue from both boat purchases and ongoing customer relationships.
The amended lending arrangements support the financing infrastructure underlying these operations.
With its term loan maturity extended to July 2029, floor plan maturity extended to March 2029, and inventory financing capacity increased to $547 million, OneWater has secured additional time and flexibility to manage its capital structure.
The company plans to use that flexibility to support disciplined inventory management while addressing the challenges affecting the marine retail industry.
KEY QUOTE:
“Extending maturities for both facilities and expanding our floor plan capacity reflect our progress in strengthening our balance sheet and the continued support of our lending partners. The amendments give us added flexibility to effectively manage our inventory as we navigate this challenging retail environment. As we move into fiscal 2027, we remain focused on maintaining proper inventory levels and fortifying the balance sheet.”
Jack Ezzell, Chief Operating Officer And Chief Financial Officer Of OneWater Marine

JBS has agreed to acquire Brazilian consumer products company Flora for $542 million, expanding into beauty and personal care while adding to its household cleaning business.
Flora is owned by J&F Group, JBS’s controlling shareholder. The transaction therefore brings a business from its controlling shareholder into the company.
The purchase includes assumed debt, with $367 million in equity consideration payable entirely through JBS treasury Class A shares, Brazilian depositary receipts or a combination of both.
JBS expects no change to its net leverage ratio based on Flora’s earnings contribution and the transaction structure.
Flora generated R$2.9 billion, approximately $531 million, in annual net revenue for the 12 months ended September 2026. Its brands include Minuano, Francis, Neutrox and OX.
The company operates five factories, seven distribution centers and a research and development center, employing more than 4,200 people.
Flora originated as JBS’s hygiene and cleaning division before separating in 2007. The businesses have maintained commercial ties, including JBS’s supply of beef tallow for cleaning and hygiene products.
JBS intends to connect its ingredients and collagen capabilities with Flora’s brands, distribution and consumer products expertise.
The acquisition complements Genu-in, established in 2022 to develop collagen applications, and research activities at JBS Biotech and BioTech Foods.
JBS also announced an $11 million acquisition of Canal Rural, an agribusiness-focused Brazilian media company, on a cash-free, debt-free basis. The final price will be adjusted for closing net debt.
Both acquisitions are expected to close in December 2026, subject to customary conditions.
The transactions broaden JBS’s activities beyond its global food portfolio, with Flora providing an established platform for expansion into adjacent consumer categories.

By John Dyer Posted in Equities

Paladin Energy Ltd (ASX:PDN, TSX:PDN) ( Paladin or the Company ) announces the successful completion of its fully underwritten A$525 million equity raising, comprising (i) an A$499 million ASX institutional placement of new Paladin fully paid ordinary shares ( Shares ) ( ASX Placement ), and (ii) a Canadian “bought deal” private placement to raise C$25 million (~A$26 million) pursuant to the Listed Issuer Financing Exemption (as defined herein) ( TSX Bought Deal ) (together, the Offer ). 1
As announced on 12 November 2026, Paladin also intends to invite Eligible Shareholders (as defined herein) to participate in a non-underwritten Share Purchase Plan to acquire Shares at the same price as the ASX Placement to raise up to a further A$50 million (before costs) ( SPP ).
Highlights
Successful bookbuild for a fully underwritten equity raising to raise A$525 million (before costs), comprising:
A fully underwritten ASX Placement of approximately 64.0 million new Shares priced at A$7.80 per Share to raise ~A$499 million (before costs); and
A fully underwritten TSX Bought Deal of approximately 3.3 million new Shares priced at C$7.62 per Share to raise ~A$26 million (C$25 million) (before costs)

Opportunity for Eligible Shareholders with registered addresses in Australia or New Zealand to participate via a non-underwritten SPP to raise up to a further A$50 million (before costs)
The equity raising positions Paladin for its next phase of growth, funding the ongoing development of the Patterson Lake South Project ( PLS Project ), potential resource growth and mine life extension at Triple R, and advancing exploration opportunities across the broader Athabasca Basin region portfolio.
Paladin MD and CEO Paul Hemburrow said:
“We are pleased with the support received from high-quality existing and new institutional investors for the equity raising. This capital allows us to maintain the strong momentum we have generated at the PLS Project as it advances towards targeted first production in 2031 and accelerate exploration and growth across Paladin’s broader Athabasca Basin region tenure package.”

The SPP will be conducted at the offer price of A$7.80. The SPP is targeted to raise up to A$50 million (before costs) and is not underwritten.
Paladin reserves the right (in its absolute discretion) to scale back applications under the SPP if demand exceeds A$50 million, raise a higher amount or close the SPP at an earlier date. candidates.text:
HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 9:47 AM
HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments
HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital (HASI) has priced a $500 million registered public offering of green junior subordinated notes bearing an interest rate of 7.850% and maturing in 2057. The financing will support the company’s sustainable infrastructure investment strategy, including projects involving renewable energy, storage, and energy efficiency.
The offering was priced on November 9, 2026, with settlement expected on November 24, subject to customary closing conditions.
HASI estimates that net proceeds will total approximately $493.3 million after underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.
The notes will be guaranteed on a subordinated basis by several affiliated entities.
These include Hannon Armstrong Sustainable Infrastructure, Hannon Armstrong Capital, and certain related holding companies.
Junior subordinated notes generally rank below senior indebtedness in the order of claims against a borrower.
The structure provides HASI with long-term financing while establishing the specific priority of the securities relative to other obligations.
HASI intends to use the immediate proceeds to temporarily repay portions of existing borrowings.
These may include obligations under its Standalone Commercial Paper Program, unsecured credit facility, and Credit-Enhanced Commercial Paper Program.
The company will allocate an amount of cash equal to the offering’s net proceeds toward acquiring, investing in, or refinancing eligible green projects.
Projects may include those with qualifying disbursements made during the 12 months preceding the issuance date.
The company may also allocate funds toward eligible projects with disbursements expected within two years following issuance.
Before the full amount has been allocated to qualifying investments, HASI may retain funds in short-term interest-bearing instruments or apply them toward temporary debt repayment.
This structure is intended to provide flexibility in managing the financing while maintaining a commitment to eligible sustainable infrastructure investments.
HASI invests across multiple categories of energy transition infrastructure.
Its portfolio includes utility-scale solar projects, onshore wind generation, energy storage, distributed solar and battery systems, renewable natural gas, and energy efficiency.
The company manages more than $19 billion in assets.
Its investment strategy combines financing expertise with long-term relationships involving energy developers and infrastructure operators.
Renewable energy and storage projects can require substantial upfront capital before generating recurring revenue.
Infrastructure investors provide financing through debt, equity, and structured capital arrangements to support these developments.
HASI’s business focuses on deploying capital into projects that offer financial returns alongside measurable environmental benefits.
The latest green notes offering provides additional financial resources for these activities.
It also expands the company’s long-term financing through securities scheduled to mature in 2057.
A group of investment banks is serving as joint book-running managers, including Mizuho Securities, BofA Securities, Goldman Sachs, Truist Securities, Barclays, BMO Capital Markets, Credit Agricole, ING, KeyBanc, M&T Securities, Natixis, Rabo Securities, Scotiabank, and SMBC Nikko Securities.
The offering reflects HASI’s continued use of capital markets financing to support its investment program.
By raising $500 million through green junior subordinated notes, the company aims to fund eligible sustainable infrastructure assets while managing its existing borrowing arrangements.

Torus launches Foundry, raises $500M for AI inference boom
Torus raised $500 million led by Magnetar to scale Foundry, modular AI inference sites built at its SLC factory.
Edited and Reviewed By
Ashley Okawa

Torus, a Salt Lake City energy infrastructure manufacturer, launched Foundry, a prefabricated modular AI compute system, and raised $500 million in growth capital led by Magnetar on Nov. 11. Participating investors include ICONIQ, Origin Ventures, Ridgeline Partners and Trinity Capital.
Foundry packages power, storage, cooling, networking and compute into a single modular unit that installs at existing commercial and industrial sites in 12 to 16 weeks, a fraction of the multiyear timeline typical for a hyperscale data center campus. Each site delivers 1 to 20 megawatts of capacity, with the smallest unit roughly the size of a cargo van. The system taps spare grid capacity that utilities have already allocated to existing sites, avoiding the infrastructure upgrades that often trigger rate increases.
The raise follows a $200 million investment from Magnetar in September 2025 , making this the second nine-figure investment the Evanston, Illinois-based asset manager has made in Torus in just over a year.
Betting on inference over training
The launch targets a shift in AI economics: Data center demand for inference, the process of running trained models rather than building them, is projected to grow at a 35% compound annual rate through 2030, compared with 22% for training, according to McKinsey . Unlike training, inference runs continuously and benefits from sitting close to users, pulling demand toward smaller, distributed sites rather than centralized campuses.
“Most providers are bringing power to the chips. Foundry brings the chips to power,” says Nate Walkingshaw, founder and CEO of Torus, who previously served as chief experience officer at Pluralsight before founding Torus in 2021.
“One of the biggest challenges in scaling AI infrastructure is access to power, and the solution isn’t simply generating more of it, but making better use of what’s already available,” says Dave Snyderman, managing partner and global head of alternative credit and fixed income at Magnetar. “Torus has spent years building the energy infrastructure and expertise to address this challenge. Foundry builds on that foundation by bringing compute to available power, helping unlock capacity within the existing grid.”
Photo courtesy of Torus
Foundry ships in three configurations: a powered shell without GPUs, a turnkey bare-metal unit with GPUs included, and a single-tenant sovereign model for enterprises that want exclusive hardware. Torus launched the product with its first customers, bare-metal GPU cloud provider Hydra Host and an unnamed AI cloud provider, and plans to have more than 47,000 GPUs running in Foundry units by the end of 2027.
Manufacturing scale in Utah
Foundry units are built at GigaOne, Torus’s 545,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Salt Lake City, where the company employs nearly 400 people. GigaOne opened its first production line in early 2026 and added a new line roughly every 21 days through the year; the Foundry line is online and expected to reach 500 megawatts of IT load, with plans to expand to 1 gigawatt.
The $500 million will fund continued expansion of GigaOne along with Torus Reserve and Foundry deployments nationwide. The company says each Foundry unit uses a waterless closed-loop cooling system that requires no water or sewer connection and donates GPU time to medical research through Folding@home.

candidates.title: SoftBank-Led Agile Robots Raises $500M Series F at $8.5B Valuation
candidates.snippet: SoftBank-Led Agile Robots Raises $500M Series F at $8.5B Valuation Wowtale
candidates.text:
A German company that has deployed more than 20,000 industrial robot solutions now has a plant that can build up to 10,000 humanoids a year. Munich-based Physical AI company Agile Robots has raised a $500 million Series F led by SoftBank Group, valuing it at $8.5 billion and bringing total funding to $2 billion.
Agile Robots announced the round on Nov. 12. SoftBank Group led, with NVIDIA, Hitachi Group (Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures) and T.Capital among the participants. The company says the investors span the automotive, artificial intelligence, digital and industrial technology sectors. SoftBank is a longtime backer: its Vision Fund 2 led the company’s $220 million Series C in September 2021 at a valuation above $1 billion, so the new valuation is more than eight times that. According to Bloomberg, a round of about $800 million, with SoftBank anchoring more than $300 million, was under discussion in June, and the round closed smaller at $500 million. Hitachi Ventures also joined Graphon Labs’ $35 million Series A this month.
The company builds humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and hands, and the software and AI models behind them, aimed at automotive, consumer electronics, healthcare and service customers that want to automate tasks that have relied on human dexterity and judgment. It was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and says it has deployed 20,000 industrial robotic solutions across automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. It has more than 3,500 employees from almost 60 countries, including more than 2,000 R&D experts, and over 650 patents, and develops and builds its hardware and software in-house from more than 20,000 square meters of lab space.
Founder and CEO Zhaopeng Chen said the company wants to bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing. The money will go to global expansion, a stronger presence in key markets and more production capacity. Agile Robots plans to strengthen its presence in the United States and speed up development of new robotics applications, while continuing to build out production capacity, including in Germany. A new site opened early this year in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots a year. Dennis Chang, managing partner at SoftBank Investment Advisers, said Agile Robots combines deep robotics expertise with the ability to execute at industrial scale, and that SoftBank looks forward to continuing to partner with Chen’s team.
Acquisitions have widened the business. In November 2023 it took over the operations of insolvent Munich robotics company Franka Emika , which now runs as Franka Robotics and serves as an AI robotics research platform. Last November it announced the acquisition of thyssenkrupp’s Automation Engineering business , and in April it closed the deal . The unit now operates as industrial deployment specialist Krause Automation, and the company said at the time it would add about 650 experts and 10 locations in Europe and North America. BÄR Automation and Idealworks are also subsidiaries, and its humanoid lineup includes Agile ONE. The company has not disclosed revenue.
Humanoid competition is heating up on both sides of the Atlantic. The closest comparison is fellow German company NEURA Robotics , based in Metzingen, which also builds the full stack from cobot arms and mobile platforms to its 4NE1 humanoid and the Neuraverse platform. In June it announced a Series C of up to $1.4 billion led by Tether at a reported valuation of about $7 billion, with the full amount contingent on performance milestones, a different structure from Agile Robots’ $500 million. In the US, Figure AI is valued at $39 billion and has tested its robots at a BMW plant, and Apptronik , partnered with Google DeepMind, raised $935 million in a Series A alone at a $5.3 billion valuation. Agility Robotics has built more than $300 million in multiyear contracts by renting robots to warehouses as a service and is going public through a SPAC merger at a $2.5 billion valuation. While those companies lean first on AI models or specific sites, Agile Robots starts from the manufacturing and delivery experience of 20,000 deployed industrial robot solutions.

candidates.title: Agile Robots Raises $500 Million From SoftBank and Nvidia
candidates.snippet: Agile Robots Raises $500 Million From SoftBank and Nvidia trendingtopics.eu
candidates.text:
Robotics
Agile Robots Raises $500 Million From SoftBank and Nvidia
Jakob Steinschaden , co-produced by AI 12. November 2026, 07:43
© Agile Robots
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
While Europe is still debating whether humanoid robots will ever make it onto the factory floor, SoftBank and Nvidia are putting half a billion dollars on the table for it: Agile Robots, the Munich-based robotics company, has just closed a funding round of $500 million (about €450 million). The round lifts its valuation to $8.5 billion (about €7.6 billion), the German news agency dpa reported.
The Round at a Glance
Hard Facts
Agile Robots
Valuation
$8.5 billion (about €7.6 billion)
Amount
$500 million (about €450 million)
Stage
not disclosed (most recently a Series C in 2021)
Investors
SoftBank Group (lead), Nvidia, Hitachi, T.Capital
Total raised to date
about $2 billion (about €1.8 billion)
Existing investors
including SoftBank Vision Fund and Xiaomi
SoftBank is not a new backer: The Japanese company already led the $220 million Series C in 2021 that made Agile Robots a unicorn. How much SoftBank is contributing this time is not known. The other names are no surprise, either. Nvidia had already announced its investment in Agile Robots in Berlin in October, and the company has been working since September on physical A.I. for manufacturing with Hitachi, which is investing through its venture arm. T.Capital is the investment company of Deutsche Telekom.
What the Money Is For
Zhaopeng Chen, the founder and chief executive, wants to use the capital mainly for three things: entering the U.S. market, new industrial applications and manufacturing in Bavaria. Early this year, Agile Robots opened a new plant in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, that is designed for up to 10,000 humanoid robots a year. The company is taking the technology straight from the lab into industrial series production, Mr. Chen said.
According to The New York Times , the round is also meant to prepare for a possible initial public offering. There is no timetable for that. Physical A.I. could help Europe close its gap with the United States and China in artificial intelligence, Mr. Chen argued there.
What Agile Robots Does
Agile Robots was started in 2018 as a spinoff of the German Aerospace Center, known as DLR, in Oberpfaffenhofen. Mr. Chen had worked there on, among other things, especially sensitive robot hands. Today the company sells almost everything that moves in a factory: robot arms, robot hands and grippers, driverless transport systems, complete production cells and the humanoid robot Agile ONE, along with its own control platform.
By its own account, Agile Robots employs more than 3,500 people at more than 25 sites, over 2,000 of them in development. More than 20,000 automation solutions are installed worldwide, it says, and it holds more than 650 patents. Its customers include large companies in the automotive, consumer electronics, health care and logistics industries.
Agile Robots has also grown through acquisitions, including that of Franka Robotics, a Munich maker of robot arms. For A.I., the company relies on partners: A research partnership with Google DeepMind has been running since the spring, followed in October by a humanoid platform based on Nvidia’s robotics models and a logistics project with Audi. Besides Germany, the company also manufactures in China and India, and its earlier investors include Xiaomi, the Chinese electronics company.
SoftBank Is Buying Its Way Into Robotics
For SoftBank, Agile Robots is one piece of a bigger bet. Masayoshi Son’s company agreed in 2025 to acquire ABB’s robotics division for $5.4 billion (about €4.9 billion) and has taken a large stake in Skild AI, an American start-up working on a universal A.I. model for robots. In that strategy, ABB supplies the bodies and Skild AI the brain.
The Competition
Money is currently flowing into many robot makers. In Germany, Neura Robotics , of Metzingen, raised up to $1.4 billion (about €1.3 billion) in the summer, from investors including Tether, Amazon and, likewise, Nvidia. The Munich start-up RobCo has become a unicorn. In the United States, Apptronik raised $520 million (about €467 million) at a valuation of about $5 billion, and then there are Figure, 1X and Tesla with Optimus, as well as Unitree of China.
High Valuation, Few Numbers
What stands behind the $8.5 billion valuation remains open: Agile Robots does not disclose revenue or earnings, and the number of installed solutions says little about how many humanoid robots are actually in use. In June, moreover, there had still been talk of a round of about $800 million. Why it has now become $500 million is not known.
There is also skepticism in principle. At the invest.austria conference, Nikolaus Keuth of EY recently spoke of a “big graveyard of pilot projects” in humanoid robotics: The technology is often not ready yet, expectations are too high, and without a real business case one is only chasing a fantasy. The panel there agreed that the race for the factory floor is still open.

By Markus Elsasser
