candidates.title: Modular Data Center Startup Mavria Raises $130M, but Grid Hookups Remain Unproven
candidates.snippet: Modular Data Center Startup Mavria Raises $130M, but Grid Hookups Remain Unproven Tech Times
candidates.text:
By
Shannon Harwood
Published: Nov 10 2026, 2:10 AM EST
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share on LinkedIn
Share on Reddit
Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp
Mavria
Mavria, a data center startup whose founders include former Energy Department officials, announced Monday that it raised $130 million at a $1 billion valuation to build data centers in a factory. The company was founded in June 2026 , according to co-founder Seth Cohen, and its first unit, Terrain 01, is being built in Houston .
Terrain comes in 5 MW units, according to Dealroom , which cites the Wall Street Journal's reporting. Mavria's own announcement gives no capacity figure , and the company has not named customers or published capacity, pricing or delivery timelines.
For the frontier AI labs, cloud providers and data center developers that Mavria targets, the open question is power, not factory speed. DatacenterDynamics reported that Mavria says Terrain can bypass grid delays by plugging into local distribution lines to soak up excess capacity, but the company's announcement makes no grid connection claim . That makes size the number to watch in Texas, where Senate Bill 6 covers loads of at least 75 megawatts at a single site: one 5 MW block is about 7% of that line, while a 100 MW campus would need 20 blocks.
How Terrain Packs Power, Cooling and Compute Into One 5 MW Block
Mavria says Terrain replaces on-site custom construction with factory-based repeatable manufacturing . Customers' compute runs inside it, and the company says it supplies infrastructure without operating a cloud or selling compute .
HuggingNews reports that the units use direct liquid cooling and integrated power distribution for customer-owned compute. Mavria's announcement mentions neither the liquid cooling nor the block size.
Liquid cooling matters at this size because AI racks outrun air. Wikipedia's computer-cooling entry puts air cooling up to 23 kW per rack, while NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack draws 190 to 230 kW , according to earlier TechTimes reporting. At those figures, 5 MW supports roughly 22 to 26 such racks before cooling and power-conversion overhead, and Mavria has not said which hardware Terrain targets.
Factory integration removes on-site assembly work, not the utility connection. NVIDIA's DSX POD moves cabling, power distribution and cooling piping into a factory, shortening connection time from roughly six months to 14 days , yet the pod still arrives at a prepared site that must already have high-voltage power , a coolant loop and a network handoff. Dealroom likewise notes that factory production cannot by itself solve power availability or site-connection delays.
The tradeoff is standardization. Mavria says Terrain should bring more predictable delivery and lower costs , but it has published no pricing , so the benefit remains a claim.
Related
NVIDIA Cuts AI Factory Deployment to 14 Days With DSX POD at GTC Berlin
FluidStack Closes $1.5B: Revenue Soars From $1.8M to $660M Projected While Owning Zero Chips
Can Factory-Built Data Centers Really Use Spare Local Power Capacity?
Distribution networks step transmission voltage down to primary lines of 4 to 35 kilovolts , with 12.47, 25 and 34.5 kV common in the United States. The utility-consulting firm Logic20/20 says smaller enterprise and colocation sites typically under 20 megawatts connect at the distribution level, a band that includes a 5 MW block.
Spare capacity on a feeder is finite, and high ambient temperatures limit the power ratings of transformers, cables and lines. Mavria's announcement names no utility , connection voltage or energization schedule for a Terrain block.
The market backdrop is real but disputed. Sightline Climate estimated in February that 30% to 50% of large data centers due online in 2026 would be delayed, citing power constraints, equipment shortages and local opposition, with about 5 GW under construction against at least 16 GW planned. Axios noted that most affected projects were delayed rather than canceled, with nine canceled projects tracked. SemiAnalysis argued in June that the headline claim rests on a flawed denominator and on speculative early-stage announcements.
Texas's 75 MW Large-Load Line and Abbott's Audit Pause Make Block Count Decisive
Senate Bill 6, signed June 20, 2025, directs the PUCT to create interconnection procedures for large loads, and its definition allows the PUCT to lower the 75 MW threshold. The Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) standards are to include a transmission screening study fee of no less than $100,000 for covered loads, and the commission voted March 12 to publish a draft rule implementing them.
On Aug. 3, Gov. Greg Abbott directed a comprehensive audit of data center projects advancing through the interconnection process run by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which Foley says effectively pauses approvals. ERCOT is tracking more than 1,800 large-load projects totaling over 474 GW of potential demand, about 90% of it for data centers, though many are preliminary and may never be built.
Block count still matters. A campus of 15 or more blocks would reach the statutory 75 MW line, and the PUCT can lower it. Abbott's directive applies to data centers in the ERCOT queue regardless of load size , while purely behind-the-meter, on-site-generation projects that do not interconnect through ERCOT may not be subject to it. The legal summaries reviewed do not say whether a small site on a utility's distribution line would enter the ERCOT queue and fall under the audit, and Mavria has not said where customers will place Terrain.
Politics add uncertainty. Of 45 data center ballot measures tracked across 10 states, 33 had passed by the morning after the Nov. 3 election, according to Data Centers on the Ballot.

Mavria, a startup that wants to build AI data centers in a factory instead of one custom project at a time, has come out of stealth with $130 million raised to date across pre-seed and seed rounds.
Its latest round values the company at $1 billion. Paradigm led it, with participation from AMP PBC, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier and Dream Ventures.
Mavria calls itself “the industrial platform behind American AI.” In an introduction published November 9, co-founder and CEO Adam Blake argued that the AI race is moving from the lab into the physical world. Intelligence needs data centers, data centers need power, and power needs factories, equipment, supply chains and skilled workers, yet much of that infrastructure is still built one custom project at a time on timelines measured in years. America’s labs and clouds have extraordinary ambitions for compute, he wrote, but not the industrial capability to match.
Mavria’s answer is “infrastructure as a product.” It wants to bring engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and capital together so that every project makes it better at delivering the next. Its first product is Terrain, a factory-built data center platform meant to bring compute online faster, with more predictable delivery and lower costs, by replacing custom field construction with repeatable manufacturing. Mavria is building it for frontier labs, cloud providers and data center developers, and says Terrain 01 is in production in Houston now. Press reports describe the platform as 5-megawatt blocks in which power, cooling, controls and IT pods are designed, integrated and tested as one system before shipping, and the Wall Street Journal described it as modular data centers that can be moved by truck.
The founders worked together at the U.S. Department of Energy, where they saw how unprepared American infrastructure is for what is coming. Blake built one of the largest commercial solar companies in the U.S. and sold a software business to Vista Equity Partners. Nick Poradek is an engineer who sold his last company to Liberty Energy and then helped build Liberty’s manufacturing platform. Seth Cohen started as a lawyer at Kirkland and ended up at the center of the effort to restart American nuclear power. The rest of the team has run utilities, led a modular LNG manufacturer with more than a thousand employees, developed major energy projects and scaled technology companies.
“The next decade will show whether America can build at anything close to the pace its AI companies are moving,” Blake wrote. “We’re building Mavria because we don’t want the answer to be no.” The capital will go toward securing critical supply chains, scaling manufacturing and growing the team. Mavria is starting with data centers but says its ambition extends across the physical infrastructure AI depends on, and it is hiring across engineering, manufacturing and operations.
Plenty is still unverified. Mavria did not say how much of the $130 million came in the latest round. Some outlets reported a $100 million round, and a filing with the SEC reportedly shows $75 million sold after a first sale in mid-October. Capacity per unit, pricing, delivery times and customer names have not been disclosed. At least one outlet reported the first facility is not yet running, with testing due in early 2027, which differs from the company’s account. Cohen reportedly said the company was founded in June, which would mean a $1 billion valuation with no disclosed customer deployment.
Racing to industrialize AI infrastructure
Modular AI infrastructure already has several players. Armada, which sells modular data centers for defense and energy customers, raised a $230M Series B in May at a $2 billion valuation. Crusoe raised a $3.9B Series F at a $30.9 billion valuation, and FluidStack raised $1.5B at $18 billion. Singapore’s DayOne and EPG have also reportedly raised large sums for prefabricated data center modules. On the power side, gas-turbine startup Parallax exited stealth with $117 million.
The idea of building in a factory is spreading beyond data centers. Fab2, which wants to mass-produce chip fabs, raised $500M , Valar Atomics raised $1B to bring manufacturing economics to nuclear, and Re:Build raised $2.1B to reindustrialize U.S. manufacturing. Paradigm also co-led drone-delivery company Zipline’s $1.5B round this month, and Sequoia’s recent overhaul points the same way, toward AI and reindustrialization.

The Woodlands-based Mavria , which mass-produces factory-built modular AI data centers, just emerged from stealth mode with $130 million in funding at a $1 billion valuation.
Mavria raised the money in pre-seed and seed rounds led by Paradigm, an investment firm that concentrates on early-stage startups developing “pioneer” technology. Participants in the funding rounds include AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Dream Ventures and Liquid 2 Ventures, co-founded by former NFL quarterback Joe Montana.
The company’s inaugural product, Terrain, is a prefabricated data center designed for AI labs, cloud computing providers and data center developers. Mavria says its platform avoids ground-up construction, delivering infrastructure more quickly and at a lower cost.
Mavria tells the Wall Street Journal that the first Terrain unit is being built at a Houston-area factory. The 5-megawatt Terrain system features power distribution, direct liquid cooling, controls and server racks.
“America sets the pace at the intelligence frontier. But the race is moving from the lab into the physical world,” Adam Blake, co-founder and CEO of Mavria, wrote in a blog post .
“Intelligence needs data centers. Data centers need power. Power needs factories, equipment, supply chains, and skilled workers, but much of that infrastructure is still built one custom project at a time, on timelines measured in years.”
Blake and Mavria’s two other co-founders, Nick Poradek and Seth Cohen, most recently worked at the U.S. Department of Energy. There, they focused on reforming the nuclear power sector.
From start to finish, it can take roughly three to six years to build a data center at an estimated cost of $10 million to $37 million per megawatt. Based on those figures, a 100-megawatt data center might cost as much as $3.7 billion.
Here are brief bios of Blake, Poradek and Cohen, who co-founded Mavria in May.
Adam Blake
Blake most recently was a senior advisor to U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright. He is co-founder and former CEO of Zego, a provider of energy management technology for property managers. Zego spun out from Brightergy, a commercial solar company. Blake is founder and former CEO of Brightergy.
Nick Poradek
Poradek , chief operating officer at Mavria, was also an advisor to the U.S. energy secretary. He is founder and former CEO of Spring-based Edera Energy, co-founder of The Woodlands-based craft-ice brand Clarity Ice, and founder and former CEO of The Woodlands-based Edera Capital. Poradek sold Edera Energy, a manufacturer of oilfield equipment, to Liberty Energy, a fracking company. Wright is Liberty’s founder and former chairman and CEO.
Seth Cohen
Cohen , chief strategy officer and chief legal officer at Mavria, was head of nuclear law and policy at the Department of Energy. He is also a former NASA advisor and a former attorney at Kirkland & Ellis.
“We believe in rapidly deploying infrastructure as a product, rather than custom-building every project,” Blake said. “We’re bringing together engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and capital so that every project makes us better at delivering the next.”

Silver Point Capital: $130 Million Financing Supports Riverside’s Hoover CS Acquisition
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 2:17 AM
Silver Point Capital: $130 Million Financing Supports Riverside’s Hoover CS Acquisition
Silver Point Capital’s Direct Lending business has provided a $130 million financing facility supporting The Riverside Company’s acquisition of Hoover Circular Solutions, a provider of packaging, fleet management and logistics services.
Silver Point served as the sole lender for the facility. The financing supports Riverside’s investment in a business serving refining, chemical, energy and industrial customers globally.
Headquartered in Houston, Hoover CS operates a mixed rental fleet of specialized assets across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific. Its services combine packaging equipment with fleet management and logistics support for customers handling industrial materials.
The company’s Catalyst Packaging business provides closed-loop logistics for fresh and spent catalysts used in refineries. Its Chemical Packaging business supplies intermediate bulk containers and intermodal ISO tanks for specialty and hazardous chemicals.
These operations support material handling and transportation requirements across refining and chemical applications. Silver Point cited Hoover CS’s longstanding customer relationships and the role its services play in customers’ operations as factors underlying the financing.
Riverside focuses on businesses at the smaller end of the middle market through private equity and flexible capital strategies. Since its founding in 1988, the firm has completed more than 1,100 investments. Its international portfolios include more than 140 companies.
Founded in 2002, Silver Point oversees more than $52 billion in investable assets across public and private credit strategies and employs more than 400 people.
Its Direct Lending business manages more than $18 billion in investable assets and finances both private equity-backed and sponsorless borrowers. Its mandate covers acquisitions, refinancings and growth capital, among other transactions.
The Hoover CS facility adds to that acquisition financing activity, with Silver Point providing a customized lending solution intended to support operating improvements and growth under Riverside’s ownership.
KEY QUOTE:
“Hoover CS has built a differentiated platform with long-standing customer relationships and solutions serving critical needs for refining and chemical customers. We are pleased to partner with The Riverside Company and provide a customized financing solution to support Hoover CS as it strengthens operations and accelerates growth.”
Anthony DiNello, Head Of Direct Lending At Silver Point Capital

Imprint, the payments, loyalty, and customer intelligence platform brands use to make every transaction more valuable, has raised $130 million in new financing, valuing the company at approximately $1.9 billion. The round was led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from existing investors Hedosophia, Ribbit Capital, Spice, Thrive Capital, and new investor Positive Sum. The funding will support the company’s expansion into new payment options and AI capabilities that help brands recognize and reward customers wherever and however they choose to pay.
Imprint now serves more than two million members and partners with brands representing more than $500 billion in annual U.S. consumer spending. Since the beginning of the year, Imprint has launched programs with Albertsons Companies, Fanatics, Kroger, and Shell, with the Fanatics program debuting this week. Across Imprint’s partner portfolio, total cardholder spending more than doubled between 2025 and 2026. The share of spending on Imprint cards at partner checkouts tripled over the past year. Imprint also recently added $1.5 billion in incremental warehouse capacity and priced its second AAA-rated asset-backed securitization, with investor demand nearly five times the offering size.
As AI changes how people discover, compare, and buy, brands face new challenges in maintaining direct customer relationships. Agentic commerce is projected to mediate up to $1 trillion in U.S. retail revenue by 2030. Imprint brings payments, loyalty, and customer intelligence together so brands can learn from everyday spending and deliver recognition and rewards that give customers reasons to return.
“From AI chats to personal agents, every digital touchpoint is quickly becoming personalized. In this future, the brands that invest in understanding who their customers really are, and building relationships with each individually, will win,” said Daragh Murphy, founder and CEO of Imprint. “Imprint helps brands create financial products to earn a place in their customers’ everyday lives, and make them feel like a regular, uniquely recognizing and rewarding them for their loyalty. The latest round supports our growth as we build more ways for brands to meet customers where they are, regardless of how they want to shop or pay.”
To help brands adapt as more consumers use AI assistants to manage their finances and make purchases, Imprint has released a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI agents to securely access members’ rewards, virtual cards, and transaction history, along with tools for members to review and authorize agent-initiated purchases. Internally, Imprint’s AI platform has tripled engineering velocity, the rate at which the company turns ideas into production software, in the past 18 months.
“AI will make every option easier to compare, which makes earning a customer’s preference more valuable than ever,” said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, CEO and Partner at Positive Sum. “Imprint gives brands a way to earn that preference every day through payments and rewards. Daragh and the team built the full-stack technology themselves, have proven their ability to win marquee partners, and are growing quickly. That combination gives us conviction that they can capture a much bigger opportunity from here.”
Founded in 2020, Imprint built the technology behind co-branded credit cards from the ground up. The company owns its stack across origination, risk, servicing, and rewards, giving brands control over their financial products and the flexibility to tailor rewards, offers, and experiences to their customers.

Schiffman, EVP, Chief Financial Officer and Director of Fanatics, said, “With Imprint, we can offer a card that creates a new way to deepen our relationships with fans and provide a value proposition to sports fans that doesn’t exist in the market — and that is rewarding their passion — in a product that feels distinctly Fanatics. I’m proud of what we’ve built together and excited to keep building,” said Rachel Ehrlich, General Manager at Fetch.

candidates.text:
When AI shopping assistants find, compare and pay for products, brands risk losing their direct relationship with customers. McKinsey projects that agentic commerce could mediate up to $1 trillion in U.S. retail revenue by 2030. Imprint , which builds co-branded credit cards so brands can stay part of everyday spending, has raised $130 million.
Co-branded cards, built from the ground up
Imprint is a payments, loyalty and customer intelligence platform that helps brands make every transaction more valuable. Founded in 2020 and based in New York, it builds co-branded credit cards with brands and owns its stack across origination, risk, servicing and rewards. That gives brands control of their financial products and room to tailor rewards, the company says.
Since the start of the year it has launched programs with Albertsons Companies, Fanatics, Kroger and Shell, with the Fanatics card debuting this week. Booking.com is also a customer. Imprint reports more than two million members and partners whose annual U.S. consumer spending exceeds $500 billion. Total cardholder spending across its partners more than doubled between 2025 and 2026, and the share of spending on Imprint cards at partner checkouts tripled in a year. It also added $1.5 billion in warehouse capacity and priced its second AAA-rated asset-backed securitization, with demand nearly five times the offering size. These figures come from the company.
For the AI era, Imprint released a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI agents securely reach members’ rewards, virtual cards and transaction history, along with tools for members to review and authorize agent-initiated purchases. Imprint Access, launching today, gives customers who are new to credit or rebuilding it, backed by a refundable deposit, the same ongoing rewards as a brand’s unsecured card, with a path to upgrade. The Federal Reserve estimates 32 million Americans have little or no credit history.
A law graduate from Dublin who came to cards through WeWork
Founder and CEO Daragh Murphy is Irish, studied law at University College Dublin and was a vice president of operations and strategy at WeWork, according to Irish media. He founded Imprint in 2020 with Gaurav Ahuja and Michael Pechman. Ahuja, a partner at Thrive Capital , is reported to have helped incubate the company and to serve as chairman. Imprint raised a $75 million Series C at a $600 million valuation in October 2024, and press reports put its December 2025 Series D at $150 million and a $1.2 billion valuation.
Valuation up from $1.2B
Imprint said it raised $130 million at a valuation of about $1.9 billion. Existing investor Khosla Ventures led. Existing investors Hedosophia , Ribbit Capital , Spice and Thrive Capital took part, and Positive Sum joined as a new investor. The money will fund new payment options and AI capabilities, so brands can recognize and reward customers however they choose to pay. The release did not name the round.
CEO Murphy said brands that invest in understanding each customer and building individual relationships will win as every digital touchpoint becomes personalized. Patrick O’Shaughnessy, CEO and partner at Positive Sum, said AI makes every option easier to compare, so earning a customer’s preference matters more, and that the team’s full-stack technology and marquee partners gave the firm conviction. Fanatics CFO Glenn Schiffman said Imprint’s technology made it possible to design a card around fans.
Competitors
In U.S. rewards cards, Bilt Rewards is the most visible rival. It started as a card that turns rent into points and raised $250 million in July 2025 at a $10.75 billion valuation, led by General Catalyst and GID. It was reported to be ending its relationship with Wells Fargo and moving its cards to Cardless. No new round since 2026 could be confirmed.
Large issuers that have long run retailer co-brand programs, such as Synchrony and Bread Financial , compete for the same brands. Imprint pitches its own technology stack as the edge in designing products. Among companies we have covered, Ramp approaches cards through corporate spend management and raised $1.85 billion at a $60 billion valuation last month.

General Flash Announces $128 Million in Funding to Scale U.S. Production of Critical Metals
News provided by
General Flash
Nov 17, 2026, 08:55 ET
Share this article
Share this article
New energy-efficient, emissions-free process for metallization to scale from the company's pilot line near MIT to 1,000 metric tons per year of commercial production in 2027
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- General Flash, which has developed a fundamentally new way to make critical metals, today announced it has raised $128 million in equity capital across its Seed and Series A rounds to scale domestic production of metals essential to national security and American manufacturing. Investors include Lux Capital, Construct Capital, Overmatch Ventures, GreatPoint Ventures, Pillar VC, Lowercarbon Capital, Ensemble VC, Ravelin and leading angel investors.
Critical metals and minerals like tungsten, titanium, zirconium, tantalum and rare earths go into semiconductors, defense, aerospace and advanced manufacturing. In the 20th century, the United States developed most of the techniques used to make these materials but allowed production to move overseas, and today it depends heavily on foreign supply. Although these minerals are mined around the world, China accounts for more than 80% of refining capacity for many of them. Starting January 1, 2027, Department of War rules will bar Chinese supply for many of these critical materials from U.S. defense supply chains.
General Flash's process converts metal oxides directly into high-purity, semiconductor-grade metal, with no emissions. It is faster and lower cost than conventional refining and gives the U.S. a way to build cost-effective refining capacity at home instead of relying on foreign supply. The company's Solid-State Flash Electrolysis (SSFE) process is metal-agnostic and can be used to refine materials like tungsten, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, zirconium, germanium, yttrium, niobium, molybdenum, and rare earth elements.
The funding will support commercial-scale production by summer 2027, in what will be one of the largest and most advanced critical materials production plants in the world.
"Critical metals are foundational to every advanced industry," said Ric Fulop, Co-Founder and CEO of General Flash and member of the visiting committee of the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering and research scientist at the MIT Center for Bits and Atoms. "We started General Flash because we believe there's a better, cleaner and more efficient way to make these materials. We've already demonstrated it at our multi-ton pilot facility near MIT, and this funding fully finances production of our first large plant in the U.S."
"Every advanced industry runs on critical metals, and the way we make them has barely changed in decades," said Peter Hebert, Co-Founder and Partner at Lux Capital. "General Flash has a genuinely new process, proven at pilot scale, and a founder who has built and scaled a manufacturing company before. We believe it can become one of the most important American industrial companies of the next decade."
"Foundational industries like metals production rarely sprout new companies, but that is exactly what is needed today as demand for onshore critical metals suppliers has skyrocketed," said Dayna Grayson, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Construct Capital. "General Flash is showing that critical metals can be made in America with a cleaner, more efficient process, and that the next generation of heavy industry can be built here."
"America's defense supply chain depends on metals that are refined almost entirely overseas, and new Department of War rules make that dependence impossible to ignore. General Flash gives the U.S. a way to make these materials at home, at scale, and that matters for national security," said Jordan Blashek, General Partner at Overmatch Ventures.
"General Flash is solving one of the most pressing challenges facing the U.S.: secure access to critical materials," said Andrew Perlman, Founding Managing Partner at GreatPoint Ventures. "Its technology can strengthen the American supply chain while bringing down costs, and its founders have exactly the kind of big vision we're proud to back."
About General Flash
General Flash makes critical metals using a new solid-state process that converts metal oxides directly into metal, with no emissions. Based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the company operates a 20-metric-ton-per-year pilot facility near MIT and is scaling to commercial production for defense and commercial customers. Its process is being developed for tungsten, tantalum, titanium, hafnium, zirconium, germanium, yttrium, niobium, molybdenum and rare earth elements. Learn more at generalflash.com .
About Lux Capital
Lux Capital is a venture capital firm based in New York City and Silicon Valley with $8 billion in assets under management. Since 2000, Lux has backed founders at the experimental frontier of science and technology. Lux invests early, often years before markets take shape, and partners with founders from the first $100K to the last $100M.
About Construct Capital
Construct Capital is an early-stage venture capital firm investing in the transformation of Foundational Industries, including manufacturing, mobility, supply chain, energy, and defense, that power half of the U.S. economy but have been underinvested for decades. With advances in AI, automation, and advanced manufacturing, Construct sees a generational opportunity to transform the physical economy and unlock a potential $50+ trillion public market opportunity. Founded in 2020 by Dayna Grayson (formerly NEA) and Rachel Holt (formerly Uber), Construct manages $1 billion in assets across three core funds and two select funds. Learn more about Construct's investment thesis at constructcap.com/construct-point-of-view .

Corma Raises $125M Series A at $1B Valuation to Scale Defensive AI
Published
November 16, 2026
By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Key Points Corma raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
View more
Corma raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
Corma argues coding-focused models suit offensive security while defense needs continuous log and event analysis.
Compute capacity rather than model quality is Corma's immediate constraint on serving demand and its waitlist.
Defensive-cybersecurity company Corma announced on November 16, 2026 that it had raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation. NEA led the round, with continued participation from Sequoia Capital , Khosla Ventures and Coatue, bringing Corma’s total funding to $185 million.
Corma said the new capital would accelerate scaling of its foundation models, expand compute capacity and support selective hiring. The Series A follows its emergence from stealth on August 10, 2026 with $60 million in seed funding.
The company characterized demand from the world’s largest organizations as overwhelming and identified securing enough compute for that demand and its waitlist as one of its central challenges. Corma’s ability to expand access therefore depends on obtaining additional infrastructure as well as advancing its models.
How the Corma Workforce Operates
The company deploys those models through the Corma Workforce , a system designed to work autonomously alongside human security teams. It operates within customers’ existing security and IT stacks, including identity, cloud, endpoint, security information and event management, and firewall or intrusion-detection tools. Its work spans investigations, connecting evidence and taking action across those systems.
Employees can assign tasks through Slack or Teams, ask questions, review findings and approve actions. The design adds AI-led execution to a customer’s current operating environment while keeping human review in the workflow.
Corma reports live deployments across healthcare, finance, energy, critical infrastructure and retail, with 99% of security tasks completed autonomously and successfully, 100 times faster end-to-end completion and 95% lower cost per completed task.
One anonymized Fortune 1000 services-company CISO quoted on the product page said end-to-end response time fell 94% in a comparison with the customer’s former service provider, which the customer subsequently replaced with Corma.
Why Corma Uses Defense-Specific Models
Corma’s launch statement argues that improvements in coding and software reasoning map more directly to offensive security than to the broader defensive workload. Vulnerability research and exploit development are code-reasoning problems against bounded targets; defense instead requires continuous analysis of audit logs, events, configurations and network flows. It also involves connecting weak signals across systems and long periods while making thousands of accurate, consistent decisions each day under changing conditions.
That distinction is the basis for Corma’s focus on domain-specific foundation models. Its stated development program includes rethinking model architecture, extending context to detect faint anomaly signals, adversarial self-play and continuous learning that can establish baselines over months and years.
CEO Alon Pluda and the Corma team said the next generation of its foundation models would be shared soon, without giving a release date. The financing supports that next phase of model development and selective hiring, but the immediate scaling constraint is compute: broader deployments require enough additional capacity to serve current demand and organizations on the waitlist.

candidates.title: Defensive AI agents co Corma raises $125m at $1b valuation - Globes
candidates.snippet: Defensive AI agents co Corma raises $125m at $1b valuation Globes - Israel Business News
candidates.text:
Israeli AI language model cybersecurity company Corma , today announced the completion of a $125 million Series A financing round, at a $1 billion valuation, led by NEA, alongside existing investors Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures. The company has now raised $185 million, having emerged from stealth just three months ago with a $60 million seed round led by Sequoia.
CEO Alon Pluda founded the company last year, after leaving Miggo Security, which he cofounded, following a dispute with his cofounders. Pluda is a graduate of the IDF Intelligence Corps’ prestigious Psagot program. He completed his service in 2022, following several years as a career officer in various technical roles at the core of Unit 8200’s technological operations. He founded Corma, which has 20 employees in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, with the aim of more effectively addressing AI-driven cyberattacks. The company achieves this by developing language models from scratch, rather than relying on existing models such as those from Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepSeek.
Pluda explains, "General-purpose language models are effective for tasks like software development or research and they are also excellent at identifying bugs and cyber vulnerabilities, which is precisely why hackers and attackers use them so efficiently. However, they are weak when it comes to defense. Defense requires a different kind of expertise: the ability to find a 'needle in a haystack' within the complex landscape of enterprise data systems, specifically regarding code and software maintenance, such as telemetry, logs, and events."
In Pluda’s view, this is why the language models currently on the market are highly advanced in their capacity to facilitate powerful cyberattacks, yet remain insufficiently developed for the purpose of defending organizations. Fluda explains that Corma addresses this gap by developing its own language model, which is focused entirely on a single task: perimeter defense for organizations. The company also develops AI agents that are integrated into client organizations, working alongside existing cybersecurity teams.
Pluda adds, "We don’t just provide CISOs with a dashboard or software to manage. We provide AI agents that empower them, enabling them to perform their jobs orders of magnitude better."
The company trains its models with the goal of achieving "superintelligence" for defensive cybersecurity - a capability that will allow security teams to operate at the speed and scale required to counter the advancement of AI-driven cyberattacks.
The company’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) is estimated to be in the tens of millions of dollars, and its client base includes companies from the Fortune 100 and Fortune 500 lists.
"Since its initial unveiling in August, demand for the company’s models has surged among organizations ranked in the Fortune 100, Fortune 500, and Fortune Global 500. To meet this demand, the company has increased its server capacity 24-fold," the company stated.
Corma works with large organizations, including companies in the healthcare, financial services, energy and critical infrastructure, retail, and telecommunications sectors. These organizations are increasingly delegating their security tasks to Corma’s autonomous workforce, which operates using a foundational model developed by the company.

candidates.text:
Ameresco: $125 Million Financing From Nuveen With Expansion Capacity To $225 Million Supports European Energy Infrastructure Growth
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 5:24 PM
Ameresco: $125 Million Financing From Nuveen With Expansion Capacity To $225 Million Supports European Energy Infrastructure Growth
Ameresco, an energy infrastructure company specializing in reliable power and infrastructure modernization, has secured a $125 million committed financing facility with Nuveen Energy Infrastructure Credit to support its expanding operations in the United Kingdom and Europe. The five-year revolving facility includes an option to increase financing capacity by an additional $100 million, potentially providing Ameresco with access to $225 million in total capital.
The facility matures in November 2031 and will provide dedicated financing for energy infrastructure projects and working capital requirements across Ameresco’s European business.
The financing has been structured with limited recourse to Ameresco and does not affect the company’s senior secured corporate leverage ratios.
This arrangement is intended to create a more self-sustaining capital structure for European operations while preserving financial flexibility at the parent-company level.
The facility will also allow Ameresco to expand available borrowing capacity as its project pipeline and working capital requirements increase, subject to the relevant terms.
The investment comes amid substantial growth in Ameresco’s European business.
European revenue increased from $62 million in 2022 to $529 million in 2025, representing more than an eightfold increase over that period.
The region now accounts for approximately 25% of Ameresco’s total revenue.
Ameresco attributes its European expansion partly to increasing electricity demand, higher energy costs, and growing customer interest in renewable energy infrastructure.
The company sees further opportunities in battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS, as European markets expand their use of technologies that can store electricity and provide greater flexibility to power networks.
Battery energy storage can help electricity customers manage demand fluctuations, integrate renewable generation, and strengthen energy resilience.
Ameresco believes its technology expertise and flexible approach to infrastructure development position it to support these requirements across European markets.
The company provides energy infrastructure solutions spanning behind-the-meter systems, utility-scale energy resources, and modernization of buildings and public infrastructure.
Its projects integrate multiple energy technologies according to customer needs rather than focusing on a single equipment or generation category.
Nuveen Energy Infrastructure Credit’s participation builds on an existing financing relationship with Ameresco.
The investment manager specializes in providing capital to companies and projects operating across energy infrastructure markets.
The new facility provides a dedicated financing source to support project execution without requiring Ameresco to rely exclusively on existing corporate financing arrangements.
Ameresco has delivered more than $15 billion in solutions and contracted over 5 gigawatts of energy resources since its founding in 2000.
Headquartered in Massachusetts, the company serves public and private sector customers throughout North America and Europe.
The financing strengthens Ameresco’s ability to pursue additional energy infrastructure projects while supporting the working capital demands associated with expanding operations.
By securing a five-year facility with the potential to grow to $225 million, Ameresco is positioning its European business to support additional demand for power infrastructure, renewable energy, and energy storage solutions.
KEY QUOTES:
“We are pleased to be working with Nuveen again as a trusted financing partner. This facility gives our European business dedicated, long-term capital to support project execution and working-capital needs as we expand across the region. The scalable structure gives us the flexibility to add additional capacity as our European operations grow.”
Josh Baribeau, Senior Vice President And Chief Investment Officer At Ameresco
“This facility gives us the capital to support the planned growth of our European business which has grown from $62 million in revenue in 2022 to $529 million in 2025, now representing approximately 25% of Ameresco’s revenues. Driving this growth has been the growing demand for renewable energy given increasing electricity demand and costs throughout Europe. We also see a significant opportunity for us to bring our battery energy storage (BESS) expertise to the European market, which is just beginning to utilize this technology. Our technology expertise and agnostic approach positions Ameresco to build out the energy infrastructure that European customers need.”
George Sakellaris, Chairman And CEO Of Ameresco
“We look forward to continuing our partnership with Ameresco and providing long-term capital solutions to support its growing European business. Supporting energy infrastructure companies like Ameresco that advance the low-carbon transition and strengthen energy security is central to our strategy.”
Don Dimitrievich, Portfolio Manager Of Nuveen Energy Infrastructure Credit

candidates.snippet:
Altius Minerals has agreed to acquire the TNR Gold shares it does not already own in a transaction with an estimated total value of $122 million, including shares in a newly formed exploration company.
The post Altius Announces Estimated $122 Million TNR Gold Acquisition And Exploration Spinoff appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
Altius Announces Estimated $122 Million TNR Gold Acquisition And Exploration Spinoff
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 3:23 PM
Altius Announces Estimated $122 Million TNR Gold Acquisition And Exploration Spinoff
Altius Minerals has agreed to acquire the TNR Gold shares it does not already own in a transaction with an estimated total value of $122 million, including shares in a newly formed exploration company.
The agreement will add royalty interests associated with Argentina’s Los Azules copper, Mariana lithium and Josemaria copper-gold projects.
Each eligible TNR share will be exchanged for 0.0072 Altius shares and 0.25 shares of TNR SpinCo. Based on November 10 prices and the assigned spinoff valuation, the implied consideration is approximately $0.48 per TNR share, representing a 60% premium.
That amount comprises approximately $97 million in Altius shares and $25 million in SpinCo shares.
SpinCo will hold the Shotgun Gold Project in Alaska and related assets and liabilities. Altius will retain a 0.5% net smelter return royalty on Shotgun.
Altius initially expects to own approximately 12% of SpinCo and will invest another $2.2 million to increase its stake to approximately 19.9%. It will also provide technical support.
The acquired royalties include an effective 0.36% net smelter return interest in Los Azules and an effective 1.35% interest in Mariana.
Los Azules is targeting a financing decision in mid-2027 and first production in 2030. Mariana has begun production and is ramping toward an initial target of 20,000 tonnes annually of lithium carbonate equivalent.
Shareholders controlling approximately 28% of TNR’s outstanding shares have signed support agreements.
Closing is expected around the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder, court, exchange and regulatory approvals. A shareholder meeting is expected in December 2026.
McCarthy Tétrault is serving as Altius’s legal counsel.
KEY QUOTES
“This transaction adds a significant development stage royalty over the Los Azules project, which offers the potential for decades of increased copper exposure within our portfolio. It also results in the consolidation of an operating stage royalty relating to the Mariana lithium brine project. Both of these assets feature attributes that are hallmarks of Altius’s long-term royalty investing strategy. With long to ultra-long potential resource lives, they provide growth optionality over multiple commodity cycles as well as projected cost curve positions that ensure long-term resiliency. We are also pleased to support the TNR SpinCo as it applies the historical project generation and royalty creation strategy that brought the Los Azules and Mariana royalties into its portfolio.”
Brian Dalton, CEO Of Altius Minerals
“The Arrangement Agreement with Altius is a pivotal milestone that fully validates the significant value we have created for TNR Gold shareholders. Altius is a premier and highly respected partner in the mining and royalty sector, and this Transaction delivers a compelling outcome for our shareholders, and we are thrilled to be making this announcement.”
Kirill Klip, Executive Chairman Of TNR Gold

candidates.title: German Start-up Vaeridion Lands €120 Million To Build Electric Plane
candidates.snippet: German Start-up Vaeridion Lands €120 Million To Build Electric Plane Aviation Pros
candidates.text:
Carsten Hoefer
dpa
(TNS)
Munich — German start-up Vaeridion has raised over €120 million ($135 million) in funding from the European Union and investors to develop an electric aircraft, the Munich-based company said on Thursday.
Vaeridion said it had raised €30 million from venture capital investors in its latest funding round. The European Commission had previously made €94.5 million available from its Innovation Fund.
The company is developing a nine-seat passenger aircraft for regional air travel called the Microliner. Vaeridion says it has already received purchase commitments for 130 aircraft.
With the €30 million from investors, Vaeridion wants to build a prototype that is eligible for certification. The EU money is intended for final assembly and for setting up production at the German aviation research and development centre at Oberpfaffenhofen airport. The hub is home to a large branch of the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), and several companies have set up operations nearby.
Vaeridion is aiming to provide a cheaper alternative to the more than 21,000 small, ageing turboprop aircraft that fly on regional routes worldwide. The company's electric aircraft is designed to have a range of 400 kilometres and operate without kerosene.
According to the start-up's calculations, Microliner tickets should cost roughly the same as first-class tickets on Germany's high-speed rail network.
"Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide," said chief executive Ivor von Dartel, a former Airbus manager.
The company says its first customer is the ASL Group, a business aviation operator in Belgium and the Netherlands.
Past failures
Two German electric plane start-ups have already failed. The Munich-based company Lilium went insolvent twice before giving up for good.
A second company, Volocopter, also went insolvent and was subsequently sold to Chinese investors.
Other companies are also working on electric aircraft, including the Bavarian start-up ERC System, which is developing a plane with a hybrid engine for transporting patients and other purposes.

candidates.title: General Dynamics Business Units Receive $117.6 Million In Navy Contract Actions
candidates.snippet:
General Dynamics business units received three Navy contract actions with a combined announced value of approximately $117.6 million for enterprise IT services, Virginia-class submarine materials, and undersea research.
The post General Dynamics Business Units Receive $117.6 Million In Navy Contract Actions appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
General Dynamics Business Units Receive $117.6 Million In Navy Contract Actions
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 10:53 AM
General Dynamics Business Units Receive $117.6 Million In Navy Contract Actions
General Dynamics business units received three Navy contract actions with a combined announced value of approximately $117.6 million for enterprise IT services, Virginia-class submarine materials, and undersea research.
The combined figure consists of a $56 million ceiling increase for General Dynamics Information Technology, a $41.6 million undefinitized contract action for General Dynamics Electric Boat, and a $20 million research contract for General Dynamics Applied Physical Sciences. The amounts have different funding and contract structures and should not be interpreted as $117.6 million in guaranteed or immediately obligated revenue.
General Dynamics Information Technology received a modification increasing the ceiling of indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract N0003925D7800 by $56 million, from $98.5 million to $154.5 million. The additional ordering capacity will support the Navy’s effort to consolidate legacy help desks into the Navy Enterprise Service Desk by October 1, 2027.
The consolidation supports the Secretary of the Navy’s Operation Cattle Drive mandate. Work will continue in Bossier City and New Orleans, Louisiana, with each location accounting for 50% of performance.
The GDIT contract is in its second performance year under an option period running from August 2026 through August 2027. One optional year remains and could extend performance through August 2028. The government did not report an immediate obligation associated with the ceiling increase, so the $56 million represents additional potential ordering authority rather than a funded task order.
The production contract followed GDIT’s successful completion of an Other Transaction Authority prototype effort that began in 2019. Portfolio Acquisition Executive Mission Systems in San Diego is the contracting activity.
General Dynamics Electric Boat received a $41.6 million undefinitized action under previously awarded contract N00024-24-C-2124. The action supports the procurement of long-lead materials for Virginia-class submarines.
Electric Boat will perform the reported work in Franklin, Massachusetts, with completion expected in June 2031. The Navy will obligate approximately $18.9 million in fiscal 2025 other procurement funding at award. Those funds will expire at the end of the current fiscal year.
Because the action is undefinitized, the Navy and Electric Boat will finalize certain pricing or contractual terms later. Long-lead procurement enables specialized materials and components to enter production early enough to protect submarine construction schedules. The Supervisor of Shipbuilding, Conversion and Repair in Groton, Connecticut, is the contracting activity.
General Dynamics Applied Physical Sciences received a $20 million cost-plus-fixed-fee completion contract for Advancements in Undersea Dominance and Naval Engineering.
The Groton, Connecticut-based business will conduct studies and develop naval technologies using first-principles analysis and physics-based modeling and simulation. Work will be performed in Groton through September 2031.
The Navy will obligate $5.1 million in fiscal 2026 research, development, test, and evaluation funding at award. Those funds will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year.
The five-year research contract has no options and was competitively procured through the Office of Naval Research’s long-range broad agency announcement for Navy and Marine Corps science and technology.
Across the three actions, the Navy reported approximately $24 million in funding obligated at award. This total comprises Electric Boat’s $18.9 million obligation and Applied Physical Sciences’ $5.1 million obligation. No immediate obligation was reported for GDIT’s $56 million ceiling increase.

candidates.title: Stanford Professor's Startup Noeri Raises $110 Million to Let Enterprise AI Rewrite Itself
candidates.snippet: Stanford Professor's Startup Noeri Raises $110 Million to Let Enterprise AI Rewrite Itself BigGo Finance
candidates.text:
Stanford Professor's Startup Noeri Raises $110 Million to Let Enterprise AI Rewrite Itself
Add preferred source
Noeri, an enterprise AI startup co-founded by Stanford University professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, has officially launched and announced it has closed a $110 million funding round led by Menlo Ventures, with Nvidia, Cisco and Snowflake participating as strategic investors. Founded about five months ago and headquartered in Palo Alto, California, Noeri is building "self-improving" AI systems that continuously learn from a company's own data and workflows. The systems examine a company's existing models and toolchains and propose modifications, with all changes subject to human review. The idea originated with a Stanford research team that, to save costs, trained a small AI to orchestrate older models such as GPT-4—and found it outperformed GPT-5 on certain scientific tasks. Japan's Sakana AI is exploring a similar direction.
Key Elements
Noeri Yejin Choi Carlos Guestrin Menlo Ventures Nvidia Snowflake Cisco Stanford University Sakana AI OpenAI GPT-5 GPT-4
Noeri, an enterprise AI startup co-founded by two Stanford University artificial intelligence professors, has officially unveiled itself and announced it has raised $110 million. The round was led by Menlo Ventures, with participation from Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA, while Cisco's investment arm, Nvidia and Snowflake joined as strategic investors. The company's valuation was not disclosed.
Noeri was founded only about five months ago and is headquartered in Palo Alto, California. Its co-founders are Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin. Choi was previously a distinguished scientist at Nvidia and received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2022; Guestrin is one of the co-developers of the open-source machine learning tool XGBoost, and his earlier machine learning company Turi was acquired by Apple in 2016, after which he led Apple's core machine learning and AI teams. The company's name evokes the idea of "multiple intelligences," and it is currently hiring research and engineering talent in Palo Alto and Zurich.
The company's starting point came from cost considerations at a Stanford microbiology and immunology research team. According to Choi, who spoke to Bloomberg , the team considered GPT-5 too expensive, so it trained a small AI to schedule work by older models such as GPT-4. The combination of "a small model directing older models" ended up outperforming GPT-5 on specific tasks.
Building on that discovery, Noeri is focused on so-called "self-improving" AI systems: the tool examines a company's existing AI models, software development tools and other software, identifies areas for adjustment and proposes modifications—retraining underlying models when necessary. All changes must pass human review before going live, allowing the system to continuously learn from a company's own data and workflows and gradually form specialized models that are cheaper and better tailored to specific business needs, while companies retain the models and processes they have built themselves.
Noeri is not alone on this path. Japan's Sakana AI launched Fugu in June this year, which likewise uses specially trained models to direct other AIs in completing complex tasks, and it is investing in AI self-improvement research. Noeri's difference lies in its explicit focus on enterprise scenarios and its emphasis on absorbing internal corporate data and practical experience over the long term.
The round's backers span both venture capital and industry strategic investors. The participation of Nvidia, Cisco and Snowflake reflects growing interest among large technology companies in "replacing a single flagship model with low-cost model combinations." For enterprise users, if self-improving systems can genuinely lower inference costs and improve accuracy on specific tasks, they would offer an alternative to an AI spending structure currently heavily dependent on a handful of large models. Still, because such systems involve model retraining and workflow changes, the barriers to adoption and governance costs remain key things to watch.

Nvidia Backs Noeri’s $110 Million Enterprise AI Funding Round
Founded roughly five months ago by Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, the company is building AI tools tailored to businesses’ needs.
By John Kim
Published Nov 16, 2026, 11:17 AM EST
Save Share An unmarked accelerator board rests on a laboratory workbench / TokenPost.ai
Nvidia has joined a $110 million financing for Noeri, a five-month-old artificial intelligence startup building specialized systems for companies, adding another early-stage AI investment to the chipmaker’s portfolio.
Menlo Ventures was the lead investor. Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, NEA and Nvidia also participated. Noeri has not disclosed how much Nvidia invested, the startup’s valuation or how it plans to spend the funds.
Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin started Noeri roughly five months ago. The company focuses on adapting specialized AI systems to businesses’ needs using their proprietary data.
Nvidia has also participated in other AI startup financings. Its venture arm, NVentures, invested in Reactor , bringing that startup’s total funding to $74 million, and Nvidia participated in Simplismart’s $14 million Series B .
John Kim

candidates.text:
Back to Blog
Clara Raises $105 Million to Grow Latin American Corporate Spend Management Platform
By Julie Muhn (@julieschicktanz) Posted on November 13, 2026
Categories: Daily news , Funding
Clara raised $105 million, comprising a $65 million Series C equity round and the renewal of a $40 million growth financing facility, bringing its total debt and equity funding to $838 million.
Clara will use the funding to expand its market reach and enhance its AI capabilities, including its MCP integration that enables AI agents to access financial data and execute authorized transactions.
The funding comes amid global growth in corporate card and spend management platforms, as providers expand beyond payments and expense tracking to offer integrated, AI-powered financial management tools.
Brazil-based spend management platform Clara raised $105 million this week. The round is comprised of $65 million in equity in a Series C round and the renewal of a $40 million growth financing facility from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF).
The $65 million Series C was anchored by Citius, Kaszek, and DEG, a subsidiary of Germany’s KfW Group. The round also attracted participation from 10 existing investors and three new investors, including CMT Digital and Nascent VC.
The latest investment brings Clara’s total debt and equity funding to $838 million, following several debt financing deals over the past year. In November 2025, Clara secured $70 million in structured debt financing from BBVA Spark, Covalto, and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Three months later, the company renewed a $150 million credit facility with Goldman Sachs, bringing its total debt capacity to more than $250 million.
Clara will use today’s funding to expand its go-to-market team and strengthen the automation and AI capabilities of its platform. Clara was founded in 2020 and now helps more than 45,000 businesses automate routine work, control spending, and make better financial decisions. The company’s platform offers corporate cards, bill payments, spend management, accounts payable, and accounts receivable to help businesses make and manage payments. Along with the financing announcement, Clara said it has also surpassed $100 million in annualized net revenue and maintained positive EBITDA for more than a year.
Among Clara’s capabilities is its Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, which connects the platform with AI agents to enable customers to access real-time spending reports and forecasts using natural language, as well as execute authorized transactions autonomously. The company also offers AI-powered policy enforcement that checks employee expenses against company policies in real time, global spend management tools that allow businesses to manage expenses across countries and currencies, and fleet management solutions that support fuel payments and vehicle operations.
“Clara exists to champion Latin American businesses, and we work tirelessly to give them the tools to compete and win on the global stage,” said Clara Co-Founder and CEO Gerry Giacomán Colyer. “The region has long been underserved by financial platforms designed for other markets. We’re combining AI with local expertise to solve challenges specific to doing business here and give our customers a distinct competitive edge.”
Clara’s latest funding comes as spend management platforms increasingly look beyond corporate cards and expense tracking. By combining payments, financial data, and AI-driven automation, Clara is positioning itself to help businesses manage not just how they spend money, but how they make financial decisions.
The news of Clara’s growth comes as corporate card and spend management fintechs around the world are expanding their customer bases as well as their offerings. Companies such as Ramp and Brex in the US, Pleo and Payhawk in Europe, and Airwallex in Asia-Pacific have expanded beyond corporate cards to offer more comprehensive financial management platforms. These providers have integrated payments, expense management, accounts payable, and AI-powered automation into a single offering. Clara is following a similar trajectory in Latin America, where its regional focus and growing suite of financial tools position it to compete for businesses looking to consolidate and automate their financial operations.

candidates.title: Addex Spin-out Neurosterix Closes $105 Million Series B Financing
candidates.snippet: Addex Spin-out Neurosterix Closes $105 Million Series B Financing GlobeNewswire
candidates.text:
Ad Hoc Announcement Pursuant to Art. 53 LR
Geneva, Switzerland, November 11, 2026 - Addex Therapeutics (SIX and Nasdaq: ADXN), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing a portfolio of novel small molecule allosteric modulators for neurological disorders, today announced that its spin-out company, Neurosterix, has closed a $105 million Series B financing from a syndicate of leading life science investors. Addex did not participate in the financing and its equity interest now represents 8.5% of the issued capital at a valuation of $18.6 million.
The proceeds raised will support mainly the planned Phase 2 clinical development of NTX-253, a highly selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator (PAM), for schizophrenia. The financing will also support Neurosterix’s broader pipeline of selective allosteric modulators for a range of neuropsychiatric disorders.
“The closing of this significant financing is a huge endorsement of the allosteric approach pioneered by Addex in schizophrenia as well as other neuropsychiatric disorders. Congatulations to the whole Neurosterix team, which has made enormous strides in advancing lead program NTX-253 through clinical development and ready for Phase 2, following our spin-out in 2024,” said Tim Dyer, CEO of Addex.
About NTX-253 and M4 PAMs
The M4 muscarinic receptor is a validated target for treating schizophrenia and related disorders through indirect modulation of dopamine signaling. NTX-253 is a potent, highly selective, oral PAM of M4 that fine-tunes muscarinic signaling in the brain to potentially reduce psychosis symptoms while avoiding the movement disorders and metabolic complications associated with traditional dopamine antagonists. Neurosterix has completed Phase 1 single- and multiple-ascending-dose clinical studies of NTX-253, which data supporting advancing into larger scale Phase 2 clinical studies.
About Neurosterix
Neurosterix is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on transforming neuropsychiatric care through selective allosteric modulation. The company’s approach is designed to fine-tune brain signaling with greater precision and selectivity, with the goal of developing safer, more effective treatments for people living with schizophrenia, and mood and anxiety disorders. Neurosterix’s pipeline includes NTX-253, a selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator (PAM) for schizophrenia; NTX-819, a potentially first-in-class mGlu7 negative allosteric modulator (NAM) for mood and anxiety disorders; and NTX-529, a second differentiated M4 PAM for additional psychosis- and mood-related disorders. Neurosterix has operations in Boston and Geneva. For more information, visit www.neurosterix.com.
About Addex Therapeutics
Addex Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing a portfolio of novel small molecule allosteric modulators for neurological disorders. Addex's lead drug candidate, dipraglurant (mGlu5 negative allosteric modulator or NAM), is under evaluation for future development in brain injury recovery, including post-stroke and traumatic brain injury recovery. Addex has selected a GABAB PAM drug candidate for development in substance use disorders and has successfully completed IND enabling studies. In addition, Addex is advancing a differentiated GABAB PAM compound for the treatment of chronic cough. Addex holds a 8.5% equity interest in a private spin out company, Neurosterix US Holdings LLC, which is advancing a portfolio of allosteric modulator programs, including M4 PAM for schizophrenia, psychosis and mood-related disorders and mGlu7 NAM for mood disorders. Addex has also invested in Stalicla, a private Swiss company pioneering a precision medicine approach for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.
Addex shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange and American Depositary Shares representing its shares are listed on the NASDAQ Capital Market, and trade under the ticker symbol “ADXN” on each exchange. For more information, visit www.addextherapeutics.com .

Jupiter Medical Center Foundation Raises Record $102 Million in Single Fiscal Year
Posted by cfelixcpa | Nov 15, 2026 | SF STAT! | 0 |
Fundraising milestone puts independent not-for-profit on par with academic health systems
November 3, 2026 – Jupiter Medical Center Foundation raised more than $102 million in philanthropic support during fiscal year 2026, marking the largest fundraising year in its history and a milestone aligned with much larger academic and multi-hospital health systems. The Foundation’s record-breaking success reflects a 61% increase in giving over the past three years.
More than 2,300 donors contributed between October 1, 2025, and September 30, 2026, fueling the continued transformation of Jupiter Medical Center (JMC), the region’s only independent, not-for-profit health system, anchored by a 340-bed hospital. Their support is accelerating investments in physician recruitment, advanced technology, expanded specialty services, research and future facilities designed to meet the growing healthcare needs of Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast.
“This milestone reflects a historic and transformative year for the future of healthcare for the region,” said Amit Rastogi, MD, MHCM, President and CEO of Jupiter Medical Center. “Across the country, communities are grappling with how to preserve local access to advanced care. Our donors have sent a powerful message that they want top-tier healthcare available to the community, and they are willing to invest in making that vision a reality.”
The fundraising success advances Jupiter Medical Center’s $500 million Generational Health campaign, a long-term initiative supporting the organization’s strategic vision to expand service lines, deliver leading-edge specialty care, recruit nationally recognized physicians, invest in next-generation technology and develop facilities capable of serving a rapidly growing region. The campaign has currently raised more than $293 million toward its goal and is on track to end a full year ahead of schedule because of this year’s fundraising momentum.
“There was a time when patients in our community felt they needed to travel to the Northeast to access highly specialized care,” continued Rastogi, who has overseen the hospital’s transformation since 2019. “Instead, now we have patients heading south for high-quality care at Jupiter Medical Center. Times have changed, largely thanks to the unwavering support of our donors.”
Jupiter Medical Center is currently undergoing the most transformative period. The health system has significantly expanded its clinical capabilities and physical footprint by creating and growing the Anderson Family Cancer Institute, developing the comprehensive Robson Heart and Vascular Institute, opening the state-of-the-art Johnny and Terry Gray Surgical Institute, and adding the highly specialized 92-bed Tim and Jayne Donahue Patient Care Tower. Looking ahead, the medical center plans to open its second hospital in Avenir in early 2028 and will soon break ground on the Margaret W. Niedland Breast Center expansion to increase access to advanced imaging services. Together, these investments have transformed Jupiter Medical Center into a leading regional healthcare destination. This growth reflects the hospital’s continued evolution as a comprehensive health system with increasingly sophisticated clinical capabilities across a broad range of specialties.
In January 2026, the Foundation announced a $35 million donation from Tim and Jayne Donahue to support the hospital’s Patient Care Tower. Within 90 days, the community responded by investing another $35 million in new pledges, additions to existing pledges, and donations from new donors – all inspired by the Donahues’ transformative investment. The momentum continued from there.
“Many of our philanthropic supporters have experienced the care provided at Jupiter Medical Center firsthand, either as patients or through their loved ones,” said Traci Simonsen, Chief Philanthropy Officer of Jupiter Medical Center Foundation. “Their generosity reflects trust in our mission and a shared belief that families deserve access to exceptional healthcare close to home. We are incredibly proud of what our community has made possible, and in many ways, we are just getting started. As an independent, not-for-profit health system, continued philanthropic support is essential to our mission in order to meet the needs for generations to come. Every gift helps build the future of healthcare for our community.”
Donor support is helping expand high-demand areas, including oncology, heart and vascular care, urology, gastroenterology, pulmonology, neurosciences, orthopedics, and women’s and infant’s services. The investments are intended to help patients access increasingly sophisticated care.
As healthcare organizations nationwide face increasing financial pressures, the Foundation’s record-breaking fundraising year demonstrates the powerful role philanthropy can play in helping independent hospitals remain innovative, responsive, community-focused and offer services philanthropic dollars can help provide.
For more information about Jupiter Medical Center, visit jupitermed.com, call (561) 263-2234, or follow Jupiter Medical Center on Facebook and Instagram @jupitermedicalcenter or on ‘X’ @JupiterMedCtr. For more information about Jupiter Medical Center Foundation, or the Generational Health campaign, visit jmcfoundation.org or call (561) 263-5728.

candidates.title: UC Davis spinout Delix Therapeutics raises USD 100m Series C after Phase Ib MDD data
candidates.snippet: UC Davis spinout Delix Therapeutics raises USD 100m Series C after Phase Ib MDD data AllSci
candidates.text:
Massachusetts-based Delix Therapeutics closed a USD 100 million Series C financing to take zalsupindole into Phase II. The company said a Phase Ib trial in adults with recurrent major depressive disorder (MDD) produced an approximately 50% mean reduction in Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale scores at Day 8, maintained through Day 36. ​
Johnson & Johnson, through Johnson & Johnson Innovation – JJDC, Inc., and SV Health Investors' Dementia Discovery Fund led the round. Existing investors RA Capital, UC Investments, Artis Ventures, OMX Ventures, Dolby Family Ventures, and Bail Capital participated, as did new investors including Adage Capital Management, Hamilton Square Partners Management, Vestal Point Capital, and YK Bioventures. Christian Jung of SV Health Investors and a JJDC representative have joined the board. The company's previous financings include a USD 70 million Series A in September 2021 and a convertible note financing of more than USD 30 million in January 2022 .
Zalsupindole is an orally bioavailable neuroplastogen inspired by 5-MeO-DMT (mebufotenin). Delix says it is engineered to promote structural and functional neuroplasticity without hallucinatory, dissociative, sedative, or other psychotomimetic effects. The company reported no such effects across more than 120 participants studied to date. It expects to start a placebo-controlled Phase II proof-of-concept trial in recurrent MDD in the first half of 2027, with a trial design that includes at-home administration.
Proceeds will also fund additional development candidates and expansion of the company's neurodegeneration program, which the company says has shown preclinical efficacy signals. The platform traces to the lab of David E. Olson at the University of California, Davis , which identifies Delix as a spinout. David E. Olson co-founded the company.

candidates.text:
XLIO Secures Additional $100 Million to Build Startups for Corporate Acquirers
News provided by
XLIO Ventures
10 Nov, 2026, 13:30 GMT
Share this article
Share this article
Global Made to Order™ startup builder to add Austin office, led by CEO Ron Kornfeld
AUSTIN, Texas , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XLIO has secured an additional $100 million to make its total available funding facility $150 Million. The funds will be deployed to build Made to Order startups for leading technology companies. CEO Ron Kornfeld will lead its new Austin, Texas office.
Made to Order gives organizations a different route to access new technology. Rather than buying an existing company and adapting it, a client defines the exact capability it needs. XLIO then funds and builds a dedicated startup to deliver it, located and incorporated wherever best suits the client. Once the company hits agreed KPIs, usually within one to three years, the client acquires both team and technology. Deals typically range from $10 million to $50 million.
The new funding allows XLIO to run more Made to Order engagements in parallel and to extend the model into both new sectors and geographies.
The Austin office, at 801 Barton Springs Rd, Austin 78704, Texas, puts XLIO close to the engineering talent, founders and corporate buyers that Made to Order is designed for. Austin-based startups raised a record $7.19 billion in venture funding in 2025, up 64.8% on 2024, according to Crunchbase.
That startup economy in the region has deep roots. IBM, Texas Instruments and Motorola opened operations in Austin between 1967 and 1974, and Dell was founded in the city in 1984. Their early presence built the engineering talent base that later drew the headquarters of companies such as Tesla to the region and now feeds a new generation of startups.
"Austin's startup economy is vibrant," said Ron Kornfeld, CEO of XLIO Ventures. "There's deep engineering talent here, a steady stream of experienced founders, and a business community that backs new companies. I've moved here because I want our clients to share in that. Made to Order lets a business tap into Austin's talent and pace to get the exact technology it needs, built by a team focused on nothing else. This funding means we can help many more of them gain a foothold here."
About XLIO
Founded in 2020 and headquartered in London and Seattle, XLIO Ventures gives organizations a new route to acquire the technology they need. Through its Made to Order™ model, XLIO funds and builds a dedicated technology company around a single client's exact need, then transfers it to the client through acquisition only once agreed performance goals are met. Led by CEO Ron Kornfeld and backed by private equity, XLIO works with technology vendors and other large organizations that build advantage by investing in their own proprietary technology. Learn more at xl.io.
Media contact
Andrew Moloney, XLIO Ventures, press@xl.io
