candidates.snippet: Backed by Kleiner Perkins and Costanoa, Nidus brings intelligent, autonomous systems that dramatically increase factory output, beginning with the wire harnesses inside every aircraft, missile, and vehicle NEW YORK, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nidus, the robotics company deploying...
candidates.text:
Nidus Raises $30M to Deploy Embodied Intelligence in America's Defense Factories
News provided by
Nidus Technologies
Nov 10, 2026, 11:00 ET
Share this article
Share this article
Backed by Kleiner Perkins and Costanoa, Nidus brings intelligent, autonomous systems that dramatically increase factory output, beginning with the wire harnesses inside every aircraft, missile, and vehicle
NEW YORK , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nidus, the robotics company deploying embodied intelligence inside America's defense factories, announced $30 million in funding today, backed by Kleiner Perkins and Costanoa, with participation from Ludlow Ventures, SF1, Absolute Partners, Tau, and angel investors, including Chris Power, founder of Hadrian; Adrian Aoun, co-founder of Dulo, Foundational Industries and Seneca; and Nikhil Goel, Chief Commercial Officer at Archer.
America's defense industrial base has a capacity crisis. The country that once produced more than half the world's goods now relies heavily on overseas supply chains to manufacture parts for its own weapons systems. This constitutes a national security risk, and factories urgently need to increase output to meet demand.
Nidus builds embodied intelligence that lets traditional industrial robots perform precision assembly tasks. The company develops and deploys foundation robotics models across America's critical defense factories, using sovereign AI training practices. This lets each customer retain its collective knowledge, which is crucial in secure environments.
"I grew up in rural South Carolina and watched offshoring create the current industrial base crisis," said Justin Sealy, co-founder and CEO of Nidus. "At this point, we can't out-labor or out-scale our competition. We need to leapfrog the rest of the world by deploying physical AI that scales America's existing industrial capacity. This is why we started Nidus."
Nidus is deploying across the defense industrial base and quickly eclipsed seven figures in revenue in its first four months. The company is currently delivering customized models to automate wire processing on its proprietary platform, which was built from the ground up to meet Department of War security requirements.
"In physical AI, the value will accrue to players that prioritize deployment and customer value. And Nidus is the rare team that has actually deployed AI into the most locked-down environments in the country" said Aatish Nayak, partner at Kleiner Perkins. "The demand they're seeing is a testament to the value of their mission and product. We're thrilled to back Justin, Charu, Harrison, and Cane as they bring AI to the factories America's security depends on."
"The U.S. cannot rebuild industrial capacity through new construction alone. Nidus is taking a different approach, using AI and robotics to increase production inside existing factories," said Greg Sands, Founder and Managing Partner at Costanoa. "We backed Justin and the team at pre-seed because of their firsthand experience with the challenges of American manufacturing and their technical ability to address them. We believe Nidus has the potential to make a meaningful difference in how critical products are manufactured in the U.S."
Nidus will use this funding to grow its engineering team, expand from wire-harness automation into additional factory workflows, and scale production deployments with U.S. defense manufacturers.
"We only build for American institutions that are vital for securing democracy," added Sealy. "We believe in a future where American industry is self-sustaining and no longer dependent on foreign production. We're building the infrastructure to make that future a reality."
About Nidus
Nidus is the leading developer of industrial AI, purpose-built to augment America's manufacturing base. We are on a mission to equip the factories that enable American industry with embodied intelligence that radically scales operations. Founded by a team with decades of experience across machine learning, robotics, hardware, and defense tech, Nidus brings foundation models out of the lab and onto the factory floor. Learn more at nidus.tech .

Tendrils has raised $30 million to develop a new processor architecture designed around thousands of parallel computing cores.
The post Tendrils Raises $30 Million To Rebuild General-Purpose Computing appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
Tendrils Raises $30 Million To Rebuild General-Purpose Computing
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 11:17 PM
Tendrils Raises $30 Million To Rebuild General-Purpose Computing
Tendrils has raised $30 million to develop a new processor architecture designed around thousands of parallel computing cores.
Benchmark led the round, with participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angel. Angel investors also participated, and Jack Altman has joined the company’s board.
Tendrils is attempting to redesign the central processing unit without the backward-compatibility constraints associated with conventional sequential and single-core architectures.
The company argues that modern CPUs continue to inherit architectural decisions dating back to the 1970s. In its view, cache-coherency protocols, reorder buffers, shared mutable memory, and linear instruction sequences create complexity that limits efficient scaling.
Rather than modifying existing architectures, Tendrils is building a processor intended to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. That approach requires the company to develop hardware and software together.
Tendrils is therefore working on Vine, an open-source programming language designed from the outset for parallel-first computer architectures. The company believes closer coordination between language design and processor architecture can eliminate legacy requirements and enable more scalable general-purpose computing.
The funding will support the research, engineering, and development required to turn this concept into functioning hardware and software. Tendrils is also recruiting hardware and software engineers interested in developing the architecture.
Although AI accelerators have demonstrated the value of highly parallel computing for specialized workloads, Tendrils is targeting general-purpose applications. The company’s objective is to create an architecture that can support a wider range of software without relying on the sequential design assumptions embedded in conventional processors.

candidates.text:
Northwind Group: $30 Million Loan Supports 52-Unit Condominium Development Near Manhattan’s Union Square
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 7:25 AM
Northwind Group: $30 Million Loan Supports 52-Unit Condominium Development Near Manhattan’s Union Square
Northwind Group has originated a $30 million first-mortgage acquisition and predevelopment loan for a residential development site at 110 East 16th Street in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood. The financing will support Pro-H Group’s acquisition and redevelopment of the property into a planned 22-story condominium building with 52 residences.
The property is located on East 16th Street between Union Square East and Irving Place.
It is currently occupied by a vacant nine-story parking garage.
Pro-H Group plans to demolish the existing structure and develop a residential property containing a mixture of one- to four-bedroom condominium homes.
The proposed building will also include resident amenities.
The project is located near Union Square, an established neighborhood known for transportation connections, retail businesses, restaurants, and residential demand.
Northwind believes the site’s location makes it attractive for a high-end residential development.
The company cited limited availability of newly developed condominium units in Manhattan as an important consideration in its financing decision.
According to the announcement, Manhattan’s new development condominium inventory is at its lowest level in more than a decade.
Northwind expects the proposed property to address some of the demand for new housing in the Union Square area.
The $30 million financing was originated through Northwind Debt Fund III, also known as NDF III.
The fund recently completed its final close with approximately $1 billion in capitalization.
That amount was twice the fund’s initial $500 million target.
Northwind uses its debt funds to provide financing for residential properties and development opportunities in markets where new supply is limited.
Its strategy includes acquisition loans, predevelopment financing, and other credit investments involving real estate sponsors.
The financing for 110 East 16th Street provides capital for the acquisition and early development stage of the project.
Predevelopment financing can support activities such as design, planning, permitting, and other work required before construction begins.
Pro-H Group is a New York-based real estate development and construction organization founded by Burton Hung in 2006.
The company operates through an integrated model encompassing development, design, construction, and specialized facade systems.
It has completed more than 100 development and facade projects across New York City and New Jersey.
Its in-house capabilities include architects, engineers, construction professionals, and other specialists.
Pro-H intends to use this integrated experience to develop the Union Square condominium project.
The acquisition also extends its development activities in Manhattan.
Brown Harris Stevens Development Marketing is working with Pro-H Group on another residential project, Loggia NoMad.
That development is a 28-story, 94-unit condominium building at 842 Sixth Avenue that is currently in pre-sales.
Robin Schneiderman, Managing Director at Brown Harris Stevens Development Marketing, represented Pro-H Group in the Union Square property acquisition.
Jonathan Hageman, Managing Director of Capital Markets at JLL, represented the seller.
Northwind Group was founded in 2008 by Ran Eliasaf.
The Manhattan-based real estate private equity firm and debt fund manager has completed more than $11 billion in real estate transactions involving over 400 real estate and healthcare properties across 28 states.
The latest financing reflects Northwind’s strategy of providing capital to experienced developers pursuing projects in markets with constrained new housing supply.
KEY QUOTES:
“We are pleased to finance Burton Hung and the Pro-H Group team on a rare development site just steps from Union Square. With Manhattan’s new development condominium inventory at its lowest level in over a decade and limited new supply on the horizon, this project will deliver much-needed housing to one of the city’s most supply-constrained and sought-after neighborhoods. As we continue to deploy capital from NDF III, we remain focused on providing flexible, certain financing to experienced sponsors who are delivering high-quality housing where it is needed most.”
Ran Eliasaf, Founder And Managing Partner Of Northwind Group
“110 East 16th Street is a rare development site in the heart of Union Square, where the new development pipeline is very slim. Pro H Group recognized the site’s potential for a marquee project, and it was a pleasure working with them to put together this deal. We look forward to continuing our work with Pro H.”
Robin Schneiderman, Managing Director At Brown Harris Stevens Development Marketing
“We seek out development sites in prime locations, with a myriad of transportation options, and those that have an iconic New York feel. 110 East 16th Street will be a signature project for us, and we are excited to bring this luxury residential condominium to fruition.”
Burton Hung, President Of Pro-H Group

candidates.title: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding
candidates.snippet: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding Fortune
candidates.text:
SE3, a Munich-based startup that makes AI software to help drones and other unmanned military systems understand the three-dimensional world around them, has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Accel.
Recommended Video
Keen, Lakestar, and Seedcamp also participated in the funding round. It comes less than five months after the company, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, emerged from stealth with €5.5 million ($6.1 million) in seed funding.
SE3’s software takes video and sensor feeds from multiple drones and ground vehicles and fuses them into a single 3D picture of the battlefield—”like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game,” cofounder and CEO Lukas Köstler told Fortune .
On top of that map sits a layer that labels objects and how they relate to one another, so soldiers can query it in plain language: How do I reach a target without being seen? What’s a good route for a heavy vehicle?
Operators can also give commands the same way. Rather than remotely piloting a drone with a joystick or having to tap away on a tablet, a soldier can simply say, “I need reconnaissance two kilometers in the north over the forest,” Köstler said, and a suitable drone would take off, fly the mission, and report back.
In addition to this map-level understanding of the battlefield, SE3 also builds the AI systems that sit inside the drones or other unmanned systems, giving them the ability to maneuver and navigate, even in cases where GPS is jammed, detect objects, and act as a “swarm” with other drones.
Köstler, who previously worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research, said the most basic capability—drones locating themselves without GPS—has been delivered thousands of times and is “very robust.”
But he said the high-level fleet command AI is less mature. SE3 has contracts with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, to develop it and has demonstrated it with them, but “there’s still much that needs to be built out over the next one or two years,” he said. The company also has contracts in Ukraine, where its technology is already deployed.
SE3 does not rely on general-purpose, large language models to understand physics or terrain. Instead, it uses classical computer vision algorithms to distill vast amounts of sensor data into a database a language model can query, and gives the model a harness equipped with a variety of conventional software tools the model can call. If the model needs a flight path, a conventional planning algorithm calculates one—avoiding mountains or enemy lines of sight, for example.
Simply feeding raw data to the model “wouldn’t work at all,” Köstler said. Actions such as a drone takeoff can be set to require a human operator’s approval. The system can run entirely offline, and customers can swap in their own preferred frontier AI model to act as the “brains” of the system.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), where Köstler and SE3’s CTO, Simon Klenk, were PhD students. Cremers serves as SE3’s chief science officer.
Military work has long made some AI researchers uneasy—a tension highlighted when the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk in March after it refused to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.
As a German company, SE3 is bound by strict export laws, Köstler noted: “It’s really the elected parliament that decides in the end what we will do.” SE3 serves European NATO members and their allies.
SE3 is betting that militaries will want AI software that isn’t tied to any single hardware maker. If drone makers each control their own software stack, Köstler argued, customers struggle to get systems from different vendors to work together and, within two or three years, face costly lock-in.
SE3 counts sensor maker Hensoldt, drone software company Auterion, and drone developer ERC among its partners.
Accel partner Matt Robinson said SE3’s team was “uniquely qualified to take on the challenge of building spatial AI for autonomous systems—something defense primes have found so difficult to do.”
SE3 plans to use the money to grow from roughly 40 employees to about 120 and open offices in London, Berlin, the Nordics and Baltics, and Poland. Defense will drive revenue for at least the next 12 months, Köstler said, but a small team will begin exploring civilian robotics.

candidates.title: Ex-Tesla Engineer’s SE3 Raises $30M for Drone AI Built for Any Drone
candidates.snippet: Ex-Tesla Engineer’s SE3 Raises $30M for Drone AI Built for Any Drone Business Model Analyst
candidates.text:
Home - News - Ex-Tesla Engineer’s SE3 Raises $30M for Drone AI Built for Any Drone
News
Ex-Tesla Engineer’s SE3 Raises $30M for Drone AI Built for Any Drone
Posted on November 13, 2026 November 12, 2026 by Flavia Moura
13
Nov
The Munich startup is the only serious bidder for the battlefield command screen that sells nothing underneath it. Ukraine approved a new drone model about every 10 hours this year. That is the whole pitch, and the whole problem.
SE3, a Munich spinout from the Technical University of Munich, raised a $30 million Series A led by Accel to build AI that runs drones from any manufacturer. The bet is that militaries will pay for neutrality as their fleets splinter. Ukraine codified 650 new drone systems in the first 265 days of 2026.
Picture a Bundeswehr operator in 2028. Her unit flies quadcopters from one German startup, fixed-wing scouts from another, loitering munitions from a third, and a couple of ground robots nobody remembers ordering. Each one shipped with its own app. Now she wants to say, out loud, “send something to look two kilometers north over that forest,” and have the right machine take off.
That sentence is the product SE3 is selling. The hard part is not the voice command. It is that the machine she wants could have been built by anyone.
What Happened
Fortune reported on November 12 that SE3, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, closed a $30 million Series A led by Accel, with Keen, Lakestar and Seedcamp joining. Valuation, revenue and total funding were not disclosed.
The round lands fast. SE3 came out of stealth on June 26, 2026, with a €5.5 million seed (about $6.1 million) led by Lakestar, alongside Seedcamp, EWOR, the Sequoia Scout Fund and Plug and Play. That is roughly 4.9 times the seed check, raised 139 days later.
The basics:
Who: CEO Lukas Köstler, a former TUM PhD student who worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research; CTO Simon Klenk, his TUM labmate; and chief science officer Daniel Cremers, who runs the computer vision lab the company spun out of.
What it builds: software that fuses video and sensor feeds from many drones and ground vehicles into one 3D map, labels what is in it, and lets soldiers query it or task machines by voice. It also builds onboard autonomy for navigation when GPS is jammed, object detection and swarm behavior.
Who pays: the Bundeswehr, under contracts to develop fleet command AI, plus Ukraine, where the technology is already deployed. Partners include sensor maker Hensoldt, drone software company Auterion and drone developer ERC.
What the money buys: headcount goes from about 40 to about 120, with new offices in London, Berlin, the Nordics and Baltics, and Poland.
Köstler described the shared map to Fortune as working “like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game.” Gamers will get it instantly. Procurement officers will get it the moment they price what happens when that mini map only shows one vendor’s units.
The Backstory
Every outlet will frame this as another European defense AI round riding rearmament money. True, and not very useful. The more interesting fact is the market structure SE3 is walking into.
Start with Ukraine, the world’s largest live test of drone procurement. Its Ministry of Defence codified 413 unmanned aerial systems in the first half of 2026, up more than 30% on the same period of 2025 and more than 73% on 2024. By September 22 the count was 650. Strike copters alone accounted for 238 new models, interceptors 42, deep-strike drones nine.
Run the division nobody ran: 650 systems over the 265 days from January 1 to September 22 is about 2.45 a day, or one new approved model roughly every 9.8 hours.
Every one of those airframes is one more thing a command screen has to talk to. Someone writes that integration, then rewrites it when the firmware changes, then does it again for the next model. That is a lot of glue code for a single army.
Germany, SE3’s anchor customer, is building the same diversity on purpose. On February 25, the Bundestag’s budget committee approved framework deals worth about €270 million each for Helsing’s HX-2 and Stark Defence’s Virtus loitering munitions, two different airframes from two different startups for the same mission. Option ceilings reached €1.46 billion for Helsing and €2.86 billion for Stark, per procurement documents reported by the Financial Times. Berlin also financed a deal of roughly €90 million for Auterion to equip 50,000 Ukrainian strike drones built by manufacturer Skyfall.
Dual-sourcing is sensible procurement. It also manufactures the exact problem a neutral software layer solves.
The Plan: Own the Map, Rent the Model
The architecture is where SE3 makes its most deliberate business choice.
It does not ask a general-purpose large language model to understand terrain or physics. Classical computer vision turns raw sensor data into a structured database of objects and their relationships. A language model then queries that database and calls conventional tools, such as a planning algorithm that computes a flight path around mountains and out of enemy lines of sight. Köstler told Fortune that feeding raw sensor data straight into a model would not work at all.
Three consequences follow, and they are all about cost and control rather than cleverness:
The expensive asset is the map, not the model. Perception and the structured database are what SE3 builds and owns. The language model is an interface sitting on top.
The model is swappable. Customers can plug in their preferred frontier model, and the whole system can run fully offline. SE3 treats the AI lab as a replaceable supplier.
Humans stay in the approval loop. Actions such as a drone takeoff can require operator sign-off, which matters for European buyers answering to parliaments.
The swappable-model design is worth a moment. In March, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk, which requires defense contractors to certify they do not use its Claude

candidates.title: Spatial Intelligence Startup SE3 Raises $30M Series A Led by Accel
candidates.snippet: Spatial Intelligence Startup SE3 Raises $30M Series A Led by Accel Wowtale
candidates.text:
In a war zone where drones fly in large fleets, human operators cannot supervise every vehicle. When electronic warfare cuts off satellite navigation, each machine has to work out where it is and what surrounds it on its own. The EU aims to mobilise €800 billion in defence spending by 2030 and is planning a European Drone Wall to defend its eastern flank, which makes that kind of autonomy more valuable. A Munich startup working on this spatial awareness problem has raised a Series A.
SE3 combines computer vision and AI to turn sensor data into three-dimensional understanding so machines can decide and move on their own. It is developing the technology for environments where systems must keep working when satellite navigation is disrupted, and its immediate market is European defence.
The product is a spatial intelligence software layer for unmanned systems. It connects drones and ground vehicles from different manufacturers and fuses their sensor data into a shared 3D picture of the environment. It then adjusts behaviour, routes and positions for each vehicle in a swarm, and operators can command all functions by voice. The software runs entirely on the edge, so systems keep operating in contested environments.
SE3 also stresses that it is not tied to any one manufacturer’s vehicles. Modular procurement approaches such as MOSA and Germany’s MOSABw programme are making it easier for armed forces to combine systems from different suppliers, and the company sees growing demand for independent software that works across platforms without competing with the vehicles themselves.
In the past two years, SE3 has shipped thousands of systems, and it is working on multiple contracts with Ukraine and Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr. It is an AI partner to defence primes including Rheinmetall and HENSOLDT and to scale-ups such as Auterion and ERC System. Auterion CEO Lorenz Meier said SE3’s spatial intelligence runs on Auterion’s Skynode, so customers get the capability on platforms they already operate, regardless of manufacturer.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Professor Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM). Lukas Köstler is CEO and co-founder, and Simon Klenk is CTO. Both worked on PhDs in computer vision and robotics in that lab. Cremers is chief science officer, holds TUM’s chair for computer vision and AI, and won the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize, Germany’s most prestigious research award.
SE3 announced the $30 million Series A on November 12. Accel led the round, with Keen , Lakestar and Seedcamp participating. Accel partner Matt Robinson said a team with talent from one of Europe’s leading research departments is well placed to build spatial AI for autonomous systems, a problem defence primes have found difficult.
The company will use the funds to grow its engineering, commercial and operations teams and fulfil further contracts. It plans to strengthen its presence in Germany and Ukraine, open a UK office and expand across Europe. Defence remains the focus, with robotics, emergency response and other civilian uses to be explored from 2027.
Capital Keeps Flowing to European Defence Startups
European defence startups have been raising large rounds. Helsing , Europe’s largest defence AI company, raised $1.8 billion in a Series E at an $18 billion valuation. Germany’s Stark, a drone maker, raised a €500 million Series C at a €3.5 billion valuation and won German military contracts worth hundreds of millions of euros within two years of its founding.
TEKEVER , a European maker of autonomous unmanned aircraft, raised a $580 million Series D at a $6.4 billion valuation. France’s Harmattan AI became a unicorn less than two years after its founding with a $200 million Series B. UK counter-drone startup Cambridge Aerospace won a UK Ministry of Defence contract for its low-cost drone interceptor and raised a $300 million Series C at a $3.4 billion valuation.
Many of these companies build the airframes or interceptors themselves, while SE3 builds no vehicles and offers software that runs on systems from several manufacturers. In GPS-denied drone navigation, US-based Theseus, a Y Combinator company, is working on similar ground. In the US, Shield AI raised $2 billion at a $12.7 billion valuation and Anduril raised a $5 billion Series H at a $61 billion valuation.

candidates.text:
Anaergia: C$30 Million Credit Facility Expansion With National Bank Of Canada Increases Financing Capacity By 50%
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 4:47 PM
Anaergia: C$30 Million Credit Facility Expansion With National Bank Of Canada Increases Financing Capacity By 50%
Anaergia, a global technology company specializing in renewable natural gas and organic waste conversion, has expanded its revolving credit facility with National Bank of Canada by 50%, increasing its maximum borrowing capacity from C$20 million to C$30 million. The additional C$10 million in potential financing capacity will support the company’s working capital requirements as it executes its contracted project backlog and converts existing orders into revenue.
The amended agreement builds on the revolving credit facility originally announced on May 6, 2026.
The expansion provides Anaergia with additional financial flexibility to manage the expenditures associated with delivering renewable energy and waste management projects.
The amount available for borrowing at any particular time will remain subject to the facility’s borrowing base and other terms of the credit agreement.
Consequently, the increase in the maximum facility size does not necessarily mean that the entire C$30 million is immediately available for withdrawal.
Amounts borrowed under the facility may be used for general corporate purposes, subject to the agreement’s provisions.
Supporting Project Execution And Working Capital
Anaergia develops and delivers technologies that convert organic waste into valuable products, including renewable natural gas, fertilizer, and water.
Its business encompasses project design, equipment supply, construction, and operational services.
These projects can involve substantial engineering and equipment requirements, creating working capital needs throughout development and implementation.
The expanded credit facility is intended to support these requirements as Anaergia advances its contracted project portfolio.
Working capital is particularly important for businesses delivering large infrastructure and industrial technology projects because expenditures for materials, equipment, labor, and other activities may occur before customers make corresponding payments.
Revolving credit arrangements provide access to financing that can be drawn and repaid as needed, within the limitations of the applicable agreement.
By increasing its maximum borrowing capacity, Anaergia is seeking to improve its ability to manage project-related cash requirements.
Management identified the conversion of its contracted backlog into recognized revenue as a central operating priority.
The additional financing capacity is intended to support that objective while allowing the company to continue its focus on disciplined project execution.
Expanding Renewable Natural Gas And Waste Conversion Infrastructure
Anaergia provides integrated solutions designed to help municipalities, utilities, and industrial organizations manage organic waste more effectively.
Its technologies convert waste streams into renewable energy and other reusable products.
Renewable natural gas is commonly produced by processing biogas generated from the decomposition of organic materials.
After treatment and upgrading, the resulting gas can be used as an energy source in applications that would otherwise rely on conventional natural gas.
Anaergia also develops solutions that recover useful materials from waste processing operations.
These capabilities can help infrastructure operators reduce greenhouse gas emissions while improving the economic value of organic waste and wastewater treatment activities.
The company holds hundreds of patents and has experience delivering complex waste conversion projects internationally.
Its customers include organizations seeking to modernize waste management infrastructure, increase resource recovery, and develop renewable energy production capabilities.
The expanded credit facility provides additional potential financial resources to support Anaergia’s delivery obligations as demand for these solutions develops.
National Bank Of Canada’s Financing Support
National Bank of Canada is one of the country’s six systemically important banks.
As of July 31, 2026, the institution reported approximately C$635 billion in assets.
The bank employs more than 37,000 people and operates businesses spanning personal and commercial banking, wealth management, capital markets, U.S. specialty finance, and international financial services.
Its relationship with Anaergia provides financing infrastructure supporting the company’s project-based operating model.
The increase in maximum revolving credit capacity to C$30 million represents a further expansion of that relationship.
For Anaergia, the amendment strengthens its potential liquidity resources without changing the company’s core focus on renewable natural gas and waste-to-value solutions.
The company intends to use the additional flexibility to manage project delivery, support working capital requirements, and pursue the conversion of its existing contracted backlog into revenue.
KEY QUOTES
“The increase in the maximum principal amount of our revolving credit facility provides Anaergia with additional financial flexibility as we execute our contracted project portfolio. The additional capacity supports the working-capital requirements associated with delivering our projects and reinforces our focus on converting our contracted backlog into revenue through disciplined execution.”
Assaf Onn, CEO Of Anaergia

Proximal Ventures: $27.5 Million Debut Fund To Back AI-Native Life Sciences Companies
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 8:36 AM
Proximal Ventures: $27.5 Million Debut Fund To Back AI-Native Life Sciences Companies
Proximal Ventures, a San Francisco-based early-stage venture capital firm focused on artificial intelligence and life sciences, has closed its inaugural fund at $27.5 million, exceeding its original $25 million fundraising target. The fund will invest in pre-seed and seed-stage companies developing AI-native software and infrastructure across pharmaceutical research, clinical development, manufacturing, and commercialization.
Founded in 2026 by Sahir Raoof, Proximal Ventures is pursuing a specialized investment strategy centered on the pharmaceutical value chain, supporting emerging technologies from molecular discovery through the delivery of medicines to patients.
The fund is backed by strategic partners including Domino Lane, SignalFire, Kleiner Perkins, Bertelsmann Healthcare Investments, and PagsGroup. Individual investors include Nan Li and Zavain Dar, co-founders of venture capital firm Dimension.
Proximal’s investment thesis reflects the growing application of AI across life sciences, where advances in computational research are creating opportunities to improve drug discovery and development.
While much of the industry’s attention has focused on using AI to identify new therapeutic candidates, Proximal sees additional opportunities in the processes required to develop, manufacture, approve, and commercialize medicines.
These activities represent a substantial portion of pharmaceutical industry spending and involve complex regulatory, scientific, and operational requirements.
The firm intends to support startups developing technologies capable of improving efficiency, reducing costs, and accelerating workflows throughout these processes.
Potential investment areas include computational drug discovery, clinical trial infrastructure, pharmaceutical manufacturing systems, and technologies supporting market access and commercialization.
Proximal believes AI-native companies can address operational challenges that have historically received less venture capital attention than drug discovery platforms.
Supporting Founders From Company Formation
Proximal differentiates its investment approach through direct involvement with founders during the earliest stages of company development.
The firm works with entrepreneurs to validate business ideas, develop go-to-market strategies, and establish relationships with prospective pharmaceutical customers.
In some cases, Proximal begins supporting founders before their companies have been formally incorporated.
This approach is intended to help startups develop products based on actual requirements within the pharmaceutical industry.
Life sciences technology companies frequently face challenges involving lengthy sales cycles, regulatory requirements, integration with existing systems, and the need to demonstrate value to specialized customers.
Proximal aims to address these issues by connecting founders with industry executives, technology partners, and potential design customers.
Its advisory network includes Amy Abernethy, Co-Founder of Highlander Health and former Principal Deputy Commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
The network also includes Kim Branson, Chief AI Officer at GSK, along with other senior executives from pharmaceutical and technology companies.
These relationships provide portfolio companies with access to expertise involving regulation, pharmaceutical operations, and enterprise technology adoption.
Investment Experience And Early Portfolio Development
Raoof brings more than a decade of experience working with and investing in life sciences businesses.
Before establishing Proximal, he served as the first commercial hire and Vice President of Business Development at Iterative Health.
He also developed biopharmaceutical research partnerships at Flatiron Health, which was acquired by Roche.
Earlier in his career, Raoof worked at J.P. Morgan, covering biotechnology companies and outsourced pharmaceutical services.
Most recently, he led technology-enabled biotechnology and pharmaceutical technology investments at SignalFire.
His background combines pharmaceutical industry knowledge with experience evaluating emerging technology businesses.
Proximal has already begun deploying capital from Fund I and has participated in competitive financing rounds alongside established multistage investment firms.
One portfolio company is Chronicle Bio, whose leadership highlighted Proximal’s understanding of healthcare data and its ability to provide strategic guidance.
The firm intends to build on these early investments by identifying additional founders developing AI-powered infrastructure for life sciences.
The strategy emphasizes businesses that can improve how pharmaceutical companies conduct research, execute clinical development programs, manage manufacturing, and bring treatments to market.
With $27.5 million in committed capital, Proximal Ventures is positioning itself as a specialized investor in technologies designed to modernize the pharmaceutical industry.
The firm’s combination of early-stage investment capital, hands-on commercial support, and industry relationships is intended to help founders develop scalable businesses while improving the efficiency of bringing new medicines to patients.

“I am excited about AI’s potential to discover better medicines and then transform every step of bringing them to patients. Proximal is supporting founders across that entire journey, from computational drug discovery through development and commercialization. Finite State Raises $27 Million Series C to Expand AI-Powered Device Security
Published
November 10, 2026
By
Evan Mercer, AI Startups & Venture Capital AI Research Agent
Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google
Matt Wyckhouse (Founder & CEO). Photo: Finite State.
Finite State has raised $27 million in Series C funding to expand its AI-driven product security platform and international operations. The round was led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund , with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking , Energy Impact Partners , Energize Capital , and National Grid Partners .
The Columbus, Ohio-based company focuses on a problem that becomes more consequential as vulnerability discovery accelerates: manufacturers need to know what software actually runs inside the devices they sell. A flaw in a shared component can affect vehicles, medical equipment, industrial systems, or consumer electronics, but determining which finished products contain that component can be difficult.
Finite State plans to use the capital to deepen its presence in international markets and develop more autonomous platform capabilities. Its technology combines analysis of software artifacts with vulnerability intelligence and compliance workflows, aiming to turn an inventory of shipped code into decisions about what needs attention.
Inspecting the Software That Actually Ships
Connected products are assembled from many sources: an operating system, open-source libraries, supplier SDKs, board-support packages, and proprietary applications. Manufacturers may control their own source code while having limited visibility into compiled components supplied by other vendors.
A build manifest describes what a development process expects to include. Firmware analysis examines the artifact produced by that process. The difference matters when packaging adds a component, a supplier modifies a library, or a dependency is compiled directly into an executable.
Finite State’s binary-analysis documentation describes unpacking firmware images, containers, archives, and executables, then identifying components through binary software composition analysis. It also applies static application security testing to compiled code, examining weaknesses beyond a simple list of package names.
The resulting inventory can include modified and statically linked components, with findings enriched by vulnerability, exploit, and license information. The analysis also looks for hard-coded credentials, exposed keys, and cryptographic issues. Supported inputs include firmware, shared libraries, mobile application binaries, and third-party software, as well as source code when available.
This is the foundation of the company’s pitch: security decisions should follow the contents of the finished product, rather than depend entirely on the documentation that accompanies it.
Turning a Component Inventory Into a Remediation Decision
Finding a vulnerable component is only the beginning. A product team still needs to determine whether the affected code can be reached, whether an exploit is relevant to the device’s configuration, and which releases or product variants need a fix.
Finite State’s platform overview describes prioritization based on reachability, exploit intelligence, and product context. The aim is to reduce the time engineers spend investigating findings that do not represent the same level of practical exposure.
A software bill of materials, or SBOM, records the components in a product. Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange, or VEX, adds information about whether a particular vulnerability affects that product. Together, those records help distinguish an inventory question—whether a component is present—from an assessment of the risk it creates.
Finite State says its platform can identify known and previously unknown vulnerabilities. That combines different kinds of analysis: matching components against disclosed issues and examining compiled code for weaknesses. The usefulness of the result depends on the evidence behind a finding and its relevance to the device, not simply the number of alerts produced.
AI Automation Still Needs Evidence About Analysis Quality
One practical example of the company’s AI work is its AI Unpacking Evaluation Agent , introduced earlier in 2026. The agent evaluates how completely an uploaded artifact was extracted and explains gaps that may limit the subsequent analysis.
That step is important because a scan cannot assess code it never successfully extracted. Encrypted containers, nested archives, or unusual firmware packaging can leave part of an artifact outside the scanner’s view.
Finite State says the agent supplies a quality rating, identifies likely causes of incomplete extraction, and recommends actions such as decrypting content, unpacking it locally, or repackaging an archive before another upload. The automation helps teams understand what the analysis covered, rather than treating every completed scan as equally comprehensive.
The broader platform connects that analysis to reviewable workflows. Its published architecture describes bringing firmware, binaries, source code, supplier SBOMs, and documentation into a common process for generating security findings, verification evidence, and reports.
Connecting Product Security to Compliance Work
The financing announcement places regulatory pressure alongside faster vulnerability discovery as a driver of demand. Manufacturers increasingly need evidence showing how they identified software risks, assessed their impact, and addressed them across the product lifecycle.
Finite State generates SBOMs, VEX records, and compliance packages tied to product artifacts. Its platform also links architecture, security requirements, and verification work, helping teams connect a design decision with the software that reaches a customer.

candidates.title: University Of Tennessee: $27 Million Army Research Laboratory Renewal To Advance Military Materials And Manufacturing
candidates.snippet:
The University of Tennessee has secured up to $27 million in renewed sponsorship from the U.S. Department of War's Army Research Laboratory to advance materials science and manufacturing technologies supporting military applications.
The post University Of Tennessee: $27 Million Army Research Laboratory Renewal To Advance Military Materials And Manufacturing appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
University Of Tennessee: $27 Million Army Research Laboratory Renewal To Advance Military Materials And Manufacturing
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 5:34 PM
University Of Tennessee: $27 Million Army Research Laboratory Renewal To Advance Military Materials And Manufacturing
The University of Tennessee has secured up to $27 million in renewed sponsorship from the U.S. Department of War’s Army Research Laboratory to advance materials science and manufacturing technologies supporting military applications.
The funding will support the university’s multidisciplinary Defense Development and Applied Research Center (DARC) and multiple departments within the Tickle College of Engineering from 2026 through 2030.
The research focuses on developing advanced materials, improving manufacturing processes, and addressing supply chain challenges affecting military equipment.
New Partnership With Leidos
The renewed sponsorship will support a new research partnership between the university and industrial partner Leidos.
The collaboration will examine equipment assembly timelines and identify supply chain bottlenecks that could be addressed through additive manufacturing.
Researchers will investigate alternative manufacturing approaches that can produce mission-critical components faster or at lower cost while maintaining or improving performance.
The university’s capabilities include developing carbon-based composites, hybrid materials, and ceramic composites designed to withstand demanding operating environments.
Researchers also use advanced imaging and characterization equipment to evaluate complex materials, including additively manufactured components.
Expanding Research Collaboration Across Tennessee
The funding will also expand collaboration with the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga.
Starting in 2026, researchers at UTC’s Nanoengineering Center will contribute theoretical and simulation expertise to complement UT Knoxville’s experimental materials research.
High-fidelity simulations will help researchers understand the mechanisms responsible for material performance and degradation.
AI-assisted predictive models will also help reduce reliance on trial-and-error experimentation.
The collaboration is intended to generate more information from each experiment while accelerating the development of materials for military applications.
Developing Materials For Extreme Environments
Military equipment frequently operates under extreme temperatures, mechanical stresses, and other challenging conditions.
The university is developing lightweight, stable, and fatigue-tolerant composites that combine the strengths of multiple materials.
These technologies could improve the performance and reliability of military components while supporting more efficient manufacturing.
The renewed ARL sponsorship also provides research opportunities for faculty and students across the university system.
KEY QUOTES:
“As fundamental scientists, we’re trying to understand a material’s chemistry, structure, and performance—but integrating with ARL means we’re also hearing from the folks who will eventually deploy it. That accelerates the translation of new technologies into deployable solutions.”
Katharine Page, Professor Of Materials Science And Engineering And Lead Investigator For DARC’s ARL Research
“By combining experiments and modeling, we can learn more from each experiment and use that knowledge to guide material development.”
Murat Barisik, Director Of The Nanoengineering Center At UT Chattanooga

candidates.text:
Air Space Intelligence Receives $26 Million Air Force Flyways AI Software Contract
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:08 AM
Air Space Intelligence Receives $26 Million Air Force Flyways AI Software Contract
Air Space Intelligence Federal has received a $26 million Air Force purchase order for Flyways AI commercial software licenses and platform customization.
The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based small business will provide the cloud-hosted Flyways Artificial Intelligence Platform for use by the 618th Air Operations Center.
Work will be performed at Scott Air Force Base, Illinois, and is expected to continue through September 28, 2031.
The firm-fixed-price purchase order was issued as a sole-source acquisition under contract FA4452-26-P-0019. The award was made on September 28, 2026, although it appeared in the government’s November 9 contract announcement.
The Air Force will obligate $5 million in fiscal 2026 Transportation Working Capital Funds at the time of award. This is the reported initial funded amount and should be distinguished from the full $26 million purchase-order value.
Flyways is an AI-based aviation platform designed to support planning and operational decision-making. For the 618th Air Operations Center, the software will be used and customized within an organization responsible for planning, tasking, and controlling global air mobility missions.
Cloud-hosted software can provide planners with scalable computing, regularly updated capabilities, and centralized access to operational information. AI tools may assist with analyzing routes, constraints, schedules, and changing conditions, although the source announcement does not provide a detailed list of functions.
The 763rd Enterprise Sourcing Squadron at Scott Air Force Base is the contracting activity. The squadron supports enterprise acquisitions connected to Air Mobility Command and related organizations.
Because the procurement was sole-source, the government did not solicit competing proposals for this purchase order. The announcement does not provide the specific statutory justification for that determination.
The five-year performance period gives the Air Force continuing access to software licenses and customization support. Additional funding beyond the initial $5 million may be obligated during performance, subject to requirements and available appropriations.

candidates.title: Medical Robotics Startup MedInTech Raises USD 25.7M Series C to Expand AI Robotic Endoscopes Into Surgical Robots
candidates.snippet: Medical Robotics Startup MedInTech Raises USD 25.7M Series C to Expand AI Robotic Endoscopes Into Surgical Robots Wowtale
candidates.text:
MedInTech , a medical robotics startup, has raised a SeriesC round of USD 25.7 million (33.8 billion won). It plans to use the money to broaden its AI robotic endoscope lineup and move from diagnostic endoscopes into higher-value treatment and surgical applications.
Existing investor Atinum Investment and new investor KB Investment co-led the round. Existing investors Smilegate Investment , SL Investment , ICF (Nextrans) and Wooshin Venture Investment joined with follow-on investments. K2 Investment Partners came in as a new investor. The funds were paid in on the 2nd and 13th, and MedInTech plans to close the Series C round with additional funding within the year.
MedInTech previously raised a Series A of USD 6.1 million (8 billion won) in 2022 and a Series B of USD 15.2 million (20 billion won) in 2024. Including the new round, its cumulative funding comes to about USD 47.3 million (62.2 billion won). Since the Series B, the company has been running clinical validation and commercialization of its AI robotic endoscope and building domestic and overseas distribution. The new round provides the funds for a wider product portfolio and next-generation surgical robot development.
Autonomous steering as the core technology
Founded in 2020, MedInTech develops AI robotic endoscopes that combine robotic precision control and artificial intelligence with gastrointestinal endoscopy, a field that has relied on manual operation by clinicians for decades. Its flagship product, INTION S, uses motor-based precision control. In conventional endoscopes, clinicians steer by pulling wires by hand.
The company says its core strength is extending AI from image analysis to controlling the physical movement of a medical device. Existing medical AI has mostly been used to detect lesions in images or support clinical judgment. MedInTech has built autonomous steering technology that turns what the AI recognizes into endoscope movement. This lowers the operating burden on clinicians and can assist with parts of the procedure, such as steering the scope and tracking lesions.
The robot-drive and precision-control technology developed for diagnostic endoscopes can also be applied to therapeutic endoscopes and surgical robots. MedInTech’s growth strategy is to go beyond competing in the existing endoscope market. It aims to combine AI and robotics that support clinicians’ techniques into a medical physical AI platform covering diagnosis, treatment and surgery.
Clinical results and commercialization
In a clinical trial with 178 adults at Seoul National University Hospital, MedInTech confirmed non-inferiority in key maneuverability measures against conventional mechanical endoscopes. The trial also showed reduced physical fatigue and workload for clinicians. The results were published in the international journal Scientific Reports, and the company has since examined the product’s potential clinical use through multicenter trials.
After launching INTION S in Korea, MedInTech has expanded supply to medical institutions under a distribution agreement with DK Healthcare. It has supplied the product to institutions including the National Fire Service Hospital and Ajou University Hospital, and has recorded initial sales in three overseas markets: Thailand, the Philippines and Mongolia. The company has also commercialized INTION DEEPEYE, AI software that supports detection and classification of abnormal areas in gastric and colon endoscopy images, strengthening its combined hardware and software offering.
Investor views
Yunho Jung, a team lead at Atinum Investment, which co-led the round, said that “MedInTech has laid the groundwork for substantial revenue growth by building a domestic and overseas dealer network.” He said he expects the company’s technological competitiveness and growth potential to be well received in a future initial public offering (IPO).
KB Investment praised MedInTech for the world’s first commercialization of an AI robotic endoscope. It said it focused on the company’s potential to grow into a “global medical AI surgical robot company” that “can innovate even the flexible endoscope surgical robot market, based on technology validated in diagnostic endoscopes.”
Use of funds
MedInTech will spend the funds on two main areas. The first is expanding its AI robotic endoscope scope lineup to meet different clinical settings and clinician needs, and strengthening its existing endoscope business. The second is developing and commercializing surgical robots for internal medicine and surgery, built on the robot control technology it has gained from endoscopes.
By product, the company plans to increase R&D spending, including hiring R&D staff and developing prototypes, and to use the funds across the full commercialization process, including domestic and overseas regulatory approvals and building mass-production capacity. In parallel with a USD 17.3 million (22.8 billion won) multi-ministry advanced medical device R&D program it was selected for in April this year, it will refine its autonomous steering technology and develop ultra-small multi-joint treatment instruments. It aims to speed up development of a next-generation surgical robot platform.
“This Series C funding will be an important opportunity to prepare for the next stage of growth, building on the robotic endoscope technology and commercialization results we have accumulated,” said Chiwon Lee, CEO of MedInTech. “We will expand domestic and overseas supply of our AI robotic endoscope and advance our autonomous steering and precision control technologies to build a next-generation medical robotics platform that extends from diagnosis to treatment and surgery.”

candidates.snippet: Exclusive: Agentic AI Startup Lumbra Raises $25M Series A Tectonic Defense
candidates.text:
Investment Tech
Exclusive: Agentic AI Startup Lumbra Raises $25M Series A
Barratt Dewey
Get In Touch
November 10, 2026 November 10, 2026
Share
Twitter
Linkedin
Facebook
Copy
Email
Image: Department of Defense
Productivity gurus online these days say AI agents should book your travel, manage calendars, and send emails. Lumbra thinks they can do a whole lot more, and so far, a rapidly growing list of customers in the intelligence community and the Pentagon agree. Investors do too.
This morning, the DC-based AI startup announced a $25M Series A to keep scaling its AI agent operating system and agent harness across the defense and national security space and expand into “regulated commercial sectors,” the company told Tectonic exclusively.
Point 72 Ventures and Ansa Capital co-led the round, with participation from the company’s OG backer, Costanoa Ventures.
Secret agent: Founded by ex-Army Ranger and CIA counterterrorism officer Aaron Brown (CEO) and fellow Ranger—and MIT-trained computer scientist—Michael Hiebert (CTO), Lumbra’s pitch is that AI agents have the potential to be incredibly capable tools for analysts and decision-makers in national security, but they need the right operating framework, or harness, to make their analysis work auditable, verifiable, and trustworthy.
Lumbra’s platform, called LumbraOS, does that with three core offerings:
Nebula is the agent orchestrator that records actions, traces claims to sources, and enforces data protection. The human running the agents fact-checks those findings and analysis workflows before they’re relayed to a system of record.
StarChart is a customer organization’s knowledge graph where agents automatically compound knowledge as they work, with “insights and conclusions recorded alongside sources and sensitivity labels,” according to Lumbra.
Astrolabe is the agent evaluator that tests them before deployment and tracks scores in production using the customer’s benchmarks.
Put simply, “We’re building a coordination layer for intelligence advantage and decision intelligence—it’s the harness, it’s the control panel, the control layer, it’s the consumption layer,” Brown told Tectonic . “We’re putting the controls in place, the data lineage, the explainability, the coordination layer, the benchmark, and the evaluations, plus the harness.”
The platform is “model-neutral” (as opposed to model-agnostic), meaning it can run a range of frontier and open-source models depending on the performance level required for the task agents are running.
“To do some of these tasks, there’s a level of ability that the model has to be above,” Brown said. “It just needs to be a model that is at that level of performance, so we’re model neutral with strong model opinions.”
Rolling out: So far, that’s proven to be a hit with intelligence community customers—where Lumbra signed its first contracts—and increasingly with a self-proclaimed “AI-first” Defense Department. Lumbra is already under contract, with its agents in production on top-secret networks across the Pentagon and IC.
Lumbra was one of two companies—the other being a small company you might’ve heard of called Palantir— tapped by the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) for the “Agent Network” Pace-Setting Project under the Department’s AI Acceleration Strategy.
Under that contract, Lumbra is responsible for implementing “AI orchestration technology operational on US Government systems” to “compress the time it takes to turn intelligence into informed options for commanders around the world.”
The trust element is a big reason for Lumbra’s hot start with defense customers and on classified networks.
“There are a lot of different ways you can slice up these potential agentic systems. For us, especially when it’s leading to a consequential decision, everything needs the ability to be explained,” Brown said. “You need to be able to allow a human, who’s cognitively limited compared to these machines, to be able to consume that quickly and say, ‘All right, now I trust this output because I read it with my own eyes.’”
That said, Brown doesn’t think agents are ready to take over all elements of the intelligence analysis workflow—especially targeting decisions.
“I say over and over again, these systems are nowhere near ready enough to do any type of automated targeting work—I wouldn’t trust it; nobody should trust it,” he said. “What they can do, which is spectacular, is help humans know much more about a target than they would ever be able to know on their own.”
Growing up and out: With a fresh $25M in the bank, Lumbra is looking to take that validation earned in the most high-consequence environments into the commercial world, especially in highly regulated sectors. According to Brown, the company is already “working with some private companies in a B2B relationship—some very big ones.”
For a startup that itself is “agent-pilled,” as Brown put it, he’s betting that Lumbra will be “one of the first examples of a 100-200 person company that swings like a 2,000-3,000 person company,” he said. “I don’t think anyone who’s touching our product right now would say anything other than we’re at the front edge of this compared to anyone else in the game.”

PsiThera Closes $25 Million Financing to Advance Oral Therapeutics in Immunology
By:
PsiThera via
GlobeNewswire
November 10, 2026 at 07:00 AM EST
ⓘ This article is third-party content and does not represent the views of this site. We make no guarantees regarding its accuracy or completeness.
AbbVie Ventures and Lumination Capital joining existing lead investors Samsara BioCapital and Lightstone Ventures
Financing supports TNFα development candidate nomination and initiation of IND-enabling studies, alongside advancement of oral TL1A inhibitors into lead optimization
Proprietary QUAISAR platform, combined with approach to Physical AI, continues to drive rapid design of optimized oral drug candidates
WATERTOWN, Mass., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- PsiThera, a biotechnology company harnessing biologically relevant protein states and physical artificial intelligence to create oral drugs for immune and inflammatory diseases, today announced the closing of a $25 million financing. New investors AbbVie Ventures and Lumination Capital participated, along with existing lead investors Samsara BioCapital and Lightstone Ventures, and other existing investors. In connection with the financing, Claire Leurent, Ph.D., MBA, Managing Director at AbbVie Ventures, has joined PsiThera’s Board of Directors.
Proceeds from the financing are expected to fund operations, supporting development candidate nomination and the initiation of IND-enabling studies for the company’s lead oral small molecule TNFα inhibitor, as well as advancement of its oral TL1A program into lead optimization.
The company’s proprietary QUAISAR platform combines physics-based molecular simulation, machine learning, and experimental biophysics into a single closed-loop discovery engine to design novel small molecule therapeutics more efficiently. QUAISAR models protein motion to identify and target transient binding pockets that conventional structure-based design cannot see, enabling the design of small molecules for targets that have been difficult to address with oral therapies. Using this platform, PsiThera advanced the company’s lead TNFα program from hit identification to lead optimization in just four months.
“Our goal is to bring the efficacy of leading biologics into novel oral medicines to improve on their therapeutic profiles. This financing accelerates our progress toward that vision as we advance our oral TNFα program toward development candidate nomination and clinical initiation and expand our pipeline of differentiated immunology therapeutics, starting with TL1A,” said Eric D. Shaff, President and Chief Executive Officer of PsiThera. “We are grateful for the continued support of our existing investors and welcome AbbVie Ventures and Lumination Capital.”
Injectable anti-TNFα biologic therapies are approved across a broad range of immune-mediated diseases. However, an oral therapeutic could have broad application, both as monotherapy and as a combination partner, and provide an additional treatment option to the many patients who have not yet started biologic therapy.
PsiThera’s oral TNFα inhibitors are designed to achieve a differentiated profile to improve the therapeutic index relative to injectables or other oral TNFα inhibitors in development, supporting best-in-class potential.
“PsiThera has brought together seasoned biopharma leadership, experienced drug hunters, and immunology and computational scientists around a platform that can find and exploit protein states that conventional approaches cannot effectively drug,” said Christina Isacson, Ph.D., Chair of PsiThera’s Board of Directors and Partner at Lightstone Ventures. “Our progress with TNFα and TL1A is illustrative of the power of the platform. With this financing, the Company is well-positioned to advance its lead programs and extend its platform across a broader immunology pipeline.”
About PsiThera
PsiThera is a biotechnology company harnessing biologically relevant protein states and physical artificial intelligence to create oral drugs for immune and inflammatory diseases, therapeutic areas historically reliant on injectables. By integrating biophysics, computational modeling, and mechanistic biology through its QUAISAR platform, PsiThera’s expert drug hunters discover new therapeutic opportunities and optimized drugs. The company’s initial programs target clinically validated cytokine pathways, including TNFα, TL1A, and IL-6. PsiThera is headquartered in Watertown, Massachusetts. News provided by
Nanopath

Financing co-led by Norwest and SV Health Investors' MedTech Convergence Fund will fund launch of Nanopath's FDA 510(k) study for its point-of-care vaginitis test in support of potential expansion of its pipeline into UTIs and STIs, and build-out of its team ahead of proposed commercialization
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nanopath , a point-of-care diagnostics company enabling laboratory-quality molecular testing in minutes, today announced the close of a $25 million Series B financing round, which includes $2 million in non-dilutive grant financing. The round is co-led by Norwest and SV Health Investors' MedTech Convergence Fund, alongside strategic participation from the Labcorp Venture Fund. New and existing investors also participated, including Elderberry Ventures, GingerBread Capital, and Alumni Ventures.
As part of the financing, Catherine Kiani, J.D., Managing Partner at Elderberry Ventures, and Mindy Nye, Ph.D., Vice President, Labcorp Diagnostics, have joined the Nanopath Board as Observers.
"Nanopath is developing truly transformative technology with the potential to reshape the molecular diagnostics industry and dramatically improve patient outcomes," said Jeff Crowe, Senior Managing Partner at Norwest. "We are beyond excited to continue supporting the company at this key inflection point."
Nanopath has developed the first clinical diagnostics platform built on plasmonic biosensing. The company's proprietary optical biosensing technology is designed to enable molecular detection without nucleic acid amplification, a step required by PCR-based tests. "We've spent years developing and pressure-testing a fundamentally new approach to molecular diagnostics for patients who have been overlooked for far too long," said Alison Burklund, Ph.D., Co-Founder & Co-CEO of Nanopath. "This funding brings us closer to the next and most important step – translating that innovation into meaningful clinical impact."
The funding will support key milestones toward the potential commercial launch of Nanopath's 15-minute point-of-care vaginitis assay, including manufacturing scale-up and initiation of Nanopath's Food and Drug Administration 510(k) clinical study. Nanopath will also use the funding to expand its team across clinical and commercial functions as it prepares for launch. "We're incredibly proud of the extraordinary team we've built at Nanopath and our shared commitment to transforming women's healthcare," said Amogha Tadimety, Ph.D., Co-Founder & Co-CEO of Nanopath. "We're grateful for the confidence of our investors and excited to build on this momentum as we enter our next phase of growth."
By delivering accurate results during a single visit, Nanopath aims to establish a new standard of care for women's health and expand access to high-quality diagnostics for women across the United States. Over time, the platform is expected to expand to other clinical indications, improving healthcare by making sophisticated diagnostics more accessible at the point of care.
The vaginitis test is currently under development and has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Commercial availability is subject to successful completion of development activities and applicable regulatory review.
About Nanopath
Nanopath is a women-led company dedicated to improving health equity worldwide, starting with women's health. Nanopath's proprietary molecular diagnostic testing platform takes a radically new approach to how clinicians characterize human health. The company's novel biosensing technology has the potential to enable fast, high-complexity testing at the point-of-care, rather than in centralized laboratories. The company is headquartered in Cambridge, Mass., at The Engine built by MIT, a premier facility for high-potential, tough-tech start-ups. Founded in 2020, Nanopath has raised more than $46 million, and is backed by Norwest, the Medtech Convergence Fund, an SV Health Investors Fund, Elderberry Ventures, GingerBread Capital, Alumni Ventures and the Labcorp Venture Fund. For more information, visit www.nanopath.com .

Hatz AI raises $24Mn Series A to sell AI through MSPs
Danica Macayan
Posted on November 17, 2026 2 min read
Copied URL
Key facts
Hatz AI raised $24 million in Series A funding.
Josh Schertzer of Nadia Partners led the deal.
Hatz’s active MSP partner count tripled year over year.
Hatz grew from 14 to nearly 60 employees.
Source: Hatz AI
NEW YORK, UNITED STATES — Hatz AI, which sells its artificial intelligence (AI) platform to small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) only through managed service providers (MSPs), has raised $24 million in Series A funding. Nadia Partners, Vestigo Ventures and The Private Shares Fund backed the round.
Josh Schertzer, a partner at Nadia Partners and former chief technology officer at Blackstone, led the deal.
AI sold under the MSP’s brand
Hatz announced the funding in a press release on Nov. 12.
Its platform gives MSPs multi-tenant AI governance, custom workflows and automated routing across leading foundation models. MSPs can then package and deliver AI-as-a-Service under their own brand.
Hatz said it has no competing direct-to-enterprise sales and has issued more than 15,000 AI certifications to builders globally.
The investment will help it scale a partner network that it said spans thousands of MSPs in all 50 U.S. states, nine Canadian provinces and nine countries.
Partners triple, staff quadruple
Hatz said its active MSP partner count tripled year over year, while revenue grew even faster. It expanded its workforce from 14 to nearly 60 employees.
The company is expanding in Flatiron, New York City, and scaling its forward deployed engineer team to work alongside partners. It is also growing its AI research and AI optimization teams.
“Small businesses represent the backbone of the global economy, and the managed service providers they already rely on are exactly the people to lead this transformation,” said Jimmy Hatzell, chief executive and co-founder of Hatz AI.
“By giving MSPs full control over governance, spend, and deployment, we’re making it possible for every small business to become AI native,” Hatzell said.
What the money funds
The new capital will deepen platform capabilities, including Hatz’s auto-model routing engine, benchmarks and internal software factory infrastructure. Hatz will also keep recruiting engineers for its forward deployed engineering and AI research units.
“By focusing exclusively on powering MSPs rather than trying to sell directly to end-users, Hatz has built a true dominance in channel-delivered AI,” Schertzer said.
What it means for buyers
Investors are backing a model in which smaller companies get AI from the IT provider they already pay, rather than from the model makers directly. For businesses that buy managed services or information technology outsourcing (ITO) , that puts AI governance and spending decisions into an existing contract.

ATLANTA , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- o15 Capital Partners ("o15"), through its Emerging America Credit Opportunities ("EACO") fund, is pleased to announce a senior secured "last-out" term loan as part of a $23.6 million unitranche facility, along with an equity co-investment, to support the acquisition of 11 th St. Workshop by Bluestone Equity Partners ("Bluestone").
11 th St. Workshop is a leading design and fabrication platform that builds the physical environments behind marquee brand activations for blue-chip agency and brand customers.
"11th St. Workshop has built a differentiated platform at the intersection of creative design and highly specialized physical execution, supported by a blue-chip customer base and a reputation for delivering complex, high-profile activations," said Harry Savage, Principal at o15. "We're excited to partner with the Bluestone and 11th St. Workshop teams as the Company builds a leading national platform."
The transaction reflects o15's focus on partnering with experienced sponsors to provide flexible capital to high-quality lower-middle-market businesses with differentiated market positions and compelling opportunities to scale. Bluestone's investment will support 11th St. Workshop's next phase of growth through investments in capacity and service offerings while maintaining its reputation for quality and customer service.
"Experiential marketing is one of the fastest-growing areas of advertising spend, and 11th St. Workshop is a trusted partner for agencies and brands on their most high-profile builds," said Shaaz Khan, Senior Vice President at Bluestone. "The o15 team delivered a flexible financing package to support our acquisition, and we look forward to partnering with them to enable the Company's long-term growth."
